10318-damon-and-delia-a-tale:
Printed in London in 1784 for T. Hookham's circulating library, this short tale follows Damon and Delia through balls, ghosts, and love scenes. The book is a romance of manners, written for readers who borrowed novels by the volume. Its motto, from Horace, warns that Apollo does not always bend his bow.

Chapters move from introductory matter to a ball, a ghost, a love scene, and specimens of heroism, with a man of humor for comic relief. Damon and Delia must weather pride, fear, and social talk. Readers get a light, eighteenth-century love tale, quaint in style and brisk in plot.
10359-aunt-jane-s-nieces-at-millville:
Edith Van Dyne published this girls' novel in 1908, sending Patsy, Beth, and Louise with Uncle John to his farm at Millville. Uncle John, who lends money to needy young men, finds himself owner of a farm by circumstance, and the nieces soon scent a mystery. The tone is bright, comic, and moral.

A little schoolma'am, a locked cupboard, a man in hiding, and three amateur detectives carry the plot, with Peggy McNutt and Bob West among the locals. A trap is set, a courtship blooms, and good news closes the tale. Readers get a cheerful series story of country life, pluck, and detective fun.
10363-the-bravo-a-tale:
James Fenimore Cooper published this Venetian tale in the 1830s, using the supposed republic of Venice to study power in disguise. His preface complains that political words blur real rule: monarchies and republics alike can hide tyranny. Cooper does not paint famous historical figures, but the familiar workings of Venetian policy.

A bravo, or hired assassin, moves through palaces and piazzas where justice in the palace and bread in the square mask secret rule. Citizens win small freedoms only by growing strength and wit. Readers get a political romance of Venice, sharp on liberty, secrecy, and the gap between names and deeds.
1038-style:
Walter Raleigh, an Oxford critic, asks in this short essay what makes English prose good. He treats style not as fancy dress for thought but as the fit between a writer's mind and his reader's ear, worked out through sense, sound, and image. The book grew from lectures given at the turn of the century.

Raleigh ranges over metaphor, slang, archaism, and the plain word, praising writers who choose the exact term and blaming those who hide behind jargon. His examples run from Shakespeare to his own day. The essay remains a clear, bracing guide for anyone who wants to write prose that lives.
10434-wyandotte-or-the-hutted-knoll-a-ta:
James Fenimore Cooper published this frontier tale in the 1840s, in an edition dated 1871, set during colonial warfare and the Revolution. Its preface warns that a nation that hears only its own praises risks false patriotism, and that the Revolution, though just, had evil aspects too. Cooper pleads for truth over flattery.

An isolated family at the Hutted Knoll faces border war, Native neighbors, and divided loyalties, with a Native character named Wyandotte at the heart of the tale. Suffering, honor, and the costs of war fill the story. Readers get a serious, questioning Cooper novel of the frontier and its moral shadows.
10670-with-zola-in-england-a-story-of-ex:
Ernest Alfred Vizetelly tells the story of Emile Zola's exile in England in With Zola in England. Zola, the great French novelist, fled France after championing truth and justice in the Dreyfus affair, and found himself a stranger in a foreign land. Vizetelly, who knew him well, records the flight, the hiding, and the daily life of exile.

The book opens with verses on light, truth, and justice denied, and follows Zola's patience under threat and insult. It is both a memoir and a defense of a writer punished for speaking out. Readers get a close, personal account of one of the most famous literary exiles of modern Europe.
10745-the-story-of-the-champions-of-the-:
Howard Pyle, the American artist and author, retold the Arthurian legends in four volumes, and this second volume, first published in 1905, tells of the champions of the Round Table. Pyle wrote and illustrated the book himself, and this reissue keeps his pictures and decorations in their original form. The tales follow Arthur's knights in quest, combat, and courtly adventure.

Pyle's versions have long ranked among the finest retellings of Arthur for young readers, noble in tone and rich in image. The knights' deeds are told plainly, with honor and fellowship at their heart. Readers get a beautiful, classic doorway into the Round Table stories.
1080-a-modest-proposal-for-preventing-th:
Jonathan Swift, Dean of St. Patrick's in Dublin, offers a cold, logical scheme: since Ireland's poor cannot feed their children, let the rich eat them. The proposer counts heads, prices flesh, and lists the gains to landlord and nation with mock-serious care. Swift wrote it in 1729, when English rule starved Ireland.

The joke is savage because the logic is sound and the morals are monstrous: Swift aims his blade at landlords, economists, and all who treat people as figures. The pamphlet runs only a few pages, yet it stands as the most famous satire in English, and its title still names any cruel, cool plan.
1086-a-horse-s-tale:
Mark Twain tells this tale through the eyes of Soldier Boy, a horse in a frontier cavalry post, who watches soldiers, children, and a Spanish girl with a horse's blunt sense. The story moves from barracks jokes to a cruel turn in Mexico, where loyalty and pride meet a harsh fate.

Twain uses the animal narrator to mock human vanity and war, and to praise dumb courage. The horse's voice is plain, wry, and touching. The book is shorter and sadder than his famous novels, and it shows his late anger at empire dressed as a children's tale.
1093-the-beast-in-the-jungle:
Henry James tells of John Marcher, a man who lives his whole life waiting for some rare, shattering event, the "beast" he feels crouching in his future. May Bartram, his loyal friend, watches and waits with him through the years, loving him while he loves only his fate. The novella moves through drawing rooms and foreign cities.

Marcher at last sees the truth too late: his waiting was itself the event, and it cost him the love offered him. James writes the tale in long, subtle sentences that track a mind dodging its own heart. It stands as his most piercing study of a wasted life.
11333-the-pearl-story-book-a-collection-:
Mrs. Colman's Pearl Story Book, published in 1850 as part of her new juvenile series, collects original and selected tales for children. Contents include the Turtle-Doves of Carmel, about a young English musician wintering at Mount Carmel, the Red Shoes, in which little Karen's vanity makes her dance without rest until prayer brings comfort. the Young Gleaner, and Tony the Miller's Son, with shorter pieces on a chimney-sweep, a caged bird, and perseverance.

Colman, author of Innocence of Childhood, writes moral tales in which kindness and repentance are rewarded. The stories are gentle and didactic, suited to family reading aloud. The book illustrates mid-Victorian children's literature, where entertainment and instruction were expected to share every page.
1134-the-winter-s-tale:
Leontes, King of Sicily, grows mad with jealousy, accuses his wife Hermione of betraying him, and loses wife, son, and newborn daughter in one ruinous act. William Shakespeare's late romance then leaps sixteen years to Bohemia, where the lost daughter, raised by shepherds, falls in love with a prince.

The play turns from tragedy to pastoral comedy and ends with a statue that seems to breathe: Hermione, alive after all. Time, the Chorus, bridges the two halves. The play's mix of grief and wonder makes it one of Shakespeare's most moving late works.
11409-the-red-rover-a-tale:
James Fenimore Cooper's Red Rover, complete in one volume in 1855, is a sea tale in thirty-two chapters, prefaced by Cooper's defense of his marine accuracy. Cooper warns keen-eyed critics that landsmen in book-making cause imperfections, and hopes the Augustan age of literature will bring typography as accurate as a log book. The novel follows a mysterious rover captain, a disguised heroine, and naval pursuit across the Atlantic.

Cooper, America's first major novelist of the sea, writes with knowledge of ships and sailing gained from his own naval service. The Red Rover mixes pirate romance with naval adventure, its identity puzzles driving the plot. Readers of maritime fiction will find it a central Cooper romance, less famous than the Leatherstocking tales but just as seaworthy.
11414-in-the-claws-of-the-german-eagle:
Albert Rhys Williams's In the Claws of the German Eagle recounts a pacifist's wartime transformation, from Paris enthusiasm for the American Legion to falling under the spell of the Germans themselves. Contents divide into spy-hunters of Belgium, on foot with the German army, war photographers in Belgium, and love among the ruins. Chapters on a German surprise party, the third degree, a night on a prison floor, gray hordes from the north, being shot as a German spy, and no-man's-land.

Williams admits feeling in his own blood the raging beasts he condemned, shattering cherished principles. His memoir is candid about propaganda, atrocity claims, and shifting sympathies. For First World War readers, it offers an American journalist's self-questioning account, unusual for its honesty.
1154-the-voyages-of-doctor-dolittle:
Doctor Dolittle, the country doctor who talks to animals, sails off with his parrot Polynesia, his dog Jip, and his pig Gub-Gub to find the secret of animal speech. Hugh Lofting's tale takes them to Spider Monkey Island, where apes, storms, and a sea serpent await. The book won the first Newbery Medal.

Lofting wrote the tales for his children while serving in the trenches, and his doctor is kind, absent-minded, and brave. The voyages mix jokes, peril, and a plea for kindness to beasts. The book remains a beloved children's classic, though modern readers note its dated views.
11618-from-chaucer-to-tennyson-with-twen:
Henry A. Beers, professor of English at Yale, wrote this short history for the Chautauqua Reading Circle, with twenty-nine portraits and selections from thirty authors. He leaves out philosophy, history, and science, and he leaves out Anglo-Saxon verse, which he calls as hard for a modern reader as German.

Chapters run from Chaucer to Tennyson, with Scots vernacular before Burns also set aside, since Scotland was a separate kingdom until the union. A later passage quotes Johnson on Iona, where savage clans drew knowledge and religion. The book gives a brief, readable path through English letters.
11635-green-tea-mr-justice-harbottle:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu pairs Green Tea, dated 1871, with Mr. Justice Harbottle, dated 1872, both framed by Dr. Martin Hesselius. The prologue introduces Hesselius, a German physician who never practised after a dissecting knife scratch cost him two fingers and his health.

Hesselius, immense in knowledge and intuitive in grasp, becomes the narrator's master in wandering years. A later note on Harbottle cites Hesselius's essay on the interior sense and its opening. The two tales are ghost stories of haunting and judgment, told as case histories by a doctor who believes the unseen.
11693-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Grenville Kleiser's eighth volume of The World's Great Sermons, covering Talmage to Knox Little, opens with Talmage, born at Bound Brook, New Jersey, in 1832. He preached for years at the Brooklyn Tabernacle, where six hundred newspapers at one time printed his sermons.

Later preachers in the volume include Spurgeon on songs in the night, Potter on Phillips Brooks, Abbott on divinity in humanity, and Brooks on the pride of life. A passage on forgiveness says pardon does not wipe out the past, but rearranges relations between man and God. Biographical notes head each sermon.
11701-the-makers-and-teachers-of-judaism:
Charles Foster Kent wrote this study of Judaism in 1911, with maps and charts. He was Woolsey Professor of Biblical Literature at Yale. The book runs from the fall of Jerusalem to the death of Herod the Great.

Sections follow the exile and revival of the Judean community. Lamentations, Jeremiah, and Jews in Palestine and Egypt appear first. Ezekiel's message to scattered countrymen comes next. Later sections cover Ezra and Nehemiah, the Psalter, and Proverbs. Ben Sira's schools of the wise and the Maccabees close the survey. The book is a historical study, built on texts and their dates.
11909-bob-the-castaway-or-the-wreck-of-t:
Frank V. Webster's 1909 boys' book Bob the Castaway, or The Wreck of the Eagle, follows Bob Henderson through schoolboy scrapes and a voyage that ends in shipwreck. Early chapters show Bob keeping a man seated all evening, to the amusement of his schoolmates, and a practical joker, Mr. Tarbill, suffering seasickness aboard ship.

When a big wave strikes the Eagle and heels her over, the adventure turns serious, and Bob must use the steadiness his jokes had hidden. Webster, whose other boys' books include Only a Farm Boy and Tom the Telephone Boy, writes for readers who wanted humor first and danger second. His hero's good nature survives both.
11911-the-silent-isle:
Arthur Christopher Benson's 1913 book The Silent Isle, dedicated to Percy Lubbock, takes its name from a place where there is little sight or sound of water. Water, Benson writes, oozes from field to drain, trickles from drain to ditch, falls to dyke. Moves silently to the great seaward slope, a landscape of quiet, flat country.

Benson, a fellow of Magdalene College, Cambridge, writes essays on reading, writing. The inner life: how thought leaps forward after finishing a book, like a weight lifted by an elastic cord. How the true artist, like the true priest, cares only for the beautiful quality of thought pursued. The Silent Isle is a meditation on solitude, attention, and the pleasures of a reflective life.
12083-eric-or-little-by-little:
Frederic W. Farrar's Eric, or Little by Little, a tale of Roslyn School, illustrated by George A. Traver in this 1902 edition, follows a schoolboy through childhood, a new home, bullying, and cribbing. Farrar, author of The Life of Christ, Julian Home, and St. Winifred's, wrote for boys who knew school life firsthand.

Later chapters treat the second term, home affections, Eric as a boarder, and taking up, as small choices accumulate into character. The title gives the moral: boys are ruined or saved little by little, not by single great acts. Farrar's school story, earnest and sentimental, became one of the best-known Victorian tales of boyhood.
12098-the-elder-brother-the-works-of-fra:
Cambridge University Press issued this volume in 1906, edited by Arnold Glover and A. R. Waller, as part of a scholarly edition of Beaumont and Fletcher plays. Francis Beaumont died in 1616 and John Fletcher in 1625, and their joint canon shaped Jacobean theater after Shakespeare.

Six plays appear here: The Elder Brother, The Spanish Curate, Wit Without Money, Beggars Bush, The Humorous Lieutenant, and The Faithful Shepherdess. The editors print The Elder Brother from the Second Folio and add its First Quarto verse text in an appendix, with notes on variant readings. Comedy, disguise, and pastoral romance dominate. For students of early drama, the volume pairs readable texts with the textual care the period demanded.
12103-the-tale-of-mrs-tiggy-winkle:
Beatrix Potter's Tale of Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, published in 1905 for the real little Lucie of Newlands, follows a farm girl named Lucie who keeps losing her pocket-handkerchiefs. One day she comes into the farm-yard in tears over another loss.

Lucie's search leads her to Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, a hedgehog washerwoman who irons and folds the lost handkerchiefs, with Potter's watercolor illustrations showing the farm, the hills, and the tiny laundry. The tale's charm lies in its domestication of the wild: a hedgehog becomes a busy housekeeper, and a child's lost property becomes the key to a secret world.
1218-the-adventures-of-jimmie-dale:
Frank L. Packard's Jimmie Dale is a rich young New Yorker by day and the Gray Seal, a gentleman burglar, by night, stealing from crooks and leaving his seal as a mark. A mysterious woman in the case pulls his strings, while the police and the underworld both hunt him.

The tales move through safes, traps, and double-crosses at a pulp clip, with Dale's wits and his secret sanctum saving him each time. Packard wrote the series for readers who loved masked heroes. The book founded a whole line of pulp crime tales, and it still reads as fast, clean fun.
12282-the-right-and-wrong-uses-of-the-bi:
R. Heber Newton published The Right and Wrong Uses of the Bible in 1883, a work of liberal Protestant criticism. Newton, an Episcopal clergyman in New York, argued that the Bible contains God true word without being literally inerrant in every part.

Chapters distinguish the unreal Bible of superstition and proof-texting from the real Bible of history, poetry, and moral growth. Newton urges readers to use scripture for faith and conduct, not as a science textbook or a fortune book. The book stirred controversy in its day, as higher criticism reached American pulpits. It remains a clear statement of the liberal position: reverence for the Bible joined to honest scholarship about its making.
12377-the-court-of-boyville:
William Allen White published The Court of Boyville in 1898, a book of boy stories illustrated by Orson Lowell, with the first story illustrated by Gustav Verbeek. White, the Kansas editor, writes of small-town boyhood with humor and affection.

Contents open with a prologue and The Martyrdom of Mealy Jones, followed by a recent conversion and other tales of school, church, and street. A mid-book scene has a boy in five minutes sombre meditation over a curling gelatine card, plotting dark things against his undoing. White boys form courts, try offenders, and learn fairness through play. The book is a classic of American boy literature, warm without being soft.
12381-the-auchensaugh-renovation-of-the-:
This volume prints the Auchensaugh renovation of the National Covenant and Solemn League and Covenant, renewed near Douglas on 24 July 1712, with an acknowledgment of sins and an engagement to duties. A Philadelphia edition of 1880, ordered by the Reformed Presbytery, compares the text with Paisley and Belfast printings and adds a second renovation ordained at Philadelphia in 1880.

The documents bind a church community to faith, moral reform and mutual duty, adapting old federal deeds to new times and places. Their language is solemn and communal, a public vow rather than private devotion. The book matters as a record of covenanting tradition carried from Scotland to America, still renewed, still argued over, nearly two centuries on.
12445-the-water-witch-or-the-skimmer-of-:
James Fenimore Cooper's sea tale, first published in 1830, is set around New York harbour in colonial days. A graceful brig called the Water-Witch slips past patrols, and its daring captain, known as the Skimmer, becomes the talk of the coast. Naval officers hunt him, while shore folk argue over whether he is pirate, patriot or smuggler.

Chase, disguise and divided loyalty drive the story, as a young woman and her guardians are drawn into the Skimmer's orbit. Cooper uses the harbour, its tides and its trading ships to stage questions of law, duty and freedom on the water. The novel ends as a romance of the sea, with the mystery brig at its centre and the coast itself as a stage.
12516-the-way-of-an-eagle:
E. M. Dell's 1911 romance, The Way of an Eagle, follows a soldier's daughter through trust, treachery and desolation. Contents promise a devil in the wilderness, the coming of an army, a school of sorrow, and an eagle's swoop and first flight. Later come a harbour of refuge, a sleep called death and an eternal flame.

Dell builds her story in three parts, from loss and army life to comradeship, ordeal and reunion. The heroine's faith, courage and love are tested by strong men who fail and by friends who return. In Dell's high romantic manner, suffering purifies and love endures, and the eagle of the title becomes an image of rising above pain.
12678-the-house-of-mystery-an-episode-in:
Will Irwin's 1910 novel, The House of Mystery, follows Rosalie Le Grange, clairvoyant, in an episode of her career. Illustrated by Frederick C. Yohn, the book opens with an unknown girl, Mr. Norcross wasting time, a light, a first call, and a light wavering, before Rosalie enters.

Rosalie's first and second reports, a nibbling fish, streams converging, a passage through wall-paper, Annette lying and then telling truth, and papers mainly, carry a mystery of fraud, sight and money. Irwin writes a lively detective romance, fond of Boston, spiritualism and stagecraft. The novel asks how much a clairvoyant sees, and how much she performs.
12680-children-of-the-ghetto-a-study-of-:
I. Zangwill's Children of the Ghetto, a study of a peculiar people, in a 1914 one-volume edition with a preface to the third edition, charts a terra incognita for English readers. Zangwill thanks public and critics for kindly reception, and restores an original sub-title answering criticism of artistic form. He adds a glossary of Yiddish words, omitting words used once and explained at once.

The book studies, through typical figures, a race whose persistence Zangwill calls the most remarkable fact in world history, whose faith and morals largely moulded it. London's East End Jews, their homes, synagogues, loves and quarrels, fill the narrative. The novel remains a classic of Anglo-Jewish writing, sympathetic, detailed and fond of its people.
13091-hillsboro-people:
Dorothy Canfield's 1915 Hillsboro People gathers stories and Vermont verses about a small New England village, with occasional poems by Sarah N. Cleghorn. Contents run from Hemlock Mountain and Petunias, That's for Remembrance to The Bedquilt, A Saint's Hours, and Hillsboro's Good Luck. Canfield writes of farmers, artists, and village talk with warmth and irony.

One story turns on a portrait whose eyes enrage an old aunt, who swears the artist missed her uncle's look. Another, in verse, hears a woman sewing by a dim flame while bees of the past frolic in memory. Salem Hills sends a voiceless cry to ships full of homestead seekers. The book is a loving, unsentimental portrait of village life at a turning point.
13144-medieval-people:
Eileen Power's Medieval People, first published in 1924, uses single lives to teach the social history of the Middle Ages. Power, a reader in history at London and fellow of Girton, opens with Langland's praise of cloister and school as places of books and peace. Her preface warns that social history often stays vague, and she answers it with persons, not abstractions.

Chapters follow Marco Polo's father and uncle on the road to Samarcand with mules and camels, reaching Acre in 1269 and sailing home to Venice. Later pages trace William Stonor's letters and a match for Katherine Riche, his stepdaughter, aged about thirteen. Power's method is clear: through one merchant, one clerk, one girl, the whole medieval world comes into view.
13305-alfgar-the-dane-or-the-second-chro:
Rev. A. D. Crake's Alfgar the Dane, second chronicle of Aescendune, is a tale of Edmund Ironside's days. Its preface and chapters run from Father Cuthbert's diary and Alfgar, son of Anlaf, through the night of St. Brice, Danes in Wessex, and tracks in the forest, to Carisbrooke, Dorchester, and a royal deathbed. Crake writes Saxon history as boys' adventure with a moral thread.

Danish parties march unopposed, since fighting men are in Wessex, spearing stray victims in a sight that sickens Alfgar. Later, barns and stables blaze, a manor house rings with double fire, and boys and women pour water on roofs against brands. The tale follows father and son through suffering to glory, in the old chronicle style.
13388-the-religious-spirit-of-the-slavs-:
Father Nicolai Velimirovic, a Serbian priest and Belgrade theology professor, gave these three lectures at St. Margaret's, Westminster, during Lent in 1916. He sets out Slav Orthodoxy, then Slav revolutionary Catholicism, then the wider religious spirit of the Slav peoples, speaking in wartime to a London audience.

The opening lecture contrasts Tolstoi with the Russian Holy Synod, picturing one view of life as a circle and the other as a drama with a set end. Later pages dwell on repeated prayer and fixed symbols in Orthodox worship, on Jan Huss, and on Primus Trubar putting Scripture into Slovene. Velimirovic argues for a church of suffering, insight, and action rather than pride or fear.
1356-the-cruise-of-the-cachalot-round-th:
Frank T. Bullen, who sailed before the mast himself, tells the cruise of the whaler Cachalot round the world after sperm whales. The narrative follows the ship from port to hunting grounds, with whale chases, cutting-in, storms, and the hard daily life of the crew.

Bullen writes as a seaman, not a surgeon or a tourist, and his detail on whaling work is firsthand and vivid. The book, praised by seamen and critics alike, stands as the classic account of the old whale fishery. It draws readers who like sea tales told true.
140-the-jungle:
Lithuanian immigrants Jurgis and Ona arrive in Chicago hoping for work and a wedding. Upton Sinclair's Jungle, published in 1906, follows them into the stockyards, where packers grind men as they grind meat. Wages, housing, and graft crush the family step by step.

Sinclair details filth, accidents, and fraud in the packing plants with unsparing force. Jurgis turns to crime, politics, and finally socialism for an answer. The novel shocked readers and pushed food-safety reform. Its power as protest fiction has never faded. Sinclair's exposé led Congress toward the Pure Food and Drug Act within months.
14013-almoran-and-hamet-an-oriental-tale:
John Hawkesworth's 1761 tale sets two brothers against each other for the throne of Persia. Almoran schemes for power while Hamet waits, mourns their father Solyman, and plans a quiet marriage. Letters, spies, and court whispers move the story forward. Each brother must choose between ambition and duty, and each choice tightens the knot.

Moral instruction shapes every scene. Power gained by cunning brings fear rather than peace, while patience and virtue win trust even from enemies. The closing passages stage a fall from pride, with courtiers already trembling at the tyrant's name. Written in the high style of the eighteenth-century oriental tale, the book uses a distant court to argue a plain lesson. A ruler's character decides whether subjects live in dread or in quiet.
14048-the-nameless-castle:
Maurus Jókai's Hungarian romance, translated by S. E. Boggs in 1898 under the author's eye, centers on a castle with a hidden past. Count Vavel plans a marriage that shocks his circle, naming Katharina Landsknechtsschild as his bride. A baroness drops her embroidery at the news, while messengers, militia talk, and war rumors stir the household. Love and rank pull against each other throughout.

Sickroom scenes give the novel its emotional core. Ludwig, an invalid, clings to a little maid named Marie, whose wet gown and shy care bring a sudden turn in his illness. Tears, embraces, and promises follow, and the doctor's visit confirms the change. Jókai loved grand feeling and tangled plots, and Boggs's authorized text aims to give English readers the story clean. Romance, pride, and sudden reversals carry the book to its close.
14153-westways-a-village-chronicle:
S. Weir Mitchell's 1913 village chronicle follows the Penhallows from frontier clearing to Civil War. The first Penhallow crossed the Alleghanies before independence, axed forest, and waited for charred stumps to rot. Later Penhallows took to sea or army, or drifted west, while Westways village kept its name and its stories. Mitchell dedicates the book to three brothers who served in the armies of their country.

War talk and household loyalty shape the middle. A stableman who broke his leg stopping a runaway saved Leila Grey, the adopted child, and earned Penhallow's trust. Lincoln himself appears, asking a colonel what emancipation will do in the South, then correcting Rebels to Confederates with a smile: calling names only hurts and never helps. Village chronicle and national crisis meet here, and the Penhallows endure both with stubborn grace.
14410-gawayne-and-the-green-knight-a-fai:
Charlton Miner Lewis retold Gawayne and the Green Knight as a fairy tale in verse, printed in 1903. King Arthur's court feasts at Camelot on Christmas Day, shields hung idle and banners decking the hall. A Green Knight rides in to set a strange challenge. Gawayne takes up the game, and the tale follows him through four cantos. Lewis writes in rhymed couplets, with a light, old-world lilt.

Elfinhart, a fairy child of the murmuring mere, grows in grace with each season, her mirth fed by fairy tutors. Gawayne, grown weary of phantom voices, hears a call to set aside fame and fortune, which yield to moth and rust. The poem urges him to pluck the fruit of joy, love, and beauty while time runs. Its charm lies in music, wonder, and a gentle moral. Lewis keeps the old tale fresh for young readers of his age.
14662-around-the-tea-table:
T. De Witt Talmage's Around the Tea-Table, published by the Christian Herald at Bible House in New York, gathers the talk of an evening household. Talmage explains that breakfast is hurried and noon scatters the family, but at six all come to the tea-table for chit-chat.

Chapters range from the spread table-cloth and Mr. Givemfits to Sabbath evenings and a dream railway stopping at Jolly Town, Gleeville, and Velvet Junction, where lords and duchesses rise and bow and a silver spittoon sits unused. The pieces mix sermons, anecdotes, and moral essays in the easy voice of a popular preacher.
14731-hatchie-the-guardian-slave-or-the-:
Warren T. Ashton's Hatchie, the Guardian Slave, or the Heiress of Bellevue, published in Boston in 1853, is a tale of the Mississippi and the South-west. Ashton says the story began on a steamboat passage from New Orleans to Cincinnati in the summer of 1848.

Hatchie guards Emily, the heiress of Bellevue, while a suitor presses her to recover her estate by returning as his wife. The novel mixes river travel, courtship, and adventure in the antebellum South, and its portrait of slavery reflects the attitudes of its time. Reprinted in 1972 from a Fisk University Library copy, it survives as a period piece.
14886-england-s-case-against-home-rule:
A. V. Dicey's 1886 book argues England's case against Home Rule for Ireland. Dicey opens by disclaiming special knowledge of Ireland or a new cure for Irish discontent, claiming only the knowledge, or ignorance, of an educated Englishman drawn from conversation.

Chapters test Home Rule as federalism, as colonial independence, as a revival of Grattan's constitution and as it stood under the Gladstonian constitution. Dicey weighs law, parliament and union, and finds each version wanting. The book is a leading Victorian unionist argument, clear, legal and partisan, and it shows how constitutional lawyers framed the Irish question in the 1880s.
14898-in-the-amazon-jungle:
Algot Lange recounts adventures in remote parts of the upper Amazon, including a sojourn among cannibal Indians, edited in part by J. Odell Hauser with an introduction by Frederick S. Dellenbaugh. Remate de Males, or culmination of evils, opens the journey, with its social and political life and other incidents of his stay.

Up the Itecoahy River, life among rubber workers, a fatal march through forest and a fatal tambo follow, before the forest itself and the Mangeroma people take centre stage. A fight between Mangeromas and Peruvians closes the narrative. Lange writes as a traveller in rubber country, and his period terms for Indigenous peoples now need reading with care and context.
15-moby-dick-or-the-whale:
A young sailor signs aboard a whaling ship and meets a captain consumed by one whale. Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, published in 1851, opens with Ishmael's restless call to the sea. The Pequod sails from Nantucket under Captain Ahab.

Chapters mix adventure with long essays on whales, whaling craft, and the sea. Ahab's hunt for the white whale drives crew and ship toward wreck. Queequeg, Starbuck, and Stubb give the voyage its human range. The novel's depth made it a central work of American letters. Later readers found in Ahab's hunt a study of obsession, nature, and the limits of knowledge.
15086-the-framework-of-home-rule:
Erskine Childers's 1911 study makes the case for Irish Home Rule by history and by comparison. He traces the colonization of Ireland and America, Grattan's Parliament, and the Union, then tests Canada, Australia, and South Africa as models for what Ireland might gain. Finance gets long, careful chapters of its own.

Childers, later a figure in Irish politics, argues that self-rule within the empire could work, and he sets out a framework for Irish powers, finance, and Westminster seats. The book is serious, detailed, and partisan in a constructive way. It remains a key text for anyone studying Ireland on the eve of Home Rule debate.
15137-the-tale-of-mrs-tiggy-winkle:
Beatrix Potter's 1905 picture tale introduces Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, a hedgehog washerwoman who lives in a tiny house on a Lake District hill. Lucie, a little girl who has lost her handkerchiefs, climbs to find them and meets the busy hedgehog at her tubs. Potter's own drawings carry much of the charm.

Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle irons, folds, and sorts clothes belonging to Lucie's animal neighbors, from rabbits to birds. The tale ends with a gentle surprise about who the washerwoman serves. Short, funny, and tender, the book has delighted small children for over a century, and it pairs well with Peter Rabbit.
15138-a-hoosier-chronicle:
Meredith Nicholson's 1912 novel, with pictures by F. C. Yohn, tells a Hoosier story of politics, ideals, and love in Indiana. A Wordsworth motto on books as a substantial world fronts the tale, and an illustration shows Sylvia with Professor Kelton. The dedication praises wise readers who know that foolish laws are ropes of sand.

Through campaigns, colleges, and country towns, Nicholson follows young people learning how character shapes public life. His prose is earnest and Midwestern, with faith in ideas over mere statutes. Fans of early twentieth-century American fiction will find the chronicle thoughtful, warm, and rooted in Indiana soil.
1525-the-phoenix-and-the-turtle:
Shakespeare's brief, enigmatic poem gathers birds to mourn the phoenix and the turtle dove, lovers whose union was so perfect that two became one. An eagle, a swan, and a crow keep the obsequy, and the poem closes with a threnos, or funeral song, on love that outlasts death and reason alike.

Only sixty-seven lines long, the poem is dense with paradox and music, and scholars still debate its occasion and meaning. It may honour a marriage or a death, but its feeling is clear. It stands as Shakespeare's most compressed lyric, a jewel of grief and wonder.
15280-lulu-alice-and-jimmie-wibblewobble:
Howard Garis's 1912 bedtime book tells thirty-one duck stories of Lulu, Alice, and Jimmie Wibblewobble, with colored pictures by Louis Wisa. The series promises one story for each day of the month, to be read aloud at night. Rabbit, squirrel, and dog cousins fill companion volumes.

Garis writes in a gentle, funny style for small children, with duckling scrapes, lessons, and cozy endings. The Wibblewobbles quack through farmyards and ponds, learning manners and kindness. Parents reading aloud will find the book sweet, simple, and well suited to bedtime. Each tale ends with a small, kind lesson for bedtime listeners.
1539-the-winter-s-tale:
Shakespeare's late romance opens in Sicilia, where King Leontes, seized by jealousy, accuses his wife Hermione of adultery with his friend Polixenes, imprisons her. Loses his son and, seemingly, his wife and newborn daughter. Sixteen years pass, and the lost girl, Perdita, grows up a shepherdess in Bohemia.

A sheep-shearing feast, a prince in disguise, and a statue that comes to life bring the family together at last. The play moves from tragedy to wonder with breathtaking ease. The Winter's Tale is a masterpiece of forgiveness, time, and art that restores what was lost.
15422-israel-potter-his-fifty-years-of-e:
Herman Melville published this novel in 1855, built from a tattered life story of a real soldier. Israel Potter fought as a private at Bunker Hill, then was carried by war and chance into exile across the sea. Melville says he reshaped a peddler's pamphlet, said to be taken down from Potter's own lips, into this fuller tale.

The chapters follow Potter from his birthplace through battle, capture, wandering in England, and long years of poverty far from home. He returns at last in infirm old age to the land he served, unrewarded in life. Melville frames the book as a tribute to brave men whom history forgets, and the dedication to the Bunker Hill Monument makes that point plain. It is adventure, but its edge is the neglect of a common soldier.
15758-same-old-bill-eh-mable:
A doughboy humour book by Edward Streeter of the 27th Division, issued by Frederick A. Stokes Company in New York in 1919. Streeter, author of Dere Mable, writes letters home to Mable in soldier slang. G. William Breck, himself of the 27th, drew twenty-seven black-and-white pictures. The book laughs at army life from inside.

Bill marches till his pack gains a hundred and fifty pounds, grows a beard on both sides of his face, and beats buttons off with a big board. Mess lines, French towns, and drill fill the letters. Mable, back home, hears it all in Bill's own spelling. The book remains a lively record of the American soldier's wit in France.
15841-leonie-of-the-jungle:
A jungle romance by Joan Conquest, author of Desert Love, issued by the Macaulay Company in New York in 1921. Conquest dedicates the book to Madhu Krishnaghar, the splendid native of India. Two books divide the tale: The West and The East, with Kipling's line that never the twain shall meet. Leonie, a child of the jungle, stands between two worlds.

Lady Susan Hetth opens the story, scolding over a kitten found by a childish voice. Leonie grows between English order and Indian wildness, loved and feared by both. Passion, danger, and the pull of the jungle drive her fate. Conquest writes with lush, popular skill for readers who liked strong romance in strange lands.
1594-essays-in-little:
Andrew Lang's Essays in Little, published in 1891 with a portrait of the author, is a small book. It gathers short pieces on Alexandre Dumas, Stevenson's works, Thomas Haynes Bayly, Theodore de Banville, and Homer and the study of the classics. The preface frames them as little essays, written for pleasure rather than for system.

Lang's range is wide and his touch is light, moving from French romance to Greek epic in a few pages. The essays show a critic at play. The volume is a delightful Lang miscellany, best read as a companion to his longer Letters on Literature.
16004-the-evil-eye-or-the-black-spector-:
An Irish novel by William Carleton, The Evil Eye, or The Black Spector, in his collected works. Carleton's preface treats the evil eye as one of the most general superstitions ever known among men. No country on earth lacks belief in its influence, he holds. In his own young days it stood as a settled dogma of belief.

Carleton argues that education and knowledge will soon banish such idle superstitions from the public mind. His tale shows the belief at work in Irish cottages, with fear, blame, and strange sights. The Black Spector haunts the plot like a curse. The novel stands as a record of a fading faith: superstition, told by a man who watched it die.
16390-little-prudy-s-dotty-dimple:
Sophie May's Little Prudy's Dotty Dimple, published in New York by Hurst and Company and dedicated to little Nelly Clarke, follows the youngest Parlin child. Chapter one, Dotty's babyhood, opens as Grandma Read calls the children to the kitchen with news of a new little sister. Susy dances for joy, while Prudy, in delight, opens the cellar door and falls the whole length of the stairs, rolling as softly as a pincushion and escaping serious hurt.

Later chapters bring the bone man, Dotty's verses, nestlings, Fanny Harlow's party, a little teacher, a water-kelpie, brother Zip, Dr. Prudy, buying a brother, and a wedding. May writes gentle, funny stories for children. Young readers will enjoy Dotty's small mishaps and warm family circle.
16505-the-voice-of-the-people:
Ellen Glasgow's 1904 novel opens at Kingsborough on the last day of Circuit Court, as judge, jury, and crowd spill from the old courthouse into sunshine. A cow-bell sounds from the green, a red-and-white cow browses among buttercups, and the judge greets the gentlemen with a fine day. From that quiet opening grows a Virginia story of politics and the people's voice.

Glasgow writes with a novelist's eye for place, class, and ambition in the New South. The book belongs to her early Southern novels, praised as crowned masterpieces of modern fiction. Readers of American regional fiction will find it rich, humane, and sharply observed.
16596-ungava-bob-a-winter-s-tale:
Dillon Wallace sends young Bob into the Labrador wilds in this 1907 winter tale, third edition, with pictures by Samuel M. Palmer. Bob gets his trail, heads to the bush, meets a bear, is swept away in rapids, and ends alone in the wilderness. Micmac John's revenge, snow, and the tragedy of the trail follow, with Nascaupee hosts and an adrift on ice.

Wallace, author of The Lure of the Labrador Wild, writes with real knowledge of trappers, snow, and survival. The dialogue keeps its dialect flavor. Boys who love northern adventure will find a hard, thrilling tale of a lad learning the bush the hard way.
16648-holiday-stories-for-young-people:
Margaret E. Sangster compiled and edited this 1896 gift book of holiday stories for young people, issued by the Christian Herald in New York. She dedicates it in verse to boys and girls in town and on farms, at work and at play. Stories and ballads fill the book, with one tale, The Middle Daughter, first printed elsewhere.

Sangster chose pieces meant to please at holiday time: kind deeds, home joys, and small adventures, all in a gentle tone. The book is a sampler for family reading aloud, not a single long tale. Modern young readers get a sweet, old-style holiday book, and grown readers get a clear view of what 1896 thought fit for children.
16676-eveline-mandeville:
Alvin Addison's 1837 novel, subtitled The Horse Thief Rival, opens with a father's scolding: why does Eveline refuse Willard Duffel, the best offer in the county, for a mere whim? Eveline answers that she does not like him, and defends her judgment against charges of vanity and folly. The clash sets a courtship plot in motion.

Addison, author of The Rival Hunters, writes in the earnest style of early American domestic fiction. The tale turns on love, choice, and a rival's schemes. Readers of early Ohio fiction will find a lively, old-fashioned romance from the days of the early republic.
16688-hymns-songs-and-fables-for-young-p:
Eliza Lee Follen's hymns, songs, and fables for young people, revised and enlarged in Boston in 1851, open with a preface by Charles Follen. Most poems were written to instruct or please some child, and many had already appeared in print. Hymns lead the contents, from Suffer Little Children to The Lord is My Strength, followed by songs like The Little Spring and a May-day song.

Follen writes simply for children of all ages, with faith and kindness at the center. The book suits family singing and Sunday reading. Readers of early American children's verse will find a gentle, devout collection, warm without preaching down.
16823-my-neighbors-stories-of-the-welsh-:
Caradoc Evans wrote this 1920 book of Welsh stories, issued by Harcourt, Brace and Howe in New York and dedicated to his friend Thomas Burke. Chapters run from love and hate and according to the pattern into two apostles and earthbred. Treasure and trouble, Saint David and the prophets, and Joseph's house follow. Like brothers, a widow woman, and unanswered prayers appear. Lost treasure and profit and glory close the set. The opening sketch paints a big, tall God over Welsh chapels.

Evans writes of Welsh chapel life with bite and dark humor, exposing greed, pride, and piety in small villages. His stories shocked some readers with their bluntness. Modern readers will find a powerful, unsettling portrait of a chapel world, told in short, sharp tales that still divide opinion.
17059-the-submarine-boys-for-the-flag-de:
Victor G. Durham's sixth Submarine Boys book, from 1910, opens at a Dunhaven hotel where Jabez Holt mistakes a German stranger for a hair professor. Soon charts are marked, loot is found, and the boys face the Secretary of the Navy, command a gunboat for an hour, and duel through a door. Daisy Huston at last decides for the flag in the closing chapters.

The book leans harder into patriot duty than its mates, as Jack and Eph deed their lives to Uncle Sam. Sea jokes sit beside real peril, and the boys' loyalty never wavers. Young readers who follow the series will enjoy its mix of comedy, command, and flag-waving adventure at sea.
17096-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-at-:
Laura Lee Hope's 1916 camp tale starts when a wagon stops before the Brown house and Grandpa's tent sets the summer plan. Bunny and Sue sleep out, Splash the dog comes too, and camp life brings a big black bear, a ragged boy, a cross man, and a bad storm. Tom goes missing, a pie is stolen, and a cave and a smoke house hide the answers.

Uncle Tad, the old soldier of the frontispiece, adds humor with his potatoes and yarns. As always, the children help Tom and keep camp cheer bright. Young readers who like tents, boats, and small mysteries will find this a cozy, lively entry in the Bunny Brown series.
171-charlotte-temple:
Charlotte Temple, a schoolgirl of fifteen, trusts a soldier's promises and elopes to America. Susanna Rowson's Charlotte Temple, once America's best-selling novel, follows her from a boarding school to New York. Her lover abandons her, and poverty, illness, and shame follow.

Rowson pauses the tale to warn young readers against seduction and false friends. A kind stranger and a dying mother's letter frame Charlotte's repentance. The novel's sentimentality moved generations of American readers to tears. Its grave in New York became a place of pilgrimage. Rowson's moral tale warned a young republic about seduction, and its lessons echoed for a century.
17145-hallowe-en-at-merryvale:
Alice Hale Burnett's 1916 Merryvale tale gives small boys a Hallowe'en party to plan and enjoy. Toad and Chuck Brown, with Reddy, Fat, and their friends, get ready for games, then play at swinging apples, a candy pull, and fortune telling by a witch. Blowing out candles, hunting a silver coin, and a fine pie close the night.

The book is written so a boy can read it alone, in plain words and short scenes from small-town life. Its fun is homely, not scary: tricks, treats, and pals in a big white house. Young readers who like holiday stories will find this a cozy, old-style Hallowe'en treat.
17168-the-queen-of-the-pirate-isle:
Bret Harte's tale, pictured by Kate Greenaway in this facsimile of the 1885 book, stars Polly, a plump, good-humored girl of nine with no right at all to be a pirate queen. She has never been to sea, she hates violence, and she does not live on an island. Yet in play she turns beggar child, schoolmistress, preacher, and at last queen of a pirate isle, with dolls and pals for a crew.

Greenaway's pictures track each game, from tents and cliffs to fireworks in a cave. The charm lies in how fully Polly believes each part, and how kindly Harte laughs with her. Young readers will love a story that honors make-believe, and adults will enjoy its gentle wit about childhood play.
17214-the-quilt-that-jack-built-how-he-w:
Annie Fellows Johnston's Cosy Corner tale, priced at sixty cents in cloth, tells how Jack built a quilt and won a bicycle. The book sits in the same small series as The Little Colonel, The Giant Scissors, and Mildred's Inheritance, all made for young readers in handy, pictured volumes. Jack's quilt grows step by step, in the cumulative style its title promises.

Young readers follow a boy's patient handwork toward a prize he wants, with home, help, and humor along the way. The tale suits children who like making things and earning wishes. It is a warm, old-style story of work rewarded, told in Johnston's cozy, plain voice.
17228-swingin-round-the-cirkle:
Petroleum V. Nasby, pen name of David R. Locke, gathers his 1866 letters to the press in this 1867 volume, pictured by Thomas Nast. Nasby, late pastor of the Church of the New Dispensation and postmaster at Confederate Roads, Kentucky, writes in wild misspelled dialect. He dedicates the book to Andrew Johnson, pride and hope of democracy, and to Postmaster General Randall.

Letters cover elections, Kentucky talk, dreams, visions of Jackson, and the Freedmen's Bureau, with a psalm of gladness and a wail of anguish in turn. The dialect satire bites at Johnson's swing around the circle and at postwar politics. Readers of Civil War humor will find a loud, partisan, and historically rich comic voice, best read with its age in mind.
17265-companion-to-the-bible:
Rev. E. P. Barrows wrote this Companion to the Bible for teachers of Bible classes, ministers, and lay readers who want a thorough, orderly study. Part One gives evidences of revealed religion, stressing historic facts: genuineness, integrity, and inspiration of the books. Parts Two and Three introduce Old and New Testament books in turn, and Part Four sets out principles of reading scripture in human language.

Barrows keeps his notes concise and condensed, ready at hand for class use. His tone is scholarly and devout, from the old school of biblical study. Bible students who want a classic study aid, with each book placed and summed, will find this a solid, well-ordered companion.
17395-the-book-of-art-for-young-people:
Agnes Ethel Conway and Sir Martin Conway wrote this book of art for young people, published in London by A. and C. Black, first issued in September 1909 as The Children's Book of Art and reprinted in 1914, 1927, and 1935. Sixteen full-page pictures in colour accompany the text. A frontispiece shows Red Riding Hood from a picture by G. F. Watts in the Birmingham Art Gallery.

Chapters run from an introduction and the thirteenth century in Europe, through Richard the second and the Van Eycks, to the Renaissance, Raphael, Venice, the north, and Rembrandt. Readers get a gentle, picture-led history of painting for young people. The Conways' book still works as a first gallery companion.
17574-my-beautiful-lady-nelly-dale:
Thomas Woolner, Royal Academician, published this poem, My Beautiful Lady, Nelly Dale, in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne in 1887 with Cassell and Company. Its introduction describes Woolner's song as showing the issue of a noble earthly love, one with the heavenly. That issue is a life of high endeavour, in which those who would be something more than feasters hear the voice of duty as the note of war.

Readers get a Victorian verse narrative of love raised to moral purpose, by a sculptor-poet of the Pre-Raphaelite circle. The poem suits readers of Victorian poetry and of Woolner's double career. Its idealism marks its period plainly.
17620-the-point-of-honor-a-military-tale:
Joseph Conrad wrote this military tale, published in New York in 1908 by the McClure Company, with pictures by Dan Sayre Groesbeck. Copyright dates run 1907 and 1908. The tale opens with Napoleon the First, whose career had the quality of a duel against the whole of Europe, yet who disliked duelling between officers of his own army.

A frontispiece promises that a hero will fight no more duels now, and pictures show a sylph-like form on a couch and the clash of arms in a prim garden. Readers get a Napoleonic tale of honour, rivalry, and two officers bound by a duel. The book suits readers of Conrad's shorter fiction and of military honour.
1788-sir-john-oldcastle:
The True and Honorable History of Sir John Oldcastle, attributed in part to William Shakespeare, dramatizes the life of Lord Cobham, the Lollard knight who defied the church under Henry V. Oldcastle, his servant Harpoole, and a cast of bishops, judges, mayors, and French agents carry a plot of heresy, arrest, and escape.

The play defends its hero against the comic Oldcastle of the Falstaff plays, presenting him as a good lord wronged by priests. Its authorship remains shared and uncertain. That is part of its value: a history play from Shakespeare's circle, arguing about faith and loyalty at a time when both could cost a man his life.
18163-patriotic-plays-and-pageants-for-y:
Constance D'Arcy Mackay gathered one-act plays and pageants for schools, camps, clubs, and festivals in this 1912 volume. Each play treats the youth of an American hero, and the plays can stand alone or link into a larger pageant. Full directions cover simple costumes, dances, and music, so a schoolroom stage can carry them.

The pageant of patriots moves from Pocahontas and a Pilgrim interlude to Ferry Farm, George Washington, Daniel Boone, Benjamin Franklin, and Abraham Lincoln. Outdoor and indoor forms suit days such as the Fourth of July, Washington's Birthday, and Lincoln's Birthday. Teachers get ready material for teaching history through acting, song, and shared celebration.
18479-the-campaigns-of-the-british-army-:
Rev. G. R. Gleig wrote this narrative of the British campaigns at Washington and New Orleans in 1814 and 1815. Gleig served as chaplain-general to the forces and wrote The Subaltern and The Story of the Battle of Waterloo. Gleig compiled the new edition of 1879 not from memory alone, but from a journal kept while engaged in the enterprise, noting adventures and remarks as they occurred.

Chapters follow the cessation of hostilities in Europe, embarkation for America, encampment near Passages, and the march toward Bordeaux and Bayonne. At sea, Bermuda, the Chesapeake, and the Patuxent lead to Nottingham, Marlborough, the march to Washington, Bladensburg, and Washington itself. Readers get the War of 1812 from the British side, in a plain journal narrative that admits the expedition's issues were not of the most gratifying nature.
1852-lucile:
Owen Meredith, the pen name of Robert Bulwer-Lytton, wrote Lucile as a novel in verse. It opens with Hamlet's lines about the stricken deer and the hart ungalled, and is dedicated to his father with diffidence. The poem follows Lucile, a young woman loved by two men, through France and the Alps, with long passages on nature, faith, and the choices of the heart.

The verse is fluent and romantic. Its set pieces — Alpine springs, the thirst of seraphs quenched at their sources, and the spirit that fashioned fair France — show Meredith at his most musical. Readers who like verse novels will find Lucile a full example of the form, sentimental by design and sincere in its feeling.
18545-a-mummer-s-tale:
Anatole France wrote this novel as Histoire Comique, here in the English translation by Charles E. Roche, published by John Lane in London and New York in 1921. It belongs to the collected English edition of France's works, edited by J. Lewis May and Bernard Miall.

The story opens in an actress's dressing room at the Odéon, where Félicie Nanteuil is being dressed for the stage while the theatre doctor rests nearby. The novel follows life behind the footlights, where acting, vanity, and private feeling meet, and where the stage and the dressing room shape each other.
18701-choice-readings-for-the-home-circl:
M. A. Vroman published this family reading book at Nashville, first entered in 1905 and reissued in 1916. Formerly called Sabbath Readings for the Home Circle, it gathers moral and religious stories and poems meant to be read aloud on Sundays. The compiler chose only pieces fit for the Sabbath, avoiding sectarian points so any household could use the book.

Lessons stress obedience to parents, kindness to brothers, sisters, and friends, care for the poor, and gospel duties, shown through tales of keeping or breaking them. By its sixth edition the book claimed one hundred thirty thousand copies sold. It stands as a popular record of family reading of its day.
18735-the-little-red-hen-an-old-english-:
Florence White Williams retold and illustrated this old English folk tale for Saalfield in 1918. A little red hen lives in a barnyard, scratching for worms in her picketty-pecketty fashion and calling her chicks to every tidbit she finds.

One day she finds a wheat seed and learns that, planted and ripe, it can become flour and then bread. She asks the pig, the cat, and the rat to help plant it and cut it, and each answers, 'Not I.' So the hen does each task herself through the long summer, and the tale turns on who earns a share of the bread. The picture book teaches industry and fair shares in plain, cheerful scenes.
18861-temple-trouble:
H. Beam Piper published this science fiction story in Astounding Science Fiction in April 1951. Its premise is given in the opening blurb. Arranging miracles to order was a fine way for travelers from another timeline to win mining concessions. But nature sometimes answers with counter-miracles, and so can men. The story opens inside a dusky, many-pillared temple.

There stands Yat-Zar, a gigantic idol of fine workmanship, with three turquoise eyes and six arms. He holds a flame-bladed sword, a jeweled object, and a rabbit by the ears. Around this god, priests, traders, and outsiders bargain over faith and profit. Readers get a witty tale of religion used as a business tool, and of the trouble that follows when the tool bites back.
1895-armadale:
Wilkie Collins's Armadale, dedicated to John Forster in acknowledgment of his Life of Goldsmith, is a sensation novel built on a curse. Two men named Allan Armadale, one good and one scheming, have fates that tangle through forgery, murder, and a woman named Lydia Gwilt. The villain, waiting for his next opportunity, pushes his interests into the first gap of silence that opens.

Collins tells the story through letters, diaries, and narratives, and the plot turns on identity, inheritance, and poison. The novel is long and melodramatic by design. Its power lies in Lydia herself, one of Collins's most memorable creations, clever, passionate, and doomed by her own past.
19011-charlotte-bronte-and-her-circle:
Clement K. Shorter published this biography in London in 1896, with Hodder and Stoughton. It follows Charlotte Brontë from her parents, Patrick Brontë and Maria, through childhood, school, and governess life, to the Pensionnat Heger in Brussels. Later chapters treat her siblings Branwell, Emily, and Anne, her friends Ellen Nussey and Mary Taylor, and the curates at Haworth.

Shorter also covers Charlotte's lovers, her literary ambitions, her publisher William Smith Williams, her friendship with Thackeray, and her marriage to Arthur Bell Nicholls. Illustrations include portraits and a facsimile page of Emily's writing. Readers get a pioneering life of the Brontës, rich in letters and personal detail, from a biographer close to the surviving circle.
19117-sergeant-york-and-his-people:
Published in 1922, this book tells the life and war deeds of Sergeant Alvin York and his mountain people. It opens with his famous fight in the Argonne forest, where he faced machine guns alone after his comrades fell. The tale then turns back to his valley home and long-hunter kin.

York moves with care through brush and weeds, picking off gunners one by one while bullets tear the ground around him. Later chapters show his faith, modesty, and charity. Readers get a personal, dramatic portrait of an ideal American soldier, brave yet humble in victory.
19122-love-instigated-the-story-of-a-car:
Bell the Cat Surly, of the Pendennis Club, wrote this short, ornate tale. Its subject is a carved ivory umbrella handle. The narrator, fresh from drink and a friend's harrowing stories, seeks a dark cell at the club. It is wine-coloured. He places his gingham umbrella by the hearth. He rings for something to settle his nerves. The tale is told in high, mock-grand style.

His gaze falls on the carved ivory odalisque on the handle. Her sly glance leads him to dark, grotesque thoughts. Daggers, elves, and Brahman gods crowd his mind. Love, the title hints, is instigated by that glance. Readers get a curious, purple piece of clubland fantasy, brief and deliberately overblown.
19377-a-brief-account-of-the-rise-and-pr:
William Penn wrote this brief account of the rise and progress of the people called Quakers, here in a twelfth edition printed at Manchester in 1834. It declares their fundamental principle, doctrines, worship, ministry, and discipline, with a summary of former dispensations of God. An epistle to the reader opens the book.

Penn traces how Christians, once persecuted, gained worldly power under kings and emperors and turned a spiritual kingdom into a worldly one full of inventions and novelties. Quakers, he argues, return to inward light. Readers get a classic Quaker apology, plain, earnest, and foundational.
19381-among-the-farmyard-people:
Clara Dillingham Pierson wrote this book for children about farmyard animals, appearing from a New York press in the late eighteen hundreds with pictures by F. C. Gordon. Each chapter introduces a creature as a person with work to do: hens, cats, and others who help humans and help each other.

A young mother cat admiring her kittens, yellow and spotted, gives the tone: warm, homely, and full of small morals. Pierson wrote a whole shelf of such animal books, and this one shows her method at its best, teaching kindness and work through friendly beasts.
19549-the-mind-of-the-child-part-ii-the-:
This second part of a study of the mind of the child, in the International Education Series edited by William T. Harris, traces the growth of intellect. It records a child's first words with care, noting how sounds heard at home shape speech.

One child calls his nurse by a name traced to the German phrase for yes indeed, while words for soup, bathing, and rice pudding appear in baby forms. The book is an early landmark of child study, built on close daily notes rather than theory alone. A conspectus tracks the child's progress month by month before the chapters on intellect and speech begin.
19551-alice-in-wonderland-retold-in-word:
Mrs. J. C. Gorham retold Alice's Adventures in Wonderland in words of one syllable, published by a New York firm in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures. Alice falls down the rabbit hole, swims in a pool of tears, meets a caterpillar, and joins a mad tea party, all in short, plain words.

At the tea table the March Hare, the Hatter, and a sleepy Dormouse crowd one corner and cry that there is no room, though Alice finds a large armchair. The retelling was made for young readers taking their first steps in reading.
19669-twenty-years-of-balkan-tangle:
M. Edith Durham was a British traveler who knew the Balkans better than most outsiders. Twenty Years of Balkan Tangle grew from her journeys through the Near East. It opens with a sea trip among mauve islets in a dazzling blue sea. Strange tongues and stranger garments greeted her at each port. She writes that the fascination of the region took hold of her there.

Durham spent years among Albanians and their neighbors. She learned languages, recorded customs, and took sides in local causes. The Balkans of her years there were a knot of empires and new nations. Her book untangles that knot from ground level. It stays a key eyewitness source for the region.
19705-border-and-bastille:
Border and Bastille is a nineteenth-century memoir of travel and hardship. Its author thanks patrons who helped him reach the post he wanted. He admits one benefactor kindly overrated his qualifications. Such prefaces were the era's way of settling debts in print. The title joins a border crossing with a prison, the Bastille. Both promise trouble met on the road.

Memoirs of this kind fed a public hungry for foreign scenes. A border meant new laws, new tongues, and new risks. A prison meant the state showing its teeth. The author moves between gratitude and grievance in his opening. That mix often signals a life spent seeking favor abroad. The book belongs to the confessional travel shelf of its century.
19711-the-buried-temple:
Maurice Maeterlinck was a Belgian writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Buried Temple gathers his essays on moral and unseen forces. One passage asks whether an intelligent Judge must exist. It wonders whether cheating a neighbor cheats all the forces of justice too. Maeterlinck writes philosophy as quiet, searching prose.

His essays circle death, fate, silence, and the soul. The buried temple of the title is the hidden shrine within each person. Readers meet symbolist thought at its most gentle. Maeterlinck avoids system and proof on purpose. He prefers wonder that stays honest about mystery. The book is a calm entry into his meditative work.
1974-the-poetics-of-aristotle:
Tragedy works, Aristotle argues, not because its verse is beautiful but because its plot is built right, and this short treatise explains the building. Aristotle argues that poetry imitates action, not men, and that a well-made plot, with a beginning, middle, and end, matters more than fine verse.

The treatise takes up catharsis, the hero's error, and the difference between history and poetry. History tells what happened, while poetry tells what might happen according to probability and necessity. Butcher's translation keeps the Greek terms where they matter, and the book remains the starting point for anyone who wants to understand how stories are built.
19824-horses-nine-stories-of-harness-and:
Sewell Ford's Horses, from 1903, collects nine stories of harness and saddle. One hero, Skipper, joins the force at the age of six. He is clean of limb and sound of wind, without a blemish. A Green Mountain boy broke him to saddle. That boy knew more of horse nature than of trashy book learning. Ford's horses are working animals with full characters.

Ford wrote beloved animal stories set in New York and Vermont. His horses pull cabs, carry police, and haul loads. Each story tests the bond between horse and driver. The age of the horse was ending as he wrote. These tales preserve its skills and affections. Readers meet horsepower when it still had a heartbeat.
20054-the-mermaid-a-love-tale:
L. Dougall published The Mermaid, a love tale, in 1895. Its lead man, Caius Simpson, is the only son of a farmer. The farm lies on the north-west coast of Prince Edward's Island. His father worked hard, grew rich by island standards, and made his land yield well.

From that firm ground, a love story grows in a sea-bound place. Island farms, coasts, and small towns shape the lives on the page. The title hints at myth and the pull of the sea. Readers get romance rooted in work, land, and local custom.
20170-legend-land-vol-1-being-a-collecti:
Legend Land, volume one, gathers old tales of the West of England. Years ago, a rich, lovely lady came at times to one church. No one knew where she came from or who she was. Her beauty and glorious voice set the whole parish talking of her.

Such mystery figures walk through many tales in this set. Old churches, moors, and coasts of the West Country frame them. The book saves tales told by word of mouth for print readers. Readers get ghosts, saints, and wonders from a land rich in legend.
20180-mr-kris-kringle-a-christmas-tale:
Mr. Kris Kringle is a Christmas tale named for Santa Claus himself. A touch of sadness dims the children's usual gay Christmas humor. That hopeful hour, so bright for the young, carries shadow here. Years bring such shadow to joy, the tale notes at its start.

Christmas tales of this era mix gifts with grief and grace. Poor children, kind strangers, and small miracles fill many such stories. The book aims to warm hearts while it tugs at them too. Readers get a tender holiday tale in the classic sentimental vein.
2020-tarzan-the-terrible:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sends Tarzan into the hidden valley of Pal-ul-don, a lost land of ape-men, lion-men, and strange beasts. He is searching for Jane, and the search leads him through jungle craft, capture, and escape. Burroughs wrote the Tarzan books as serial adventure, and this volume keeps that breathless, chapter-ending pace.

Chapters move from the pithecanthropus and the gryf, a great flying beast, to temples, pits, and a struggle for a throne. The pace is fast and the setting is pure adventure, with Tarzan's strength and woodcraft tested at every turn. Jane's fate drives the search, and Tarzan's loyalty to her gives the wild action a steady human centre.
20214-instruction-for-using-a-slide-rule:
Instruction for Using a Slide Rule teaches a tool once vital to skilled work. Slide rules gave fast, close answers without long hand sums. Students, teachers, engineers, and architects all used them daily, it notes. Draftsmen, surveyors, and chemists found the rule just as handy at work.

Clerks and accountants used it when rough sums had to be rapid. The manual explains scales, settings, and worked examples step by step. Before electronic calculators, this slim tool ruled offices and labs. Readers get a clear fossil of practical math in the pre-digital age.
20249-legend-land-vol-2-being-a-collecti:
Legend Land, volume two, gathers more old tales of the West of England. Brent Tor rises as a lone, church-crowned peak near Lydford. It stands like a sentry watching the West for grim Dartmoor. From afar, the brave little hill looks like a burst of flame.

Burnt Tor, they say, was its old name for just that reason. Saints, giants, and ghosts crowd the tales tied to such places. Each short piece ties a story to a tor, church, or moor. Readers get a second rich helping of West Country legend and lore.
20255-the-unruly-sprite-a-partial-fairy-:
Henry van Dyke wrote The Unruly Sprite, a partial fairy tale of visions and faith. Some beings in the tale seem as substantial as mountain mists. They flicker and stray like will-o'-the-wisps over dark, wet ground. Yet something immortal clings to them, the man in the tale knows.

Without their presence, the world would be nothing to him at all. Van Dyke blends fairy lore with gentle moral and spiritual counsel. His sprite stands for the wild, bright part of the soul. Readers get a short, lyrical tale from a beloved American essayist-preacher.
20314-pearl-and-periwinkle:
Pearl and Periwinkle is a children's tale of two orphans taken into a stiff home. The children are son and daughter of the family's outcast sister. She has been half-forgotten, though only two months dead, the book notes. Adopting her children strikes Miss Hetty as almost scandalous at first.

Worse still, the pair have traveled all their young lives with a circus. Circus ways clash with a prim household's rules and manners at once. Yet pathos softens that clash as the tale goes on. Young readers get a story of orphans, pride, and slowly opening hearts.
20328-simon-dale:
Anthony Hope wrote Simon Dale, a historical novel of Restoration England. It opens by praising a great man who left an enduring name. His rule for life was charity in mind, trust in providence. And truth as the pole on which a life should turn, it adds.

Simon Dale serves at the court of Charles the Second in this tale. Hope, famed for The Prisoner of Zenda, loved courts and swordplay. Love, honor, and intrigue swirl around his young hero at Whitehall. Readers get polished historical romance from a master of the form.
20563-terry-a-tale-of-the-hill-people:
Charles Goff Thomson's Terry: A Tale of the Hill People opens with a shot in the winter hills. The frosty silence of the snow-covered hills is broken by the vicious crack of a high-powered, small-caliber rifle. A hidden hunter has fired from a thicket.

The hunter springs out and crosses the gully to a knoll. There lies a black furry bundle, the game he has brought down. Thomson builds his tale of the hill people on such scenes of hunting, hardship, and mountain custom. The hills themselves, white and silent, shape every life in the story.
20567-the-pigeon-tale:
Virginia Bennett's The Pigeon Tale is a story for children set in an old farmhouse that seems to wake up and dress itself young again. The fresh muslin curtains at the window are stiff with starch. They will not stir an inch in the breeze blowing in.

The old farmhouse, the narrator decides, is trying to look young again. To look young again: how many others wish the same. Into that brightened house comes the pigeon's tale, told in Bennett's gentle farm language. The book belongs to the shelf of quiet animal and farm stories written for young readers.
20580-napoleon-the-little:
Victor Hugo wrote Napoleon the Little as a furious attack on Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte after his coup of December 1851. Hugo, driven into exile, refused to call the new ruler Napoleon the Great's equal. This 1909 edition brought the polemic to English readers in a fresh form.

Its pages stage scenes from the fall of the republic. The representatives crowd the right lobby of the Assembly and return to their places, leaving the passage free. It was about four in the afternoon, and darkness was falling on the great hall. Hugo turns such scenes into an indictment of tyranny.
2063-the-trail-of-the-white-mule:
B. M. Bower follows Casey Ryan, a hot-tempered Irish driver who slides through city traffic, collects a ticket, and soon finds himself on the trail of a white mule and a desert mystery. The city gives way to the open West. Bower wrote Casey Ryan tales for magazine readers who loved the West in comic form.

Casey, a hero of Bower's earlier books, drives, argues, and blunders with comic energy, and the plot mixes bootlegging, prospecting, and chase. The novel is light western fun, told in Bower's brisk, slangy voice. The white mule gives the plot its mystery, since a beast so strange must be going somewhere worth following.
20709-from-pole-to-pole-a-book-for-young:
Sven Hedin, the Swedish explorer of Central Asia, wrote From Pole to Pole as a book of world travel for young people. Rather than tell his own expeditions, he takes readers on one great journey around the earth. Lands, peoples, and natural wonders pass in order along the route.

Our journey begins at Stockholm, the capital of my native country, he writes. Leaving Stockholm by train in the evening, we travel all night in comfortable sleeping cars. We arrive next morning at Trelleborg, Sweden's southernmost port, where the journey by sea begins. School readers across Europe learned geography from Hedin's ride.
20711-daily-thoughts-selected-from-the-w:
Daily Thoughts gathers short passages from the writings of Charles Kingsley, chosen for one day at a time. Kingsley was a clergyman, novelist, and naturalist whose sermons and books filled Victorian homes. A daily reading book lets his voice speak briefly each morning.

Kingsley urges readers to understand where we are, and what our work is here. He scorns superstitions about the good old times. Men fancy those days belonged to God, he says, while this age belongs only to man, blind chance, and the evil one. The selections mix devotion, nature, and social duty in his hearty style.
20716-the-tale-of-timothy-turtle:
Arthur Scott Bailey's The Tale of Timothy Turtle belongs to his Sleepy-Time Tales of the animals of Pleasant Valley. Timothy Turtle is an old, grumpy resident of Black Creek. All the wild folk know him by name, though few see much of him.

He is seen less often than Mr. Crow because he spends much of his time on the muddy bottom of Black Creek. Besides, he never flapped his way through the air to Farmer Green's fields. Bailey's animal tales taught children the habits of real creatures while dressing them in waistcoats of story.
2075-crotchet-castle:
Thomas Love Peacock, friend and trusted critic of Shelley, sets a comic novel in a country house where talkers of every stripe debate reform, poetry, and progress. The master of Crotchet Castle gathers guests who argue in set speeches. Peacock wrote Crotchet Castle in 1831, after years of friendship with Shelley and other radicals.

Peacock delights in Greek literature and in puncturing new fashions, and his characters speak for schools of thought rather than for themselves. The novel charms as satire, and as a portrait of an age arguing with itself over dinner. His talkers include a poet, a political economist, and a clergyman, each arguing his own hobby.
20808-three-people:
A baby fresh from the bath, all curls and blue eyes, opens Three People. Isabella Alden, who wrote as Pansy, asks what such a child could be but a beauty. Hands, feet, and a rosebud mouth all quiver with life and glee.

Pansy wrote Christian tales for vast numbers of young readers. Three People weaves faith into home life and the growth of its leads. Her books taught conduct through story rather than sermon. This one keeps her warm tone and clear moral aim. It shows why her tales filled Sunday school shelves and family bookcases across America for decades.
20878-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-essay-:
Thomas Carlyle's works, says John Morley, form a canon closed and set for posterity. Thirty fine volumes hold his Gospel of Silence in compressed form. Morley's essay on Carlyle, in Critical Miscellanies, weighs that vast, strange legacy.

Carlyle thundered against his age as prophet, historian, and sage of Chelsea. Morley sorts his power from his faults with cool, clear judgment. Hero worship, German thought, and French revolt all fed Carlyle's fire. This essay gives new readers a firm guide into a writer who awed and irked his century in near equal parts.
20923-a-negro-explorer-at-the-north-pole:
Word that Matt Henson stood with Peary at the North Pole reached New York in 1909, this book recalls. A Peary Arctic Club man swore Henson must have been there that day. A Negro Explorer at the North Pole, from 1912, tells Henson's own tale.

Henson, a Black explorer of rare skill, drove dogs and broke trail for Peary. Cold, hunger, and ice perils fill his plain, strong account. White fame long slighted his share in the feat. His book claims that share with calm proof, and it remains a key voice from the heroic age of polar travel.
20939-the-song-of-the-exile:
England's shores shrink astern as The Song of the Exile opens in verse of parting pain. The singer owns he has little cause to mourn, for home gave him only unrest. Birth, yes, his native land gave, but never a true home.

Visions and miscellaneous poems fill the rest of this slight volume's pages. Exile, faith, loss, and hope sound through its gathered pieces in turn. Such verse spoke to many in an age of wide migration and parting. Readers meet a voice that turns private sorrow into song, plain in feeling even when its dress is old and formal.
21105-teddy-the-story-of-a-little-pickle:
John Conran Hutcheson wrote this short children's book about Teddy. The small boy's loud demand for his grandmother startles a railway porter out of his skin.
