Teddy is an independent young gentleman of about ten or eleven in spirit, forever in minor trouble. His small misdeeds fill most of the chapters.

The porter who first meets him is a tall, good-natured giant in worn velveteen clothes smeared with oil and grease. Hutcheson, better known for sea tales, keeps this story on land and at child height. It aims at young readers who enjoy seeing a pickle of a boy get into and out of scrapes.
21129-the-heart-of-una-sackville:
Una Sackville starts a diary in May 1895, in a handsome book with a clasp and key given her by Lena Streatham. Mrs George de Horne Vaizey tells Una's story through that diary, begun just as she leaves school. Una means to write only when she wants to talk and her friend Lorna is not near.

The tale follows a young woman of the professional middle classes. She looks for love and a husband in the months and years after school. Vaizey draws the men and women around Una sharply. Written close to its 1895 setting, it records the social world of such girls from inside.
21203-the-tale-of-grandfather-mole:
Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales introduce a queer old person who has lived in Farmer Green's garden longer than anyone can say. Neighbours seldom saw Grandfather Mole, since moles spend their lives underground. The frontispiece shows him making a rush at Mr. Meadow Mouse.

Bailey wrote a whole shelf of these animal tales, from Cuffy Bear to Dickie Deer Mouse, for Grosset and Dunlap. Each gives one creature a small comedy of habits, appetites, and quarrels with the neighbours. Grandfather Mole's grumbling ways underground make him a funny, cross old character for children hearing the stories at bedtime.
21272-the-bibliotaph-and-other-people:
Leon H. Vincent's essays on book lovers appeared in Boston in 1899, several of them first printed in the Atlantic Monthly. The Bibliotaph, his opening portrait, is a book collector buried in his books, drawn not wholly from imagination. Two more papers follow the same figure among his friends, scrapbooks, and bargain bins.

Other essays read the letters of John Keats and consider Thomas Hardy and an Elizabethan novelist. A third takes up Stevenson as vagabond and philosopher, ending with his novel St Ives. Vincent pokes gentle fun at collectors while sharing their passion. The volume preserves the talk of 1890s book rooms, where bargains and editions were serious sport.
21296-mother-carey-s-chicken-her-voyage-:
Mark Strong has always longed to follow his sea-captain father to sea. At last his father agrees to take both Mark and his mother on the next voyage. George Manville Fenn warns the boy that a man's duty is to face danger. A woman, he says, keeps the nest. But the family sails together anyway. The Java Seas await them.

Pirates, sharks, serpents, volcanoes, hostile peoples, geysers, and fire at sea crowd the voyage to the unknown isle of the title. Fenn piles peril on peril in his practised way. Mother Carey's chicken, a storm petrel, gives the tale its name and its sea flavour.
21314-king-o-the-beach-a-tropic-tale:
Carey, a teenage boy, sails on the steamer Chusan to join his parents in Australia in George Manville Fenn's tropic tale. He befriends the ship's doctor and seaman Bob Bostock. Then he falls from the rigging and is knocked out, his telescope taking the worst of the fall. A gale then drives the powerless ship onto a coral-girt volcanic island.

Most passengers escape by boat, but Carey is too hurt to move, so the doctor and Bostock stay with him on the wreck. A beachcomber who calls himself king of the islands arrives with a retinue and proves vicious. When he shoots the doctor, the tale turns toward rescue.
21333-doom-castle:
Neil Munro's novel of Jacobite Scotland opens on an autumn afternoon with wintry breakers sounding and nuts dropping in the corries of Ardkinglas. Count Victor, a foreigner, comes to a strange country and is pursued almost at once. The Baron of Doom and his castle give the tale its centre.

Chapters promise a spy wanted, an apparition, a lawyer's good lady, and a woman at a window. Mungo Boyd and chamberlain Sim MacTaggart serve the household as intrigue gathers. A duel on the sands, a cell in the fosse, and the Duke's ball carry the action. Munro, a Highland writer, sets romance and conspiracy in the Argyll he knew well.
21344-the-young-bridge-tender-or-ralph-n:
Arthur M. Winfield, who also wrote the Rover Boys books, opens with Ralph Nelson, only son of a widow. His father once kept the swing bridge between Westville and Eastport on Keniscot Lake. Ralph holds the bridge tender's job himself when a smash at the bridge starts the action. Squire Paget wants the property and moves against the family.

Chapters follow a missing bill, a runaway, a midnight crime, and Ralph out on bail before the robbery is cleared up. Percy, the squire's son, hears something that matters. Winfield wrote upward-struggle tales for boys in the Alger line: honest work, false suspicion, and a rise earned by pluck.
21449-with-axe-and-rifle:
A boy watches his Irish family make a home in the wild West in W. H. G. Kingston's With Axe and Rifle. His father liked the country so well that he went back to Ireland for his bride. The boy, his brother Dan, and small sister Kathleen grow up on the frontier.

Kingston shows the settlers' grind against weather, sickness, bad neighbours, and raids. A tutor called the Dominie and Dio, a runaway slave they shelter, stand close to the family. A wicked man named Bracher and a strange hunter who keeps saving them add drama. The tale ends in sudden, glad relief.
21577-peter-simple:
Peter Simple is the fool of his family, and the navy gets him, in Captain Marryat's novel of 1834. His father, a clergyman and a noble family's youngest son, holds a rich living. Custom, Peter jokes, offers the family's greatest fool to the country's naval greatness.

At fourteen Peter is packed off, first to a stockbroker and then to sea. His slow wits prove sharper than folk think, as cruises and captures pile up. The book was Marryat's fourth, and it fixed his fame for comic sea fiction. Friendship with the loyal O'Brien gives the tale much of its heart.
21616-the-ape-the-idiot-other-people:
W. C. Morrow gathers dark tales in The Ape, the Idiot and Other People, copyrighted in 1897. The stories first ran in Lippincott's Magazine and in San Francisco papers. A fourth edition, from 1910, is the copy given here.

One tale opens on an ape who has lived in a cage since childhood, with no memory of free forests. Others treat a plague hero, a monster-maker, and a game of honour. Absinthe, dungeons, and faithful amulets supply the props of these grim pieces. Morrow writes with a cold, exact hand that made him a master of the weird tale.
21692-the-pirate-city-an-algerine-tale:
R. M. Ballantyne sets The Pirate City in Algiers, in a tale of action about 1817. A dear little old lady in Sicily opens the tale, her mouth a study of smiles. Her wrinkles, Ballantyne says, are each a separate smile around it.

Her son Lucien is meant for the Church, by his father's dearest wish. Juliet, an adopted child, is promised to a convent by her uncle the abbot. Against those quiet plans stands the pirate city itself, and its defeat by the British Navy. Ballantyne mixes comic portraiture at home with Barbary fighting abroad.
21733-the-giant-of-the-north-pokings-rou:
Arctic seas call in this Ballantyne adventure, whose subtitle promises pokings round the Pole. Ballantyne had lived in the Canadian north as a young Hudson's Bay clerk, and ice country was his home ground as a writer. His tales of the far north drew on real cold, real hunger, and real travel by sledge and boat.

The giant of the title and the voyage toward the Pole drive the story's wonders. Strange sights, hard weather, and tall tales gather around the push into the frozen seas. Ballantyne mixes fact from polar travel with a boy's love of marvels. The result is a northern yarn in his fullest storyteller's voice, equal parts camp talk and adventure.
21837-monopolies-and-the-people:
Trusts and monopolies are put on trial in this 1889 study by Charles Whiting Baker, an editor of The Engineering News. Baker promises two things: a fair survey of monopolies in every industry, and a plain discussion of their causes, growth, evils, and remedies. He admits his list cannot name every powerful combination, yet holds that the broad facts deserve wide knowledge.

The book is dedicated to all who love truth, justice, and the rights of the whole people. It appeared as the great trusts were reshaping American business and politics. Baker writes as an engineer among lawyers: facts first, then judgment. For readers of the trust era, it is a clear contemporary map of the fight that led to antitrust law.
21975-the-barbadoes-girl-a-tale-for-youn:
An orphan girl from the West Indies joins an English family in Mrs. Hofland's The Barbadoes Girl, a tale for young people reissued at Boston in 1863. Mr. Harewood tells his wife and children that the daughter of a dead friend is coming from Barbados to live with them. The children pepper him with questions. Edmund is grave and studious at twelve, Charles lively at ten, and Ellen, eight, the mildest and most modest of all.

Bacon and Addison supply the mottoes: indulged passion makes bitter work for repentance. Hofland was a prolific writer of improving tales. Her new girl's temper and the family's patience drive the lesson home. The book teaches the management of feeling through a stranger in the house, in the firm Victorian manner.
22174-andrew-melville:
William Morison wrote this life of Andrew Melville for the Famous Scots series. Melville, scholar and church reformer, led Scotland's Presbyterians after Knox. The struggle from 1574 to 1688 to keep the Presbyterian system fills the book. Morison argues that the system's benefits to Scotland justify that struggle.

Melville defied kings, rebuilt universities, and suffered exile for the Kirk's freedom. His famous rebuke of James VI, calling him God's silly vassal, echoes through the story. Morison writes in the brisk, admiring style of the Famous Scots volumes. The book gives general readers a compact life of the second founder of Scottish Presbyterianism.
22185-sonnie-boy-s-people:
James B. Connolly, the Irish-American writer of sea stories, published Sonnie-Boy's People as a set of tales. Connolly knew Gloucester fishermen and harbour towns at first hand. In the title story, Marie Welkie watches a stranger from her veranda while keeping an eye on her nephew. His fine clothes and easy assurance disturb and amuse her; his kindness to the boy pleases her more.

The stories circle Sonnie-Boy, a child among sailors, fishermen, and shore folk. Connolly writes dialect and sea talk with a reporter's ear. Humour and pathos mix in his port scenes. The collection shows why Connolly was rated among the best American sea-story writers of his day.
22264-irish-books-and-irish-people:
Stephen Gwynn wrote Irish Books and Irish People as essays on his country's letters and life. Behind everything, Gwynn says, lies a great social change. Ownership of Ireland's land was passing from landlords to the men who tilled it. That transfer, he argues, literally unenslaved three-fourths of Ireland's people, though its links to the life of the mind are obscure and intangible.

His essays connect the land change to Ireland's literary revival. Books, writers, and readers all stand in the new Ireland's making. Gwynn, a nationalist member of Parliament and man of letters, writes as an insider. The volume captures the Irish revival's confidence in the years before the Great War.
22346-exile:
Exile is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its figures belong to a strange order of scholars in robes. One of them, Oktan, stands slightly under Kinton's height of five feet ten.

Oktan has a long, supple trunk and short, bowed legs. His short, thick arms are carried high before his chest. That build leaves Kinton feeling something is out of proportion. Robes hide part of the oddness from casual eyes. Such close body detail builds an alien presence without explanation. Readers meet exiles whose forms set them apart. The tale plays on difference, strangeness, and the unease of standing near it.
22399-the-fireside-picture-alphabet-or-h:
The Fireside Picture Alphabet mixes an alphabet book with humor and droll moral tales. Its back pages advertise the publisher's other wares for children. Miss Hattie's French Bedstead and Tom Thumb's Carriage appear there.

New toys in preparation are also promised to young buyers. A manual of cricket and baseball is offered by mail. Its plans show how to lay out grounds and form clubs. Marylebone Club rules for cricket are included in that manual. Baseball rules from several clubs appear alongside them. As a whole, the volume shows how children's books were sold. Pictures taught letters while advertisements sold the next purchase.
2248-the-winter-s-tale:
Leontes, king of Sicilia, suddenly believes his wife Hermione unfaithful with his friend Polixenes, and his jealousy destroys his family. The Winter's Tale spans sixteen years and two kingdoms, from a trial and a seeming death to a shepherd's cottage where the lost baby Perdita grows up among clowns and flowers. Shakespeare then stages one of his most famous reunions.

Time itself appears as a chorus, and the statue scene at the end turns grief into wonder. The play blends tragedy and pastoral comedy in a way no other Shakespeare quite attempts. Its final forgiveness feels earned, strange, and deeply moving.
22763-suite-mentale:
Randall Garrett wrote Suite Mentale, a science fiction story about minds joined in a telepathic gestalt and the strain of sharing thoughts. The catalog record gives no year. Garrett, a prolific magazine writer, liked clever premises worked out with a light, ironic hand, and a mental suite, minds in sequence like music, is one of his neatest.

The sample is pure Garrett misdirection. A doctor gives his brief verdict, he may live. His audience is a group of men in conservative business suits, holding soft felt hats outside the door. Mallon's eyes stop on the tallest man's face. Nothing in the scene admits how strange the case behind the door has been. The story that follows thinks hard about what linked minds would do to privacy, guilt, and selfhood.
22827-patchwork-a-story-of-the-plain-peo:
Anna Balmer Myers set Patchwork, her 1920 story of the Plain People, among Pennsylvania's plain-dressing farm families. A perfect June morning opens the tale, with perfume from countless blossoms tempting everyone outdoors. Sunshine, blue sky, and lavish early summer set the scene before any conflict arrives.

Against that beauty, Myers works out the tensions of a strict, close community. Young people in plain dress face the pull of the wider world, its clothes, music, and freedoms. The patchwork of the title fits both the quilts of the region and the pieced-together lives on the page. Myers knew this world well, and her sympathy shows. The novel remains a warm, informed portrait of Pennsylvania Dutch country life.
22948-rival-pitchers-of-oakdale:
Morgan Scott opens Rival Pitchers of Oakdale, published in 1911, at noon on a sunny April day. Boys cluster on the Oakdale Academy steps at noon, talking nothing but baseball. The season is about to open, and Scott says the fever of the game already runs in their veins.

Two pitchers, one mound. The rivalry promised by the title drives this entry in Scott's Oakdale sports series, with school honor and a girl's opinion never far away. The books sold clean competition to boy readers, complete with coaching in both pitching and conduct. Period slang and period certainty fill the pages. As a record of how America taught sport to its sons, it is hard to beat.
23126-eric-or-little-by-little:
A boy counts the days in Eric, or Little by Little. A young boy capers and claps at the news. His parents come home within the week, the family will stay a short while, and then, at last, school begins for him.

Frederic William Farrar's school story follows Eric Williams through an English public school, where small surrenders to temptation accumulate, little by little, into ruin. Few Victorian novels were pressed on schoolboys so hard, or remembered so vividly, fondly and ruefully at once. Farrar, a clergyman and schoolmaster, wrote to warn, and his warning became a genre landmark. Modern readers meet the original of a hundred school stories, sermon and all, with its pathos fully intact.
23148-droozle:
A puppy snake stars in Droozle. The narrator traces Droozle to art school days and a grand tour. An unscheduled stop in the Coffin system introduced him to ballpoint snakes, Coffin Two's chief export. By liftoff, one small snake had become his traveling companion.

A pet from another planet, carried home in a traveler's luggage, gives the story its gentle engine. Art school, a grand tour, and interstellar stopovers blend in a future where tourism includes other worlds. Droozle himself, part souvenir and part companion, tests what his owner owes a creature bought as a curiosity. The tone stays light, the questions real. It is a small, fond piece of science fiction about pets and responsibility.
2316-the-choir-invisible:
James Lane Allen's Choir Invisible is a Kentucky romance of the early republic, following a young minister and the woman he loves through the wilderness settlements. The novel takes its title from George Eliot's poem about lives that shape the world unseen, and Allen writes the frontier with a poet's attention to woods, rivers, and seasons. Love and duty contend throughout.

The story's tone is elegiac: the pioneers' hopes, their losses, and their quiet faith all feed the choir of the title. Allen's prose is lush by modern standards, but his feeling for Kentucky is genuine. Readers of regional romance will find a tender, old-fashioned book.
2326-his-own-people:
Booth Tarkington's His Own People follows an American abroad who discovers that money cannot buy the old-world society he craves. The novella's hero, a wealthy Midwesterner in Europe, chases titles and acceptance while his own countrymen watch with amusement. Tarkington's satire is gentle but pointed.

The story's interest lies in its social observation: Americans performing Europe, Europeans performing disdain. Tarkington, later famous for The Magnificent Ambersons, already shows his gift here. Readers will find a short, witty comedy of manners. Tarkington later won Pulitzer Prizes for his novels of Midwestern life.
23330-one-day-at-arle:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this tale of one day at Arle, a tiny fishing hamlet on England's northwest coast, published in the late eighteen seventies. A young, handsome woman leans at a cottage door by the shore, drawing a stranger's eye at first glance.

A second look teaches more and pleases less: she is young but not girlish, tall, lithe, and braced against the lintel with a will of her own. Burnett's sketch turns a single day into a portrait of a woman shaped by sea, work, and pride. A forsaken man wipes hot tears with the back of a rough hand, saying he is not the sort to take up with the world.
23343-lines-in-pleasant-places-being-the:
William Senior, writing as Red Spinner, gathered these fishing sketches in London in nineteen twenty, after a long run of his earlier angling books had gone out of print. The pieces look back on a life spent beside rivers and lakes. They speak to readers who fish for sport rather than for a living.

Day after day on the water fills the pages: casting a fly, working a stream, playing a fish that runs hard, and losing one that should have been landed. Senior writes with warmth about guides, friends, quiet banks, and the small luck that makes or breaks an outing. The charm lies in that plain talk of skill, patience, and place, kept close to what the rod and the river actually do.
23352-comical-people:
Drawn from the designs of J. J. Grandville and the embroidered tapestry shown by Maria Fusinata of Belluno at the Great Exhibition, this eighteen fifty two picture book gives animals the dress and manners of people. Sixteen plates carry the joke, with beasts posed as lords, ladies, and town folk.

Short tales follow the plates: a ball hosted by Lady Chaffinch, a lord of the manor, a country story told by Warren Rabbitt, a portrait painter, and an alderman with high aims. The fun lies in the clash between animal form and human pride, rank, and fuss. Young readers and grown readers alike can enjoy the satire, which stays light even when it pokes at vanity.
2345-the-adventure-of-the-red-circle:
Holmes unravels a lodger's secret in The Adventure of the Red Circle, where a mysterious tenant, coded messages, and an Italian secret society converge on a London lodging house. Arthur Conan Doyle gives Watson a front-row seat as Holmes decodes the signals and unmasks a vendetta from the old country. The climax comes in a darkened room with a dead man and a living witness.

The story's atmosphere of foreign conspiracy suits the Holmes formula well. Its solution is neat and its tension steady. Mystery fans will enjoy this compact late case.
23453-the-book-of-one-syllable:
Esther Bakewell wrote this book of one syllable pieces, with coloured engravings, for young readers learning to read. A frontispiece letter of one syllable sets the rule: every word short, every tale plain, so a beginner can sound out each line without stumbling.

Bakewell dedicates the book to friends of her youth, recalling days gone by and kind words that time has not washed away. Scenes from the past, told in the simplest words, give children both reading practice and gentle feeling. Parents and teachers will value the book as a primer with heart, proving that short words can still carry memory, friendship, and a touch of poetry.
23459-fishy-winkle:
Jean C. Archer made this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty nine in the series, about Fishy Winkle and a band of runaway children. Mistress O'Hara looks blue for good reason, as nurse reports for the third time in a week that the children have all run away.

Mama checks the larder, finds pumpkin pie and dinner clean gone, and sets off with a big stick for the sea, sure the truants will be there. Yama Guchi leads the twins by the nose, and the whole crew follows wherever he goes. The rhymes stay brisk and comic, with pictures of the chase, the shore, and the scolding to come. Small children will laugh at the runaways and their grown up hunters, in a tale of mischief with a mild end.
23477-up-horsie-an-original-fairy-tale:
Madame de Chatelain wrote this original fairy tale for the Lilliputian Library, printed by Joseph, Myers and Company of London. Gilbert, a young peasant riding a stout, well fed nag to market, overtakes Sandy, an old Scotch shepherd trudging on foot. He mocks his slow pace.

Sandy, peering from under bushy brows, proposes ride and tie, sharing the horse in turns. Gilbert scorns the plan, saying he keeps a horse for himself, and rides on, leaving the old man behind. What follows in the market town turns the joke on Gilbert, as fairy justice catches up with a churlish rider. Children will enjoy the tale's brisk talk, its north country flavour, and its plain moral about kindness to fellow travellers.
23580-the-children-s-bible:
Henry A. Sherman and Charles Foster Kent, Woolsey professor of biblical literature at Yale, translated and arranged this children's Bible. It offers selections from Old and New Testaments, printed by Scribner's in nineteen thirty six from a nineteen twenty two copyright. A Curtis picture of Christ welcoming little children fronts the book.

Old Testament tales run from creation, gifts to man, first disobedience, Cain and Abel, Noah's flood, and the tower of Babel. They continue through Abraham, Lot, Ishmael, and Rebekah, in language pared for young ears. New Testament selections follow in the same clear style. Parents and teachers will value the book as a gentle first Bible, keeping great stories whole while trimming hard passages for children.
23622-about-peggy-saville:
Mrs. George de Horne Vaizey wrote this late nineteenth century girls' book about Peggy Saville, a new girl at a vicarage school near Brighton, where older children learn beside the vicar's own three. Peggy, lately from India where her parents remain, has great talent in some directions yet still adds by counting on her fingers.

Peggy gets up to tricks, and at a dance given by a titled pupil's family, a fire breaks out, from which Peggy rescues the daughter of the house. Vaizey writes emotions with timeless warmth, even where manners and references date the tale. Girls who love school stories will enjoy Peggy's scrapes, friendships, and brave act, in a book that treats a new girl's pluck as its heroine's true gift.
23699-abijah-s-bubble:
F. Hopkinson Smith's Abijah's Bubble begins at a christening where a father's voice drowns a mother's whisper. The minister starts, I baptize thee, Evang—, and Ezekiel Todd roars over him: Abijah, I tell ye, Parson. Abijah it is, though the women are furious and Deacon Libby's wife begs that she be called Abbie for short.

Abbie never minds the name, being too little to remember. Only old Si Spavey never forgets the sound, like a buzz-saw striking a log. Twice since, the name has cost her: signing as a witness to a mortgage after her father's death, and signing an application later. Smith tells her story with village humor and a fond eye for small dignities.
23742-charley-s-museum-a-story-for-young:
Charley's Museum, published in Philadelphia in 1855, tells of Charley Carter, a bright and active lad of twelve. He is the son of a farmer a few miles from Philadelphia. He is a great favorite of two uncles: Brown, a wealthy city merchant, and a sea captain brother of his mother who has sailed to all parts of the world.

Charley loves to learn about animals, whether they fly, swim, walk, or crawl. His uncle Brown shares the taste for natural history from boyhood, and the uncles and his father together give Charley the means to build a museum of his own. It is a mid-century boys' book about curiosity, collecting, and kind adults who feed a child's interest.
23781-a-little-girl-of-long-ago-or-hanna:
Amanda M. Douglas published A Little Girl of Long Ago, or Hannah Ann, in 1897 as a sequel to A Little Girl in Old New York. It opens in 1846, with New Year's bells and pistols, and closes in 1897, following Hannah Ann from girlhood to grown womanhood across fifty years.

Chapters bring an interview with a tiger, a wedding, winter happenings, and the land of Ophir. There is a visit with a poet, the king of terrors, and the beginnings of romance, counted up at cost. Douglas writes, as her dedication says, that the little girls of long ago grow old with the century, while girlhood blossoms afresh each spring.
23836-the-french-prisoners-of-norman-cro:
The Reverend Arthur Brown, rector of Catfield in Norfolk, published The French Prisoners of Norman Cross in 1895. Its epigraph mourns him that goeth away, for he shall return no more nor see his native country. The tale opens late one autumn afternoon in 1808, on the road from Peterborough to Yaxley.

A body of men marches four abreast, shabby and downcast, guarded by red-coated militia with loaded guns and fixed bayonets. They have come from battlefields and crowded ships to the dreary depot at Norman Cross, their home for they know not how long. Brown writes of prisoners of war as an honorable estate, and of captivity without shame but also without comfort.
23887-strange-stories-from-history-for-y:
George Cary Eggleston published Strange Stories from History for Young People with Harper and Brothers, in Harper's Young People Series. Eggleston, author of Red Eagle, The Big Brother, and The Wreck of the Red Bird, writes history as story, choosing strange and striking episodes to hold young readers.

The series around it shows its company: Jimmy Brown, the Canoe Club, the Moral Pirates, Toby Tyler, and Tim and Tip. Eggleston's volume belongs to that shelf of illustrated sixteenmo cloth books, a dollar each, meant for boys and girls. For modern readers it is a sample of how the nineteenth century taught history to the young: by anecdote, adventure, and wonder.
2397-the-story-of-my-life-with-her-lette:
Helen Keller's Story of My Life, with her letters from 1887 to 1901, tells how a deaf-blind child learned language through her teacher Anne Sullivan. The memoir follows Keller from the famous water pump breakthrough to Radcliffe College, with letters showing her growth as a writer and thinker. Her prose is vivid, earnest, and remarkably assured.

The book remains one of the great autobiographies of overcoming, and its letters add intimacy to the narrative. Keller's later career as an activist grew from the education recorded here. Readers of every age still find it inspiring.
24066-dr-johnson-and-his-circle:
John Bailey wrote this study of Samuel Johnson, the great eighteenth-century English writer and maker of the Dictionary, first published in February 1913. Bailey treats Johnson not only as an author but as a national figure, a man whose talk, opinions, and friendships shaped literary London. James Boswell, Johnson's famous biographer, gets a full chapter of his own.

Chapters cover Johnson's character, his works, and the friends who gathered round him, from Boswell to the wider circle of writers and talkers. Bailey draws on Boswell's Life and on Johnson's own writings to show why Johnson lasted: blunt sense, moral seriousness, and talk that people still quote. The book suits readers meeting Johnson for the first time.
24147-tecumseh-a-chronicle-of-the-last-g:
Ethel T. Raymond wrote this short history of Tecumseh as volume seventeen of the Chronicles of Canada, published in Toronto in 1915. Tecumseh sprang from the Shawnees, an Algonquian people whose name marks them as Southerners, and he joined the British in the War of 1812. Chapters follow his boyhood, his rise as orator and leader, the Prophet, Tippecanoe, and fighting on American soil.

Later chapters cover service under the British flag, the Battle of Lake Erie, and Tecumseh's last fight, in which he gave his life. Raymond sets him beside Pontiac and Brant, all three fighting, as she puts it, for their people's lost cause. Readers get a clear, brief life of a leader still honored in Canada.
24221-the-untouchable:
Stephen A. Kallis Jr. wrote this science fiction story for Analog in December 1960, with pictures by Douglas. A man named Max enters the office of General George Garvers after long delays at security checkpoints, finding the general isolated behind his guards. Garvers admits he was vague on purpose: the matter is vital, it touches security, and it needs technical help from a friend.

The tale's hook is stated up front. It can be seen and watched, but never touched. Nothing frustrates more when you need, most violently, to lay hands on it for just one second. Readers get a tense story of a guarded object, a general's secret, and a touch denied.
24336-little-people:
Henry Mayer drew the pictures and T. W. H. Crosland wrote the verses for this alphabet book for children, published in London by Grant Richards in 1901 as number eleven of the Dumpy Books for Children. Each letter brings a people of the world, from Arab, Boer, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, and German. Hungarian, Indian, Japanese, Kaffir, and Laplander follow. Mexican, Neapolitan, Odalisque, Persian, and Quakeress come next. Russian, Scotch, Tyrolean, United States, Valencian, Welshman, and Zany close the alphabet.

The Arab verse shows a man upset, with pretty shield and spear, two pistols in his sash, and flashing eyes. The book belongs to a series of small cloth volumes for children, beside Little Black Sambo and A Cat Book. Readers get a period alphabet of peoples, bright in pictures and plainly of its time.
24426-iole:
Robert W. Chambers published this romantic fantasy in New York in 1905, with illustrations throughout. A group of young New York men, among them Wayne, Lethbridge, and Harrow, cross paths with a poet. They also meet Cybele, a beautiful and elusive young woman whose presence bends ordinary life toward dream and wonder.

Much of the novel moves between city scenes, such as tea at Sherry's restaurant, and passages of heightened romance. Wayne falls deeply in love as the story turns visionary. Chambers blends light social comedy with a fairy-tale mood. Readers who enjoy his strange tales will find the same mix of charm, mystery, and yearning here.
2446-an-enemy-of-the-people:
Henrik Ibsen's Enemy of the People pits Dr. Stockmann against his whole town when he discovers the public baths are poisoned. The doctor's brother, the mayor, and the town's press turn on him as he insists on telling the truth, and Stockmann learns that a majority can be wrong. Ibsen's five-act play is a fierce study of democracy and cowardice.

The drama's famous line, that the strongest man is he who stands most alone, closes a play of great moral force. Its relevance to public health and politics has only grown. Readers of Ibsen will find a stirring, angry masterpiece.
24600-is-slavery-sanctioned-by-the-bible:
This pamphlet, number 45 in its series, asks whether slavery is sanctioned by the Bible. Its author opens by calling slavery the great national question of the day, argued at firesides, in factories, in rail cars and steamboats, and in state legislatures and Congress. The pamphlet takes up the Scriptural case directly.

It examines the texts cited for and against slavery, with notes on Hebrew words and an errata list. Written before the Civil War, it belongs to the fierce pamphlet war over the Bible and bondage. Readers of American religious history will find it a compact example of how Scripture was argued on both sides.
24653-personal-recollections-and-experie:
Milo S. Hascall read this paper before the Illinois Commandery of the Military Order of the Loyal Legion at Chicago on 14 February 1889. He had served as a lieutenant in the United States Army and as a brigadier-general of volunteers. It was printed at Goshen, Indiana, the same year. Its subject is the Battle of Stones River.

Hascall proposes to relate what happened to him, and what he observed during the battle, as a general who fought there. His recollections give the fighting from a commander's view, with the confusion, decisions, and courage of the day. Readers of Civil War history will value this plain, firsthand account.
2489-moby-dick-or-the-whale:
Herman Melville's Moby-Dick follows Captain Ahab's obsessive hunt for the white whale that took his leg, as narrated by Ishmael, a sailor who signs aboard the Pequod. The novel ranges from whaling lore and cetology to philosophy and Shakespearean tragedy, with Ahab's monomania driving the ship toward doom. The whale itself remains vast, white, and unreadable.

The book's reputation grew slowly: dismissed in its time, it now stands as the great American novel. Its chapters on whales, ropes, and crews reward patient readers. Anyone tackling American literature will meet it sooner or later.
2509-the-lani-people:
J. F. Bone sets this science fiction novel on Kardon, a distant world where a young veterinarian named Jac Kennon takes a well paid ranch post that looks too good to be true. The job promises a fine hospital, free quarters, and a five year contract, yet something about the setup troubles him from the first day.

Kennon slowly learns that the ranch stock he was hired to tend are thinking beings kept in servitude, not mere beasts. His choice to defend them puts his career, his safety, and his conscience on the line. The novel pairs planet hopping adventure with a plain question about what makes a person, and who gets to decide.
25102-nobody-s-boy-sans-famille:
Hector Malot's Nobody's Boy, translated by Florence Crewe-Jones in 1916, is the classic French story of Remi, a foundling sold to a travelling musician. Known in French as Sans Famille, it follows Remi and his master Vitalis, with their performing animals, along the roads of nineteenth-century France.

Remi faces hunger, arrest, homelessness, and the death of friends, yet keeps faith with the people who shelter him. His long search for his real mother ends in reunion, after hardship has taught him loyalty, work, and kindness. The novel remains a beloved children's classic, admired for its warmth and its unsentimental view of poverty.
25158-stubble:
George Looms's Stubble, published by Doubleday, Page in 1922, is a rural novel in three parts: Mary Louise, Myrtle, and Bloomfield. It opens on a cold April rain, as Mary Louise gathers her sewing and watches a timid visitor at the front gate.

Later scenes follow Joe and Zeke at a cabin by night, where fear, humor, and country speech mix. Looms writes about farm and small-town people with close attention to weather, work, and talk. The novel offers a portrait of rural life in the early twentieth century, told in a plain and sympathetic voice.
25299-wood-magic-a-fable:
Richard Jefferies's Wood Magic, first published in 1881 and reissued by Longmans in 1907, is a nature fable for children. A boy named Bevis, called Sir Bevis, learns to hear and understand the birds and beasts around his home, from weasels and squirrels to brook-folk and courtiers.

Chapters follow an emperor owl called Choo Hoo, a council of creatures, and traitors among them, while pigeon captains boast of their flocks. One claims three hundred and twenty-two pigeons, another a thousand, each swearing his voice is sweetest. Jefferies fills the tale with close observation of wild life, wrapped in fantasy.
25309-child-s-story-of-the-bible:
Mary A. Lathbury's Child's Story of the Bible, published in Boston in 1898 with an introduction by Bishop John H. Vincent, retells Scripture for mothers to read at home. Lathbury calls the home the first and greatest school, and mothers its earliest teachers.

She keeps the pure outlines of the sacred record and uses exact words for quoted speech, avoiding fanciful additions. Stories run from Moses and Zipporah at the well to Daniel and his friends in Babylon, who refuse the king's meat and wine because it was offered to idols. Colored plates and engravings illustrate the tales.
25339-atheism-among-the-people:
Alphonse de Lamartine's Atheism Among the People, translated in Boston in 1850, began as an essay in his monthly journal for the French people. Editors Edward E. Hale and Francis Le Baron thought its interest was not local, and offered it to American readers.

Lamartine asks why he is a republican and a partisan of equitable democracy, loving a people among whom he was not born. He traces the Revolution's fever, the Directory's moderate reaction, and Bonaparte's restoration of worship, under which priests officiated freely. The essay defends faith as a people's need, not a priestly trick.
25592-life-and-adventures-of-mr-pig-and-:
This nursery tale in verse follows Mr. Pig and Miss Crane through a comic education, embellished with designs. Young Master Pig first appears on his mother's knee, no longer sucking with patience, now cutting both his tusks.

Next he rides tied in a go cart, trotting beside old granny, then goes to Master Goat, whose excellent learning cannot make this block say A B C or hic, hac, hoc. An Oxford fop in cravat and Brutus top, hunting, and further scrapes follow, in rhymes meant to amuse small children while mocking grown-up fashions.
25780-the-fire-people:
Ray Cummings, author of The Golden Atom, writes The Fire People, first printed in Argosy All Story Weekly in October and November 1922. Contents open with the coming of the light, an unknown enemy, and the landing of invaders.

A meeting, capture, and Miela follow, with a Mercutian camp, an escape, and futile attacks. Miela's story, a plan to save the world, and a landing on Mercury lead to a captive earth man, a ruler of the light country, and a mountain conclave. The fire planet, a fight at the bayou, revolution, and a new ruler close a pulp science fiction serial.
25805-in-ancient-albemarle:
Catherine Albertson writes In Ancient Albemarle, published by the North Carolina Society Daughters of the Revolution in 1914, with pictures from drawings by Mabel Pugh. An old float bridge across the Perquimans River fronts the book, and Albertson dedicates it to state regent Mary Hilliard Hinton.

Chapters open at Wikacome in Weapomeiok, home of George Durant, then the first Albemarle assembly at Hall's Creek near Nixonton. A verse on the Perquimans River, from Great Swamp depths through marshes and fertile fields, sets a history of early North Carolina settlement, families, and frontier government.
25808-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
This index gathers the Project Gutenberg works of Thomas Carlyle, giving contents lists for his books in order, compiled by David Widger in June 2008. Carlyle's History of Friedrich II of Prussia, Frederick the Great, opens the index in twenty-two volumes of books and chapters.

Book one treats birth and parentage in 1712, book two Brandenburg and Hohenzollerns from 928 to 1417, and book three Hohenzollerns in Brandenburg to 1718. Friedrich's apprenticeship, double marriage projects, life at Custrin and Ruppin, and taking the reins in 1740 follow, letting readers navigate Carlyle's vast Prussian history. Widger drew on Gutenberg texts for a single contents guide.
25888-edge-of-the-jungle:
William Beebe, curator of birds and head of the New York Zoological Society's tropical station at Kartabo, British Guiana, gathers essays from the jungle's edge. Printed in 1921, the book follows his earlier Jungle Peace and reprints pieces from the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's Magazine, and House and Garden. All but one, on a tropic garden at Georgetown, deal with the jungle round the station at the meeting of the Cuyuni and Mazaruni rivers.

Beebe dedicates the book to the birds, butterflies, ants, and tree frogs that bore his presence in their jungle antechambers. One passage watches an ant gather sand ball by ball, and sets that small labor against Cheops, the Great Wall, log cabins, and the Panama Canal. For Beebe, the ant's work outshines them all in quiet wonder, and his essays share that sense of awe.
25902-the-history-of-england-from-the-ac:
Thomas Babington Macaulay tells the history of England from the accession of James II, in five volumes here gathered complete. The first volume opens with a grand survey, from Roman Britain and the Saxon conversion through Danish invasions, the Norman Conquest, the Wars of the Roses, and the Tudor age. Macaulay sets out the growth of limited monarchy and its checks on tyranny before he reaches James.

Later volumes follow William's reign in detail: church parties high and low, the Toleration Bill and the Comprehension Bill, oaths of allegiance, the coronation, and war with France. Ireland at the Revolution, with civil and military power in Catholic hands, gets full treatment. The history moves with sweep and vigor, and its chapter tables alone map a nation's turn from Stuart rule to a new order.
26448-the-dragon-of-wantley-his-tale:
Owen Wister's comic fairy tale, second edition 1895, tells of Wantley, where Sir Godfrey loses his temper and his daughter Elaine must manage the consequences. The dragon lurks in his den, the hero makes his first appearance and is locked up at once, and Elaine loses her heart while finding something of the greatest importance. Wister dedicates the book to his ancient playmates in Appian Way, Cambridge.

Verse at the opening praises Thackeray and Ingoldsby, whose merry books exorcised peevish woes, and bids farewell to realism as a specious pose. The plot turns on detection. Her father's cellar has been broken into, Mistletoe was chained to a rock for a week with no dragon near, and wine from the cellar reaches unexpected hands. A great white Christmas at Wantley closes the tale.
26496-rembrandt-s-etching-technique-an-e:
Peter Morse, associate curator of graphic arts at the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology, studies one Rembrandt print in this paper, number 61 of the museum's contributions. Landscape with a hay barn and a flock of sheep, signed and dated 1650, measures 83 by 174 millimeters and shows a Dutch scene along the Onderdijk Road, near St. Anthony's Dike, a short walk from Rembrandt's Amsterdam home. The image mirrors the real view, as prints do.

Morse traces how the eye circles the work. Bright highlights on trees and barn draw it first, then a woman outlined against the sky at left, sheep and shepherd below, and the creek bank. It moves on to the distant town, cows at right, and at last a horse rolling in the grass. Drypoint proves vital, with a dulled vertical needle for light shading and an angled sharp needle raising burr for rich blacks.
2665-the-professor-at-the-breakfast-tabl:
Oliver Wendell Holmes revised this first series of Breakfast Table papers a quarter century after writing them, and his preface warns that statements true then are not necessarily true now. Even the trotting horse record, he notes, has moved on since the fastest time was set down.

The Professor holds forth on science, medicine, books, and Boston life, while the boarders listen, argue, and interrupt. Holmes writes with wit, learning, and a doctor's eye. The book remains a classic of American table talk, and a record of how much a generation can change.
2666-the-poet-at-the-breakfast-table:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote this third series of Breakfast Table conversations, with a slight dramatic background setting off a few talkers and writers. The machinery resembles the two earlier series, and old acquaintances return among the silent supernumeraries.

The Poet discourses on life, science, books, and Boston society, with Holmes's wit and learning in full play. Holmes reread these papers with care, and his preface owns their familiar charm. The book delights as table talk raised to literature, and as a portrait of a brilliant circle. Boston society, science, and poetry all pass across the table.
26789-emelian-the-fool-a-tale:
George Borrow translated this Russian tale for private circulation at London in 1913, from a Thomas J. Wise pamphlet. It opens in a village where a mujik, or yeoman, has three sons, two clever and the third a fool called Emelian. Dying, the father leaves house and cattle in equal portions and a hundred roubles to each son.

Emelian's brothers take his hundred roubles to the city for traffic, promising a red caftan, a red cap, and red boots if trade prospers. Left with his sisters-in-law, Emelian lies on the stove through a terrible winter frost until threatened with losing his red clothes, then goes for water. Hewing a hole in the river ice, he catches a very large pike, which begs to be returned and promises to do whatsoever he wishes. Soon Emelian rides a horseless sledge to the forest at the pike's behest.
2688-the-clue-of-the-twisted-candle:
Edgar Wallace opens this thriller at Three Bridges, where a derailment holds up the train from Victoria to Lewes. John Lexman catches a late connection to Beston Tracey, only to find the village wagonette, his sole link to the outside world, already gone.

A twisted candle, a murder, and a web of blackmail follow, with Wallace's brisk plotting driving every chapter. The novel mixes detective work with melodrama, in the author's popular style. Readers get a fast, foggy mystery, where every clue points two ways at once. Wallace keeps the twists coming until the final chapter.
26944-the-magic-soap-bubble:
David Cory's children's fantasy follows a boy named Ned into Fairyland, where a tiny Gnomeman, a bluebird, and other small folk draw him into one odd errand after another. It belongs to Cory's Little Journeys to Happyland series, alongside tales such as The Cruise of the Noah's Ark.

Ned chases a lost magic ring, meets a king, earns gold for a feat with a well, and rides off on a donkey after a feast. The verses and short scenes are built for reading aloud, with simple jokes, bright pictures in words, and a new wonder waiting in each chapter.
26977-the-old-tobacco-shop-a-true-accoun:
William Bowen's 1921 children's fantasy tells what befell a little boy in search of adventure, starting at an old tobacco shop. Freddie meets Mr. Punch and a clock tower, two old codgers, a churchwarden, and a sailor named Lemuel Mizzen, each pulling him deeper into a tall tale.

Chapters pile up wonders: a Chinaman's head, celluloid cuffs and a silk hat, Captain Higginson and the Spanish Main. Bowen writes in a storyteller's voice, half fairy tale and half seafaring yarn, and the book keeps its promise of adventure at every turn of the shop door.
27074-the-jealousy-of-le-barbouille-la-j:
The Jealousy of Le Barbouillé, Molière's early farce La Jalousie du Barbouillé, comes from the small farces he sketched in the provinces. Only two such pieces seem genuine and have been printed with his comedies for thirty years. Molière later reused this one in the third act of George Dandin.

Le Barbouillé, husband to Angélique, opens by calling himself the most unfortunate of men, plagued by a wife who gads about and eats good dinners. He consults a doctor, while Valère courts Angélique and her father Gorgibus watches, in a brisk comedy of jealousy and bad advice.
27136-six-days-on-the-hurricane-deck-of-:
Almira Stillwell Cole's Six Days on the Hurricane Deck of a Mule recounts a mule-back journey in Honduras, Central America, in August 1891. Published in 1893 after the writer's death, for distribution among her relatives and friends, it opens with a boarding-school bicycle struggle.

Cole had planned five years in the interior of Honduras, despite storms of reproach from friends, and she traveled by steamer from New York to Colon and by rail to Panama. The book gives a lively woman traveler's view of mule trails, households, and the hurricane deck of a mule.
27491-unthinkable:
Rog Phillips wrote this science-fiction piece around a simple question: if Nature suddenly changed its ways, what we call obvious today might become unthinkable. Phillips recalls his story The Despoilers, in the October 1947 Amazing Stories, which asked whether anything lies absolutely beyond human comprehension.

In that story, humanity gets a thousand years to bear one man able to comprehend the incomprehensible. He notes that the incomprehensible is harder to portray than the merely unknown. We can describe it only by what it is not, and by comparing it with what we can grasp. The piece is a thoughtful prelude to hard science fiction.
27604-a-history-of-the-japanese-people:
Captain F. Brinkley, editor of the Japan Mail, wrote this history of the Japanese people from the earliest times to the end of the Meiji era. Baron Kikuchi, former president of the Imperial University at Kyoto, collaborated on the work. It carries 150 illustrations engraved on wood by Japanese artists, with half-tone plates and maps.

Brinkley dedicates it, by gracious permission, to the late Emperor Meiji Tenno. In a preface dated Tokyo, 1912, he says Japanese students spent three decades collecting the disjointed fragments of their country's history. Foreign historiographers alone could hardly have done the task. His chapters open with the historiographer's art in old Japan and Japanese mythology, then treat the origin of the nation.
27660-a-book-without-a-title:
George Jean Nathan published this 1918 collection under a deliberately blank title, offering seventy-four short pieces on subjects from atheism and love to satire and dramatic criticism. Each entry runs only a page or two, and the table of contents reads like a catalog of passing thoughts.

Nathan, already known as a theater critic, writes in sharp, epigrammatic bursts rather than sustained essays. Readers get quick judgments, jokes, and provocations on art, reputation, and human nature, making the book a snapshot of one critic's mind in the late 1910s. The pieces carry playful headings such as The Atheist, The Gift, and The Judgment of Solomon.
27690-nobody-s-girl-en-famille:
Hector Malot's Nobody's Girl, En Famille in the French original, was translated by Florence Crewe-Jones and published by Cupples and Leon in New York in 1922, illustrated by Thelma Gooch. Its heroine is Perrine, with her donkey Palikare.

Chapters follow Perrine and Palikare through a hard road to travel, storms and fears, and a rescue, to Maraucourt at last and grandfather Vulfran. One sleepless night, the hut on the island, and work in the factory follow, with new shoes, strange housekeeping, and a banquet in the hut. An illustration shows Perrine saying softly, at page 86: Why, it's beautiful. Malot's orphan tale moves from wandering to belonging.
27754-the-flower-basket-a-fairy-tale:
Published in London in 1816 by Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, The Flower Basket is a fairy tale written at a friend's request for the amusement of her children. Its preface defends fairy tales against the fashion for improving children's books.

The author argues that a child's mind is less led astray by open fancy than by impossibly perfect characters in realistic stories. The tale itself, offered with that apology, belongs to the early nineteenth-century debate over what children should read and what imagination is for. The preface cites a celebrated woman writer's Thoughts on the Education of a Young Princess in support of fairy tales.
2795-bob-son-of-battle:
Alfred Ollivant wrote this tale of sheepdogs and shepherds, opening with the coming of the tailless tyke. The gray dog, a son of Hagar, and Red Wull set rivals in motion, and first blood is drawn in a contest of dogs and men.

A little man, a man's son, a licking or a lie, and a white winter follow, toward the shepherds' trophy where rivals meet. Ollivant writes with rugged feeling about the dales, their dogs, and their pride. The book endures as a classic animal story, fierce, tender, and deeply English.
2798-the-queen-of-the-pirate-isle:
Bret Harte tells this story through an adult recalling a nine-year-old girl named Polly, who crowned herself queen of an imaginary pirate isle. Polly had never been to sea and lived nowhere near an island, yet she ruled her games with complete seriousness. Earlier she had played a beggar child, a severe schoolmistress, and a personal preacher, each role taken up with the same conviction.

The charm lies in how the children's make-believe meets the real world, including a Chinese boy named Wan Lee and a tunnel game that turns frightening. Harte treats childhood invention with respect rather than mockery, letting the games reveal courage, loyalty, and fear. It remains a warm portrait of how children build whole worlds from almost nothing.
28056-music-and-some-highly-musical-peop:
James M. Trotter published Music and Some Highly Musical People in 1878, in a 1968 reprint prepared from the original, with portraits and an appendix of music composed by colored men. Trotter, born into slavery in Mississippi, escaped with his mother by the Underground Railroad, taught in Cincinnati, and fought in the Civil War.

The book opens with chapters on music itself, the music of nature, and the history and power of music, then sketches remarkable Black musicians. Described as the first full music study from the United States, it remains a landmark of African American cultural history.
28074-the-buccaneer-a-tale:
Mrs. S. C. Hall published The Buccaneer, a tale, in London with Richard Bentley in 1840, in the Standard Novels series, revised by the author. The novel opens with a ship at sea, her guns of mighty strength and warlike length, deep in draught and broad in deck.

The frontispiece shows the Protector crying for guards as five or six rush in and lay hands upon Robin. The opening chapters move between the vessel and a curious carved chair where the lean, lanky Fleetword kneels. Hall's tale of adventure and intrigue belongs to the popular historical romance of the early Victorian years.
28112-alonzo-and-melissa-or-the-unfeelin:
Alonzo and Melissa, or The Unfeeling Father, first ran as a serial in 1804 in the Political Barometer of Poughkeepsie, written by editor Isaac Mitchell. Pirated copies named Daniel Jackson as author, and the 1851 Boston edition used here follows that name. The tale, printed without chapter breaks, follows two lovers thwarted by a stern father.

Melissa walks alone to a place of grief, Alonzo suffers exile and war, and both must trust Providence through affliction. The preface promises a story friendly to religion and virtue, with no indecent scenes. The book remains one of America's earliest popular novels, loved by generations of readers.
28234-lizbeth-of-the-dale:
Marian Keith wrote 'Lizbeth of the Dale, copyright 1910, as a novel of a Canadian girl growing up among eight Gordons. Miss Gordon, foster-mother to eight nephews and nieces, darns eight pairs of stockings on a porch while watching Jamie, the yard, and a girl in a blue gown coming up the lane. The gay Gordons fill the first chapter.

Later chapters follow Lizbeth through schooldays, chivalry, a budding actress, a fairy godmother, and society, from beauty to darkness to sunrise. Keith, author of Treasure Valley and Duncan Polite, writes with warmth and humour. The novel offers a gentle coming-of-age tale in rural Canada.
28327-continuous-vaudeville:
Will M. Cressy wrote Continuous Vaudeville in 1914 as a book of backstage sketches and jokes from the variety stage. Cressy, with pictures by Hal Merritt, covers the old stage door tender, one-night-stand orchestras, Tommie Ryan's horse, and the troubles of laugh getters. His pieces run from union labour to a night in Bohemia.

Other sketches treat hotel whys, playing English music halls, and joining the suffragettes, always with a performer's eye for timing. Cressy writes for readers who love the theatre's rough, funny side. The book offers a lively record of vaudeville just before it faded.
28350-lives-of-the-presidents-told-in-wo:
Jean S. Remy's Lives of the Presidents, published in 1900, retells the lives of the American presidents from George Washington through William McKinley using only words of one syllable. Hyphens break longer names into sounded parts, so a young reader can sound out each word alone.

Short lives follow in order: Washington's Virginia boyhood, Jefferson, Jackson, Lincoln, Grant, Garfield, Cleveland, and the rest, each given a few pages with illustrations. The book was meant as a first history reader, giving children the main facts of each presidency in the simplest language the author could manage.
28527-the-story-of-nathan-hale:
September 1776 opens Henry Fisk Carlton's radio play The Story of Nathan Hale, edited by Claire T. Zyve for Teachers College. The first scene takes us to Washington's New York headquarters, in the orderly room, where the famous Revolutionary hero and martyr enters the story.

The cast lists Captain Nathan Hale, Captain William Hull, General Washington, Lieutenant Pond, Simon Carter, and the British provost marshal Cunningham. Like Carlton's Connecticut play, this one is meant to be read aloud around a microphone, with no costumes or scenery. School players bring Hale's spy mission and death to life by voice alone.
28530-kings-in-exile:
Charles G. D. Roberts's Kings in Exile, published by the Macmillan Company in 1910, gathers animal stories whose heroes are wild kings dethroned. Last Bull opens the book: a buffalo listed as Kaiser at the Zoological Park, renamed by two grim old Dacotah sachems who gazed at him for hours. The name fits a race all but vanished, and a tragic bond between bull and watchers.

Other stories follow the King of the Flaming Hoops, the Monarch of Park Barren, the Gray Master, the Sun-Gazer, and the Lord of the Glass House. A lone wolf and a return to the water world close the set. Readers get vivid tales of beasts in park, forest, and sea.
2866-windsor-castle:
William Harrison Ainsworth built Windsor Castle around the castle itself, opening with Shakespeare's lines about Herne the Hunter walking the forest at midnight with ragged horns. The first book follows Anne Boleyn at Henry the Eighth's court. Later books mix history with the legend of the spectral huntsman, who blasts an oak, shakes a chain, and makes cattle yield blood. The castle grounds become a stage for both pageant and haunting.

Ainsworth fills the romance with rides, chases, and uncanny journeys, including a swim beneath the water led by Herne's demon horses. The history is colorful rather than exact, and the ghost story carries much of the excitement. Readers still pick it up for its Tudor color and its famous treatment of the Herne legend.
28688-the-silver-maple:
Marian Keith's The Silver Maple, published by the Westminster Company of Toronto in 1905, opens in the great swamp of the Oro after a storm. Snow mantles wood and plain in silence, broken only by rabbit tracks and a narrow human path. Into the cathedral aisles bursts a little figure in red mittens and a scarlet scarf, singing a rollicking Scottish song.

Seven Canadian winters have bred the boy hardy, yet awe suddenly touches his spirit, and fear visits him for the first time in the woods. Chapters follow a new name, winning his spurs, Cape Canada, a reformation, the avenging of Glencoe, and the end of a feud. Voyageurs, a well-meant plot, and the promised land complete the Canadian tale.
28922-compatible:
Richard R. Smith wrote this short science fiction story about a husband, his wife, and a drastic solution to marriage trouble. George, once Smith's college roommate, calls his life with Helen a living hell, naming her a worry-wart, a hypochondriac, a neurotic, an escapist, and a communist. His friend Ed, the narrator, suggests divorce, but George says Helen would never grant one.

The story's turn comes from the title: what does compatible mean when two people cannot live together, and what price would a man pay for peace? Smith, who had written science fiction since 1949 except for a year in Korea, writes here with dry humor and a chill. Readers get a short, sharp tale of domestic trouble solved by science-fictional means, and left unsettling.
29042-a-tangled-tale:
Lewis Carroll wrote A Tangled Tale, published by Macmillan in 1885, with six pictures by Arthur B. Frost. The tale first ran serially in The Monthly Packet from April 1880. Carroll's plan was to hide one or more mathematical questions in each Knot, like medicine concealed in jam, to amuse and perhaps instruct the magazine's fair readers.

The ten knots run from Excelsior and Eligible Apartments through Mad Mathesis and the Dead Reckoning to Oughts and Crosses, Her Radiancy, and Petty Cash. A frontispiece shows a traveler at six miles an hour, and the dedication praises a pupil tamed by addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Readers get Carroll's mathematical play at its best: stories that are also puzzles, with answers to work out.
29053-raiders-invisible:
D. W. Hall wrote this science fiction tale for Astounding Stories in November 1931, when airships still filled the popular imagination. Lieutenant Christopher Travers flies scout planes from the Blue Fleet dirigible ZX-1, sent ahead to find an enemy fleet at sea. His foes, the Black Fleet, strike without being seen, and Travers must face them on his own.

Travers pilots a small scout high above the ocean, watching toy-like ships and the great dirigible below him. Hall builds the action around fleet maneuvers, scout planes, and a lone pilot hunting an unseen enemy. Readers get a fast pulp adventure about air power, nerve, and a war fought against raiders no one can spot.
29116-cursory-observations-on-the-poems-:
Edmond Malone published these cursory observations on the poems attributed to Thomas Rowley, the supposed fifteenth-century Bristol priest. The Rowley poems, in fact the work of the young Thomas Chatterton, fooled many readers with their medieval dress. Malone examines the poems and argues about their true authorship.

This reprint, with an introduction and notes, also includes Narva and Mored, an African eclogue, and other pieces in the Rowley manner. Malone's case helped settle one of literary history's famous forgeries. Readers get an eighteenth-century detective work of scholarship, showing how spelling, language, and history unmask a brilliant fake.
29445-the-hour-of-battle:
Robert Sheckley wrote this science fiction story about Guardian ships protecting Earth from a foe able to seize a man's mind effortlessly and without warning. Edwardson stands at the port looking at the stars and asks if a hand moved. Morse, watching the Attison Detector for over an hour, blinks and looks again: not a millimeter. Cassel, behind the gunfire panel, agrees.

The slender black hand of the indicator rests on zero, the ship's guns stand ready with black mouths open to the stars, and a steady hum fills the room. The Detector joins all other Detectors in a gigantic network around Earth. Edwardson asks why the enemy does not come. Readers get a tense, ironic tale of a defense waiting for an attack that may already have begun inside men's minds.
29527-the-soul-of-a-people:
H. Fielding's Soul of a People describes the people of Burma as a friend sees them. It was first printed in 1898 and reached a third edition by 1899 from Macmillan in London and New York. Fielding opens by recalling his first years in Burma, so full of excitement that he had little time for thought beyond the day. His dedication answers critics who reproached him for speaking only well of his subjects, forgetting faults and recalling virtues.

The book takes Matthew Arnold's line as its creed: beauty rightly seen is truth rightly seen. Fielding writes of Burmese life with warmth, patience, and close detail. Readers of travel and colonial-era Burma will find a humane, if partial, portrait that values sympathy over censure.
29604-college-teaching-studies-in-method:
Paul Klapper, associate professor of education at the College of the City of New York, edited College Teaching. It is a study of methods of teaching in the college, printed in 1920 by World Book Company. Nicholas Murray Butler, president of Columbia University, wrote its introduction. Klapper's opening claims a treasure of wisdom stored in the colleges, with teachers as keepers of knowledge that frees life and moves it forward.

Its studies treat methods subject by subject, with bibliographies aimed at college teaching, seeking worthwhile contributions to pedagogy. The book aims to make teaching itself a studied art. Students of higher education will find a landmark volume from the age when college teaching first became a field of study.
29710-ireland-as-it-is-and-as-it-would-b:
Sixty-two letters make up this volume, written by the special commissioner of the Birmingham Daily Gazette between March and August 1893. The writer came to Dublin in March and travelled Ireland with a map of the places he visited. His brief was to report Ireland as it stood, and as it might stand under Home Rule, then fiercely debated.

The preface says Irish loyalists met Home Rule not with calm but with dismay, above all in the industrial towns. The letters give street talk, trade fears, and local scenes in Irish dialect, with spelling kept as printed. Read now, they are a loyalist report from the ground in 1893, sharp, partisan, and full of detail no later summary can match.
2981-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
One text now holds the whole Casanova, from Dux to his last years. Machen's translation of the rare 1894 London edition gathers every volume together. The contents run from Casanova at Dux through his Venetian years, childhood, clerical life in Naples, military career, Paris, prison, and the eternal quest across Europe. A transcriber's note warns the memoirs were not written for children.

The complete text lets readers follow Casanova without hunting across separate volumes, from his first adventures to his last years at Dux. A passage about paying a priest monthly at a tavern shows the memoir's blend of piety, fraud, and humor. The volume stands as the fullest English Casanova, long, candid, and endlessly digressive.
29978-shelley-godwin-and-their-circle:
H. N. Brailsford wrote Shelley, Godwin and Their Circle for the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge, number 77. Oxford University Press first published it in 1913, and reprinted it in 1919, 1925, 1927, 1930, 1936, and 1942. Brailsford opens with a fine frame: he traces the French Revolution's history in England from a sermon at the start to a poem at the end.

Between Dr. Richard Price's discourse on the love of our country, given in the excitement after the fall of the Bastille, and Shelley's Hellas stretch thirty-two years. Thomas Paine, William Godwin and the revolution, and Political Justice follow. Godwin and the reaction, Godwin and Shelley, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Shelley himself close the book. Brailsford traces a hope from dawn through clouding to an unearthly sunset.
30132-the-canon-of-the-bible:
Samuel Davidson, doctor of divinity of Halle and doctor of laws, traces how the Bible's books were chosen, ordered, and held across the churches. Peter Eckler published the New York volume in 1877, from the third revised and enlarged edition. Davidson had resolved to print entire a work first written late in 1875 for the new Encyclopaedia Britannica. That version, he says, had been abridged and cut against his wishes.

Chapters follow the Old Testament canon from beginning to close, the Samaritan and Alexandrian canons, and the number and order of separate books. Later chapters treat the New Testament canon in the first three centuries, the canon from the fourth century to the Reformation, and the canon in church confessions. A closing chapter, from Semler to the present, reflects on readjustment of the canon itself.
30160-christ-christianity-and-the-bible:
I. M. Haldeman, pastor of the First Baptist Church in New York City, defends the Christian faith in three linked essays on Christ, Christianity, and the Bible. His opening piece argues that if Christ is not God, he is not good, quoting the gospel question about who can be called good but God. From there he paints Christ as full of compassion, seeing people one by one, sharing weddings, tables, sickness, and grief without office hours or guards.

Charles C. Cook published the New York volume in 1912, and Haldeman draws on his earlier books on Bible study, the coming of Christ, and the signs of the times. The tone is warm, earnest, and pastoral, aimed at readers who want a plain statement of faith rather than a technical debate. Its strength lies in vivid scenes of a life spent doing good, told with conviction.
30310-special-report-on-diseases-of-catt:
The United States Department of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Industry under Chief J. R. Mohler, issues a special report on diseases of cattle in a revised edition from the Government Printing Office in 1923. Thirteen doctors of veterinary science share authorship, from Atkinson, Dickson, and Eichhorn through Hickman, Law, and Lowe to Marsh, Mohler, Murray, Pearson, Ransom, Trumbower, and Woodward. The volume stands as a federal reference work for a farming nation that depended on healthy herds.

Tables were reshaped to fit the text file, footnotes moved to the ends of sections, and spelling inconsistencies resolved where the authors' intent seemed clear, as the transcriber notes. Unresolved errors carry a mark, and chemical formulas and ligatures follow plain-text conventions. Readers will find a thorough, practical government manual, written by bureau specialists for veterinarians, farmers, and stockmen.
30334-ultima-thule:
Dallas McCord Reynolds follows a young man chasing an interplanetary post, in Analog, March 1961, with pictures by John Schoenherr. Ronny Bronston has reached a personal interview, a step beyond the usual path. On that path, an application goes onto an endless tape, feeds into a machine, and returns moments later as a neatly printed rejection. Nine out of ten men his age apply each year, almost all are rejected, and practically nobody ever wins a place.

Bronston, under no illusions, stands at easy attention inside the placement office of the Commissariat of Interplanetary Affairs, Department of Personnel. The officer, going through a sheaf of papers, looks up and calls him by his full name, Ronald Bronston, inviting him to sit. Ronny tries to look alert, earnest, and ambitious without seeming too ambitious, fearless and devoted to the task ahead. The story turns on an ambition meeting its first door.
30371-service-with-a-smile:
Charles L. Fontenay writes a science fiction story about Herbert, a gentleman robot who serves Alice with perfect manners and a permanent porcelain smile. He bows with a muted clank, presents a martini on a silver tray he made himself, and stands holding it while Alice sips and grimaces.

Herbert found silver for the tray and sand for the glass, mixed chemicals from the air for gin and vermouth, and froze ice to chill the drink. Alice praises the martini yet wishes he could drop the everlasting smile, and Herbert replies politely that he cannot alter himself in any way. The tale turns on service, charm, and the limits of a machine built to please.
30372-robert-coverdale-s-struggle:
Horatio Alger, Jr., tells Robert Coverdale's Struggle, published by A. L. Burt in New York. Alger, author of Tom Temple's Career, Tom Thatcher's Fortune, Tom Turner's Legacy, and The Train Boy, opens in a fisherman's cabin. That cabin stands in a New England fishing village on the coast. Robert's aunt asks after his uncle, supposing him over at the tavern as usual, drinking up about all he earns, with little enough left for them.

Robert, a strong boy with a face embrowned by sun and wind, promises he will not follow in his uncle's steps, not for a hundred dollars. His aunt prays God keep him in that resolution, since she does not want her sister's son to go to destruction as her husband is doing. His calico shirt, well-patched trousers, stockings, and cowhide shoes need repairs, but his fortune starts from resolve.
30376-the-snow-image-a-childish-miracle:
Nathaniel Hawthorne tells The Snow-Image, a childish miracle, published in New York by James G. Gregory in 1864, with illustrations by Marcus Waterman. After a long storm, on a cold winter afternoon with the sun shining bright, two children get their mother's leave to run outside. They play in the fresh snow. The elder, a little girl of tender and modest disposition, thought very beautiful, is called Violet.

Her brother is known as Peony, because his broad, round little face is so ruddy that everyone thinks of sunshine and great scarlet flowers. Their father, Mr. Lindsey, an excellent but exceedingly matter-of-fact man, a dealer in hardware, sturdily takes the common-sense view of all matters. An illustration shows Violet and Peony putting the finishing touches to the snow girl, and Hawthorne lets a child's wonder test a father's common sense.
30596-general-bramble:
Andre Maurois writes General Bramble, translated by Jules Castier and Ronald Boswell, first published in 1921 and in the Week-End Library in 1931 by John Lane the Bodley Head. Eighteen chapters move from portraits and diplomacy to the Tower of Babel, a business man in the army, and the story of Private Biggs.

Later chapters add an air raid, love and the infant Dundas, a great chef, a prelude to a general's evening, and Private Brommit's conversion. Justice, variations, the cure, the beginning of the end, and a danse macabre follow, with the glory of the garden and a letter from Colonel Parker to Aurelle. General Bramble's return closes the book, in Maurois's witty war portrait.
30689-the-brass-bottle:
F. Anstey first published this comic fantasy in October 1900, and its hero is Horace Ventimore, a young office worker in Westminster. As the book opens Horace sits at his office window in Great Cloister Street, thinking back six weeks to a bright August morning at a small Normandy watering place. A cheap lot soon puts a brass bottle, and the genie Fakrash, into his hands.

From there the comedy grows out of wishes that go wrong in polite, modern London. Chapters with titles like Carte Blanche, A Fool's Paradise, and A Game of Bluff trace Horace's hopes, blunders, and bargains as he tries to use old magic in a new world. Anstey's tale is light, witty, and kind, and it still charms readers who like a genie story told with Edwardian manners.
30740-men-of-the-bible:
D. L. Moody gathered seven Bible sermons in this volume, published by Fleming H. Revell in 1898. Contents are Abraham's Four Surrenders, The Call of Moses, Naaman the Syrian, The Prophet Nehemiah, Herod and John the Baptist, The Man Born Blind and Joseph of Arimathea, and The Penitent Thief. Each piece takes one life or scene and draws a plain moral lesson from it.

The opening sermon says many people fear the will of God, yet surrendering one's own will is among the sweetest lessons in the school of Christ. Abraham, Moody says, learned that lesson in four surrenders, and he could not choose for himself as well as God could choose for him. The book is direct revival preaching, warm in tone and built for listeners who wanted scripture made plain and personal.
30816-a-world-by-the-tale:
Seaton McKettrig wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in October 1963, about a writer the world loves to hate. Its opening lines present him as the best-hated author on Earth, pampered and petted because of a crime against humanity. The tale then cuts to New York, where Professor John Hamish McLeod waits in his apartment for a visit that is not quite what it seems.

Three minutes after a ship called the Galactic leaves McLeod's rooms, eight men from the Union Bureau of Investigation push in, led by a man who gets the professor's name wrong. McLeod corrects him with care, and the questions begin. The story plays with fame, blame, and the power of a tale itself, asking how a writer can be both a criminal and a pet of the very world he wronged.
30882-god-and-mr-wells-a-critical-examin:
William Archer wrote this 1917 critical examination of H. G. Wells's God the Invisible King, published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York. Archer opens by calling Wells the great adventurer of latter-day literature. Wells had already sent explorers to the moon, brought Martians to Earth, snared an angel, fished up a mermaid, and ridden a time machine into the future. Now, Archer says, Wells had set out to discover God.

Seven chapters weigh that quest: a god who grew, new myths for old, the Apostle's Creed, when a god is not a god, and back to the veiled being. Archer tests Wells's ideas with wit and close reading, asking whether a growing, personal god can hold together. Readers of Wells, or of early twentieth-century religious debate, will find a sharp and readable critique.
31062-the-cartels-jungle:
Irving E. Cox, Jr., wrote this short science fiction novel, printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1955. Its tagline sets a world of greedy Dynasts, each contending for the right to pillage and enslave, where one man's valor becomes a shining shield. Its epigraph, from Machiavelli's Discorsi of 1531, says he who overcomes an enemy by fraud is as much to be praised as he who does so by force.

The story opens with a captain walking down a ramp carrying a lightweight bag.
