To a discerning eye, the bag means only one thing: Max Hunter has quit the service, since a spaceman on leave never takes personal belongings from his ship. An editorial note calls the novel startlingly original, granting the usual utopian premise of a world of maladjustment, cruelty, and crime, only to approach utopia by a highway of the mind. It is a thoughtful space adventure.
31111-across-asia-on-a-bicycle:
Thomas Gaskell Allen Jr. and William Lewis Sachtleben, two American students, rode bicycles from Constantinople to Peking and their 1894 book tells the trip in six chapters. They cross the Bosphorus, climb Mount Ararat, push through Persia to Samarkand and on to Kuldja, and cross the Gobi Desert. They pass the Great Wall and end with an interview with the prime minister of China.

Along the way they deal with suspicious villagers, Kurdish parties, guards, snowfields, caravans, and the sheer labor of wheeling loaded machines over rough ground. The book mixes travel adventure with sharp sketches of the peoples and places met en route, and it remains a vivid record of long-distance cycling before good roads or motor travel.
31180-ellen-middleton-a-tale:
Lady Georgiana Fullerton's tale Ellen Middleton, in the Tauchnitz copyright edition of 1846, opens on October 15 in an unnamed cathedral town. There, a respected clergyman and canon walks to evening service through declining sunlight. An epigraph from Fuller's Worthies, about a bird that finds by reflection it has killed one like itself and pines away, sets the book's theme of guilt and remorse.

Fullerton, a Catholic convert writing for a wide Victorian audience, builds her story around conscience, confession, and the hope of mercy, with cathedral ritual and clerical life as its backdrop. The tale remains a moving example of the Victorian novel of moral reckoning.
31263-bark-kathleen-sunk-by-a-whale:
Captain Thomas H. Jenkins's 1902 account, published in New Bedford, tells how the bark Kathleen sailed from that port on October 22, 1901, for a whaling voyage in the South Atlantic. An infuriated bull whale rammed and sank her. A New York Journal report quoted in the book calls it the most thrilling episode ever known in the American whale fisheries, stranger than any tale in Frank T. Bullen's Cruise of the Cachalot.

The crew list names officers, boatsteerers, cooper, steward, cook, seamen, and green hands, with Mrs. Jenkins aboard beside her husband, and the volume adds accounts of two like disasters, the losses of the Ann Alexander and the Essex. The book is a firsthand whaling disaster narrative, plain and terrifying.
31510-mary-magdalen-a-chronicle:
Edgar Saltus's Mary Magdalen, a chronicle, was published by Brentano's of New York in 1919, the year given as MCMXIX, with copyright in 1891 by Saltus himself. Saltus, author of Historia Amoris, The Pomps of Satan, Imperial Purple, and The Anatomy of Negation, retells the story of Mary Magdalen. His chapters follow her life as a continuous narrative. The chronicle form lets him move from scene to scene without the machinery of a conventional novel.

Saltus writes in the rich, decadent prose of his period, treating a biblical figure as a subject for psychological portraiture. Readers will find a late Victorian retelling, more interested in character and atmosphere than in doctrine. The book stands as an example of how fin-de-siècle writers reimagined sacred stories in literary form.
31558-a-monograph-on-the-sub-class-cirri:
Charles Darwin's A Monograph on the Sub-Class Cirripedia, with figures of all the species, is volume one, on the Lepadidae, or pedunculated cirripedes. It was published in London for the Ray Society in 1851, the year given as MDCCCLI. Darwin, fellow of the Royal Society and the Geological Society, wrote the monograph before his work on species made him famous, and it shows the same patient, detailed method. The Ray Society, instituted in 1844, issued it as a work of record.

The volume describes stalked barnacles species by species, with figures to aid identification. Darwin's preface acknowledges great obligations to collectors and correspondents who supplied specimens. For readers of natural history, the monograph is a landmark of systematic zoology, and a reminder that Darwin was first a working naturalist, happiest with specimens in hand.
31601-an-empty-bottle:
Mari Wolf's science-fiction story An Empty Bottle, from 1952, opens with Hugh McCann taking the last photographic plates out of the developer in an observation room. Around the table, men and women listen in silence. McCann turns to old star charts, volume one, number one, maps of space covering systems inside a hundred light years of Sol. He turns them to the composite map of the stars as seen from Earth, and the party begins to check what has changed.

The story's headnote sets the stakes: its people longed for home, for the planet they had known, but even the stars had changed. Wolf's tale follows a crew comparing charts to the sky, hunting for a home that may no longer be where they left it. Readers will find a quiet, haunting story of displacement, told through astronomy rather than action.
31650-nathan-hale:
Jean Christie Root's Nathan Hale, in the True Stories of Great Americans series, was published by the World Syndicate Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York. It carries copyright in 1915 by the Macmillan Company. Set up and electrotyped in May 1915, it was reprinted in August 1925 and March 1929. Root tells the life of Hale, the Connecticut schoolteacher turned spy, hanged by the British in 1776, whose last words became an American legend.

The book, written for young readers, follows Hale from schoolroom to army to the fatal mission behind British lines. Root's narrative is plain and patriotic, as the series required, but it keeps the facts of Hale's short life in view. Readers seeking a first life of Hale will find a clear, accessible biography, with the hero's courage as its theme.
31688-what-shall-i-be-a-chat-with-young-:
The Reverend Francis Cassilly, S.J., published What Shall I Be? as a chat with young people at New York with the America Press in 1914. Its epigraph from Matthew quotes Christ's words to the rich young man about selling what he has and giving to the poor. The book speaks to young readers weighing what life to choose.

Its fifteen chapters move from getting a start and aiming high to the state of perfection and who are invited. Later chapters ask whether Christ wants the reader, what to do when no attraction is felt, and what if a mistake is made. The priesthood, the teacher's calling, and the parents' part all get chapters of their own.
31710-the-hills-and-the-vale:
Richard Jefferies's Hills and the Vale, with an introduction by Edward Thomas, was published at London by Duckworth and Company in 1909. Its contents move from choosing a gun and skating to Marlborough Forest, village churches, and birds of spring. The spring of the year follows, with vignettes from nature, a king of acres, and the story of Swindon.

Later essays take up unequal agriculture, village organization, the idle earth, and life after the county franchise. The Wiltshire labourer, the downs, the sun and the brook, nature and eternity, and the dawn close the book. Jefferies writes the Wiltshire country with a naturalist's eye and a countryman's knowledge.
3174-a-dog-s-tale:
Mark Twain tells this story through a dog's own voice. Her father was a Saint Bernard and her mother a collie, the narrator reports, but she herself is a Presbyterian. That joke comes from her mother, who loved fine large words and liked to see other dogs look surprised and envious at her learning. The words were show, not schooling, picked up by listening in the dining room.

Behind the comedy runs a protest. The dog saves a child, serves her master faithfully, and then loses her puppy to cold experiment. Twain uses the animal's plain telling to accuse human cruelty without preaching. The tale is short, tender, and angry, and it helped carry the case against vivisection to readers who might have ignored a pamphlet.
31752-the-gold-sickle-or-hena-the-virgin:
Eugene Sue's historical tale, translated from French by Daniel De Leon, opens the series called The Mysteries of the People. Narrated by Joel, chief of the tribe of Karnak, it is set in Gaul at the time of Caesar's invasion and centers on Joel's daughter Hena, virgin of the Isle of Sen.

The chapters move from a Gallic homestead and family stories to war cries, farewells, and the forest of Karnak, tracing how one family lives through conquest. Readers get an early installment of a long saga that links a single household to the wider clash between Gaul and Rome.
31769-uncle-daniel-s-story-of-tom-anders:
John McElroy's 1886 book Uncle Daniel's Story of Tom Anderson and Twenty Great Battles is presented as a truthful picture, in story, based on events of the late war. It is dedicated to Union soldiers and their children. It opens in the dark days of 1861, with a father who gave his children to the country and volunteers raised in southern Indiana.

The narrative centers on Daniel Lyon of Allentown, Indiana, a town of 10,000 on the Wabash River. He has seven grown sons, all well educated, fond of field sports, and inclined to a military life. Readers get a postwar Union tale that follows one family through twenty great battles of the Civil War.
31832-the-travellers-a-tale-designed-for:
The Travellers, a tale designed for young people by the author of Redwood, was published in New York in 1825 by E. Bliss and E. White. Its epigraph, from Childe Harold, invites the reader to climb slowly the many-winding way and linger to survey new loveliness from loftier rocks.

The tale itself follows young travelers through scenes meant to instruct as well as entertain, in the moral and descriptive manner of early American children's books. Readers get an early nineteenth-century story for youth, quaint in spelling and manners, that treats travel as a school for character.
32071-the-banished-a-swabian-historical-:
The Banished, a Swabian historical tale edited by James Morier, author of Hajji Baba, appeared in London in 1839 from Henry Colburn. This file holds volume one of three volumes. Morier's editor's notice frames the book modestly. He compares himself to a man at the door of an exhibition of a historical picture, assuring visitors that the show is worth their notice and time.

Morier claims no merit beyond that of trumpeter to the show, yet he states in honesty that what he was called upon to read, he sincerely approves. Readers get a nineteenth-century historical romance in an editor's presentation, with Swabia as its setting and a banished figure at its centre, as the title promises. The volume invites reading as a panorama of an earlier age.
32111-diary-of-battery-a-first-regiment-:
Theodore Reichardt's diary of Battery A, First Regiment, Rhode Island Light Artillery, was written in the field and published at Providence in 1865. Reichardt addressed his preface to his comrades of the battery, keeping a promise made to them. The days of trial, hardship, and suffering were past, he wrote. It remained only to memorise the period when they had battled for the sacred cause of the Union. The book preserves that period in diary form.

Its contents run through the diary years 1861, 1862, 1863, and 1864, followed by a roster of Battery A and closing remarks. Readers therefore get both a day-by-day artilleryman's record and a roll of the men who served. The diary's value lies in its closeness to events. It was written where the battery fought, not reconstructed long afterwards. It speaks in the voice of a gunner to his fellow gunners.
32285-adventures-of-bindle:
Herbert Jenkins's comic novel centres on Joseph Bindle, a London furniture remover with a sharp tongue and a habit of getting into scrapes. In this volume he helps Mr. Hearty publicise a new shop, sees Lady Knob-Kerrick's drawing room turned into lodgings for soldiers without her knowledge, and copes when Mrs. Bindle takes in a lodger. He also works as a porter at Fulham Square Mansions and lets one flat to two people at once.

Old faces return, including Ginger, Wilkes, Huggles, Dick Little, and Mr. and Mrs. Hearty, alongside new figures. Bindle further tries to block the Reverend Andrew MacFie's courtship of his niece, Millie Hearty. The humour comes from talk, mix-ups, and Bindle's cool nerve when each plan starts to unravel.
32491-the-wild-swans-at-coole:
W. B. Yeats's Wild Swans at Coole, published in New York in March 1919 with copyrights in 1917, 1918, and 1919, gathers poems of middle age, war, and Ireland. The title poem opens the book, followed by In Memory of Major Robert Gregory, An Irish Airman Foresees His Death, Men Improve with the Years, and The Collar-Bone of a Hare. Under the Round Tower, Solomon to Sheba, The Living Beauty, and songs to young beauty and a young girl follow.

Later poems include The Scholars, Tom O'Roughley, The Sad Shepherd, Lines Written in Dejection, The Dawn, On Woman, and The Fisherman, with The Hawk, Memory, The People, and His Phoenix. A Thought from Propertius, Broken Dreams, A Deep-Sworn Vow, and Presences close the first part of the contents. Yeats writes with clarity and music about love, loss, politics, and the passing of time.
32532-king-cole:
John Masefield's King Cole, published in New York in 1921 with drawings by Judith Masefield, retells the old king as a wandering friend of man. After a good reign and a beloved death, Cole chooses at the judging place to walk the earth, helping distressed folk by the power of spirit within him.

In ragged grey, with glittering eyes and a wooden flute, he pipes music that feeds the starved, warms the cold, and gives courage to the beaten. The poem then follows a rain-soaked circus struggling toward St. Giles's Fair, where Cole's path crosses tired showmen hauling vans and wagons up a hill at Goring.
32626-thomas-carlyle:
Hector C. Macpherson's Thomas Carlyle, in the Famous Scots series, studies a writer critics first found confusing and inexplicable. Macpherson opens with Hegel's remark that a great man condemns the world to explaining him. He notes how opinion swung between calling Carlyle an insane rhapsodist and accusing him of a craze for singularity.

Chapters follow early life, Craigenputtock and literary efforts, mental development, life in London, holiday journeyings, the rectorial address, and the deaths of Mrs. Carlyle and Carlyle himself. Later chapters judge Carlyle as a social and political thinker and as an inspirational force.
32779-above-the-battle:
Romain Rolland gathers wartime essays written above the battle. They were translated by C. K. Ogden and published by the Open Court Publishing Company in 1916. The title renders Au-dessus de la Mêlée. The book opens with Walt Whitman's lines over the carnage, a voice rising above passion to judge the war.

After eighteen months of fighting, Rolland argues that he has resisted the fury of the moment. He stands almost alone among Europe's intellectual leaders in that resistance. Essays weigh deported peasants and children, and the silence from Belgium. They weigh journals such as Die Weissen Blätter, and call on those not bearing arms to live by conscience and prepare for rebuilding.
3284-the-discovery-of-the-source-of-the-:
John Hanning Speke tells how the Nile's source was found in this classic of exploration. Born in 1827, Speke served in the Punjab and left in 1854 to explore Somaliland. He discovered Lake Tanganyika with Burton, and Lake Victoria on his own. With Grant he became the first European to cross equatorial Africa, and he died in 1864.

Speke was thirty-six when his Nile journal appeared, after entering the army in 1844. The book follows the journey to the great lake and the river flowing north from it. Readers get exploration at its hardest: fever, desertion, and doubt, with a geographical prize that settled one of the age's great questions, where the Nile begins.
32924-the-new-mistress-a-tale:
George Manville Fenn follows Hazel Thorne, a new national schoolmistress at Plumton All Saints, on her first morning. Her family, reduced in circumstances, lives in a small cottage with yellow glass and smoking chimneys. Her mother insists that Hazel, though a schoolmistress now, remains a lady, and clings to the title mamma against Hazel's plain mother.

Hazel hurries to the Gothic schoolhouse, its prim lancet windows and new buildings raised on land given by William Forth Burge. The schoolmaster Chute, gnashing his teeth as usual, resents any favour shown to the mistress over the master, and considers her as good as his. The vicar Mr Lambent, the Burges, and a visitor named Geringer move through Hazel's orbit. The tale turns on pride, poverty, and a young woman's struggle to keep her household cheerful.
32998-the-romance-of-the-red-triangle:
Sir Arthur K. Yapp's book tells the story of the Red Triangle. It tells of the service the Y.M.C.A. gave to sailors and soldiers of the British Empire during wartime. The book is dedicated to Y.M.C.A. leaders and workers at home and abroad. It traces how the triangle came to camps and ports. Its huts, canteens, and meeting places offered rest, writing paper, and a touch of home to men far from it. Illustrations show Y.M.C.A. posts in the field.

Yapp stresses work done out of sight and difficulties surmounted, and he leaves most workers unnamed. The book is both history and tribute, recording an organization that tried to meet practical and moral needs together. For readers interested in the home front and the daily life of service, it preserves a side of war that battle histories often miss.
33118-just-around-the-corner-romance-en-:
Fannie Hurst's Just Around the Corner, subtitled Romance en Casserole and published by Harper and Brothers in September 1914, gathers stories of love, money, and city life. Its contents run from Power and Horse-Power and Other People's Shoes, through The Other Cheek and Marked Down, to Breakers Ahead, The Good Provider, Superman, The Paradise Trail, and The Squall. Illustrations catch its moments, including a frontispiece surprise and a hand held light as a leaf.

Hurst, already known for sharp stories of working women and modern marriage, writes with warmth and bite about people trying to make a living and a life in the city. Romance here is cooked en casserole, slow, everyday, and mixed with practical worries. The collection suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century stories of women, work, and the bargains people strike for happiness.
33133-klytia-a-story-of-heidelberg-castl:
George Taylor's Klytia, a story of Heidelberg Castle, opens in spring in the Rhine valley. It was translated from the German by Sutton Fraser Corkran and published in Leipzig in 1883 as volume one of a two-volume Tauchnitz edition. While a cold raw wind and sharp night frost still check early buds elsewhere, the valley between the Bergstrasse and Hardtgebirge has reveled for weeks in timely spring. The Neckar valley shimmers with white and red fruit blossoms and yellow rape fields, as if spring wished to show how an ill-favored season could turn.

That garden frames a story of Heidelberg Castle, its people, and their loves and losses. Taylor writes historical romance with a German's feeling for place, letting castle, river, and blossom carry the mood. The novel suits readers who enjoy a tale set in a famous landscape, where history and feeling meet in spring light.
33137-descriptions-of-three-new-birds-fr:
James P. Chapin's Descriptions of Three New Birds from the Belgian Congo reports new species from the museum's Congo expedition. It was published as article sixteen of volume thirty-four of the Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History on October 20, 1915. The whole large collection secured between 1909 and 1915 under Herbert Lang had arrived safely. It was gathered across the Belgian Congo from Boma in the west to Aba in the northeast, much of it from remote country between Stanley Falls and the Lado Enclave.

Chapin's paper describes three birds new to science, drawn from dense equatorial forests of the Ituri, Nepoko, and Bomokandi. The birds also come from the high-grass and bush country of the Uele district. The descriptions are precise and technical, giving measurements, plumage, and place. For ornithologists, the paper remains a primary source, marking three additions to the Congo's known birds from a expedition.
33257-under-the-mendips-a-tale:
Emma Marshall's tale, published in London in 1892 in a sixth thousand printing, is set under the Mendips, in a world of country houses and city springs. Its chapters move from Fair Acres and the city of deep springs to the palace, the lady of Barley Wood, and Sunday at Fair Acres. Marshall, author of In Colston's Days, writes of family life, faith, and the quiet trials that test character.

The story's charm lies in its West Country setting, from heather hills to Clifton's Sion Hill, and in its warm, moral tone. A dark cloud over Fair Acres brings the tale's crisis, and its close restores hope through kindness and duty. For readers who enjoy Victorian domestic fiction, Under the Mendips offers a gentle, well-told story.
33261-bindle-some-chapters-in-the-life-o:
Herbert Jenkins's chapters follow Joseph Bindle, a Cockney hero praised as the greatest to enter literature since Dickens's Pickwick Papers. Published in London in 1916, the book opens with the Bindles at home, where Bindle remarks on women with the wit that made him famous. Its chapters trace his scrapes, his talk, and his good heart through London life, in a series of comic scenes.

Bindle's charm lies in his plain speech, his humor, and his refusal to be beaten by bosses, wives, or fate. Jenkins writes in a lively, theatrical style. For readers who enjoy Cockney comedy, it is a bright, laughing portrait of a working man.
3327-bulfinch-s-mythology-the-age-of-fab:
Thomas Bulfinch's Age of Fable, revised by Rev E E Hale, remains the classic handbook of Greek and Roman myth for English readers. The contents open with the origin of Greeks and Romans and the Aryan family, then the divinities of these nations and the character of the Romans. The Greek notion of the world follows, with dawn, sun, and moon, and Jupiter and the gods of Olympus.

Foreign gods and Latin names come next: Saturn or Kronos, the Titans, and Juno, Vulcan, Mars, and Phoebus Apollo. Venus, Cupid, Minerva, Mercury, Ceres, and Bacchus join them, with the Muses to close the divine company. Clear stories, plainly told, in the order Bulfinch made standard: myth for first meetings and for returns.
34170-heathen-mythology-illustrated-by-e:
Heathen mythology is gathered here from the most celebrated writers, ancient and modern, on the gods of Greece, Rome, India, Scandinavia, and other lands. Nearly two hundred engravings after designs by M. Baron embellish the work, published in London by Willoughby and Company. A preface notes how hard it is to say anything new on a subject so long pondered.

Yet the subject stays fascinating, the preface says, for each river had its nymph and every wood its god, and a visible power seemed to dwell in nature. The extracts let great writers speak on myth in their own words. The book serves readers who want myth through classic voices and pictures.
34205-some-little-people:
George Kringle's 1881 book Some Little People gathers short tales for young children about small boys and girls. The opening tale follows Lisbeth Lillibun, who lives a hundred miles from London with her brother Dickon, and learns what that distance means.

Kringle writes in a gentle, fireside voice, with simple scenes of home, play, and small mishaps. The book suits reading aloud to little ones, and its charm rests on plain talk and kind humour. Pictures fill the volume, and the tales are short enough for one sitting each. Kringle keeps his sentences short and his scenes plain, so young listeners can follow with ease.
3536-the-enchanted-castle:
Edith Nesbit writes a children's fantasy about three children, Jerry, Jimmy, and Kathleen, who spend a holiday near a great house. Jerry's full name is Gerald. Left to their own devices when illness keeps them from home, the children discover a castle garden where statues seem alive and magic works by odd rules. Nesbit dedicates the tale to Peggy, with a verse about enchantments in Soho.

The magic brings a sleeping princess, a ring that grants wishes in unexpected ways, and a garden that changes with the seasons. Nesbit keeps the children's talk natural and funny, even when wonders pile up. The book suits young readers who enjoy gentle fantasy and the same author's Five Children and It.
3638-the-devil-s-disciple:
George Bernard Shaw sets this play in New Hampshire in 1777, during the American Revolution. On a dark, wintry night, Mrs Dudgeon sits up in her farmhouse kitchen near Websterbridge, a grim woman shaped by barren faith. Her son Dick, called the devil's disciple for his rebellion against her religion, soon faces a choice that tests his scorn for respectability.

When British soldiers arrest the local minister, Dick takes his place, risking hanging for a man he barely respects. Shaw turns the rescue into a debate about faith, courage, and revolution. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw's history plays, where a scoundrel proves braver than the pious and a revolution is judged by its human cost.
3732-wolfville:
Alfred Henry Lewis tells these western tales through an Old Cattleman who has seen Wolfville grow from camp to town. The stories follow Sheriff Mace Bowman, saloon keeper Enright, Doc Peets, Cherokee Hall, and Faro Nell through funerals, feuds, dance halls, and elections, with a joke never far from a gunshot. A foundling baby left in a stagecoach, a washwoman's war, and a Thanksgiving in camp all get their chapter.

Lewis writes in cowboy slang that takes a page to catch, then runs swift and funny. The town feels lived in, with its rival halls, its faro tables, and its code of rough fairness. Readers who enjoy Bret Harte or Mark Twain will find Wolfville a genial cousin, less polished and more rowdy, with a warm heart under the swagger.
3777-tom-swift-and-his-electric-rifle-or:
Victor Appleton arms Tom Swift with a new electric rifle and sends him to Africa in this boys' adventure tale. Tom, Ned, and Mr Damon fly the airship Black Hawk across sea and savanna, hunting elephants for their tusks while a whale attack and a night stampede test the ship. On the elephant trail they mistake hippopotami for their quarry from half a mile up, then press on toward lions, antelope, and the red pygmies.

The party also seeks captive missionaries, and a rogue elephant closes the book with a charge. Appleton keeps the pace brisk and the inventions buzzing, with the rifle's strange power as the chief wonder. Young readers who like travel, hunting, and machines will find Elephant Land a lively stop on Tom's long tour.
3875-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
This complete text gathers all fifteen volumes of the Duke of Saint-Simon's memoirs of Louis the Fourteenth and the Regency, more than two million characters of court history. The contents run from Saint-Simon's birth and musketeer days through the Namur siege, the king's natural children, and his father's death, across wars, marriages, and successions to Dubois, Law, and the Regency. No other witness covers the reign at such length or with such malice and memory.

A middle passage shows Vendome audaciously presenting himself before the Duchesse de Bourgogne at Meudon, while the princess suffers it in silence and watches her chance. Two months later the king, Maintenon, and Bourgogne dine with Monseigneur, and the reckoning arrives. Readers who want Saint-Simon whole will find the fullest portrait of the Sun King's court ever written by one of its own.
4084-the-adventures-of-peregrine-pickle:
Tobias Smollett's novel follows Peregrine Pickle, a young rake whose pride and passion carry him through assemblies, quarrels, and travels. At one assembly, three gentlemen of fortune rival him for Emilia, each begging the honor of a dance.

Emilia excuses herself to each, pleading a slight indisposition that will keep her from the ball, while Peregrine watches and burns. Smollett mixes comedy, satire, and adventure across England and the Continent. Readers who enjoy bawdy, bustling eighteenth-century fiction will find a long, lively tale of a hero who learns little and suffers much.
4226-empress-josephine-an-historical-ske:
Louise Muhlbach wrote this historical sketch of Josephine, first as the Viscountess de Beauharnais and later as the wife and then the divorced empress of Napoleon. Translated from the German by W. Binet, it follows her from girlhood and an unhappy first marriage through the Revolution, prison, and deliverance.

The later books follow the courtship and marriage to Bonaparte, the Italian campaigns, the court at the Tuileries, and the slow break that ended in divorce. Muhlbach blends domestic scenes with great events, so Josephine appears both as a woman caught in political storms and as a central figure of Napoleon's world.
4250-imperial-purple:
Edgar Saltus built this volume of essays around the color purple. Purple was the dye and emblem of Roman imperial power, and the rulers who wore it. Short chapters move from the murder of Caesar to conjectures about Rome. They cover the pursuit of the impossible, Nero, and the house of Flavia. The empress Faustine closes the set.

Saltus writes in a rich, allusive style. He treats each emperor as a study in appetite, cruelty, and splendor. The book suits readers who want Roman history as vivid portraits rather than a straight chronicle. Poison, luxury, and pageantry stay in the foreground throughout.
4495-the-house-on-the-beach-a-realistic-:
George Meredith called this short novel a realistic tale, and it opens with a reflection on great officials who lay down dignities before death. Such men learn, Meredith notes, that eccentric behavior in trifles most exposes them to hostile criticism and jeopardizes popularity. It is their Achilles heel, where mother nature holds them.

The house on the beach becomes the scene for a retired man's second life, with neighbors, vanities, and the sea's indifference. Meredith treats authority in retirement with irony and pity. The tale is compact, observant, and less fanciful than his great novels, but it keeps his wit about human weakness.
4526-born-in-exile:
George Gissing sets this novel in the English Midlands in 1874. It opens at Whitelaw College in Kingsmill, as crowds gather to unveil a statue of Sir Job Whitelaw, a self-made manufacturer and founder of the college. Into that world of civic pride and new learning comes a clever young man of poor means. His brains promise more than his birth or his purse can support, while class, religion, and respectability press on him from every side.

Gissing follows his hero's efforts to rise, to love, and to hold his own beliefs without losing his place in society. The title points to the cost: a man can feel exiled at home when his ideas and his income do not match. Readers get a serious Victorian novel about ambition, conscience, and the quiet cruelty of a society that rewards polish more than talent.
459-the-white-people:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells a strange, quiet tale of a girl at a remote Scots castle in this short novel. The narrator, raised at Muircarrie among few kin, senses from childhood that she differs from other children. Visions and voices from beyond the veil visit her, bringing comfort rather than fear.

Burnett writes in a soft, first-person voice, letting mystery unfold without shock. The white people of the title are the dead, seen as near and kind. The book reads as a tender ghost story, more about love and loss than horror, and about a girl who learns that death may not end care.
4668-siege-of-washington-d-c-written-exp:
F. Colburn Adams, a captain and author of The Story of a Trooper, wrote Siege of Washington, D.C., expressly for little people, published at New York in 1867. His preface reports his publisher's fear that many persons will be offended. Quite a number of great generals, the publisher thinks, will feel their dignity disturbed by liberties his artist has taken with them. Adams calls such publisher views narrow, and insists the work was not written to offend.

It was written, he says, to amuse and instruct little people, and he respects great generals too much to believe they will feel offended. Some little generals may take exception to positions his artist assigned them, and make war on him. Close observers of the war saw those generals making war on writers all along. Readers get a children's Civil War satire, illustrated and good-humoured, about Washington under siege.
4925-the-age-of-fable:
Thomas Bulfinch's Age of Fable tells the stories of the Greek and Roman gods for readers who meet them in poetry and art rather than in worship. Olympus holds no worshippers now, Bulfinch notes, but its divinities live on in literature and taste, too closely tied to fine poetry and art to pass into oblivion.

The volume retells the ancient stories that modern poets, essayists, and orators allude to, so readers can follow those references with pleasure. No author is named in the catalog record, though the work is Bulfinch's classic handbook. Students and general readers get the essential myths in clear, readable prose.
501-the-story-of-doctor-dolittle:
Hugh Lofting tells of Doctor Dolittle, a Puddleby physician who learns animal speech, in this 1920 children's classic. When patients leave and debts grow, Dolittle turns to animal doctoring, with Polynesia the parrot as teacher. A message from Africa sends him, with his beasts, across the sea to cure sick monkeys.

Lofting writes and draws the voyage with gentle humor: a bridge of apes, a lion leader, and a rare pushmi-pullyu. Home again, Dolittle keeps his strange, kind practice. The book endures as a tale of a man who listens to beasts, and of a world where care crosses every species line.
506-the-shuttle:
Frances Hodgson Burnett weaves an Atlantic tale of two sisters and two houses in this novel. Bettina Vanderpoel, a rich American girl, crosses to England to rescue her sister Rosalie from a cruel earl at Stornham. The shuttle of the title shuttles wealth, love, and fate between New York and an old English village.

Burnett writes with rich detail, from Bond Street shops to marsh lanes. A young lord, a plain American, and a village full of watchers shape the plot. The novel charms as a transatlantic romance where a strong sister's will mends what rank and money broke.
523-court-life-in-china-the-capital-its-:
Isaac Taylor Headland, a professor at Peking University, describes late imperial China from inside the court in this study. His wife, physician to the Empress Dowager's kin, opened doors shut for years, letting him sketch the Forbidden City, its ladies, princes, and officials. Reform, the Boxer rising, and new schools frame the tale.

Chapters follow the Empress Dowager as girl, ruler, reactionary, reformer, artist, and woman, then turn to Emperor Kuang Hsu as prisoner and reformer. Headland argues the Dowager was misjudged by the West. The book serves as a rare firsthand portrait of a court on the edge of fall.
5328-writing-for-vaudeville:
Brett Page's Writing for Vaudeville, in the Writer's Library edited by J. Berg Esenwein, asks whether vaudeville writing can be taught, and answers with examples. Nine complete examples of various vaudeville forms by Richard Harding Davis, Aaron Hoffman, Edgar Allan Woolf, Taylor Granville, Louis Weslyn, Arthur Denvir, and James Madison show what experienced writers accomplished.

Page, dramatic editor of the Newspaper Feature Service, offers the book as help for writers with native gift, showing problems, methods, and finished work. Readers interested in early twentieth-century popular theatre will find a practical handbook and a record of an art form that flourished before radio and film.
5437-an-original-belle:
E. P. Roe wrote An Original Belle, published in 1900, as a novel about power, character, and a young woman's place in the world. The preface argues that true power lies less in muscle than in trained intelligence and moral quality, and the story tests that claim through its heroine. Chapters titled A Rude Awakening, A New Acquaintance, and Woman's Chief Right signal its themes.

The heroine faces schemes, surprises, and a siege of suitors, while learning what independence and hope require of her. Roe, a popular novelist of his day, writes plainly and earnestly about courtship and conscience. Readers get a late Victorian romance with a serious interest in how a woman claims her own judgment.
559-greenmantle:
John Buchan sends Richard Hannay on a Great War mission to the East in this spy thriller, sequel to The Thirty-Nine Steps. Hannay, Sandy, and Peter Pienaar must stop a German plot to raise a holy war with a prophet called Greenmantle. Disguised Dutchmen, caravanserais, and garden houses in Constantinople mark the road.

Buchan writes with brisk, boyish vigor, praising the war's strange truths over romance. His preface owns the tale was scribbled in odd moments. The novel endures as a classic of wartime adventure, where a few bold men play for empires with bluff and nerve.
5590-the-greylock-a-fairy-tale:
Georg Ebers's The Greylock opens, once upon a time, in a country more beautiful than all other lands, where the duke's castle lay beside a lake bluer than the deepest indigo. Long ago, Knight Wendelin and his squire George chanced upon this lake, finding only waste fields and bleak rocks around it. Yet shattered columns showed the shores once bore a different aspect.

The fairy tale follows knights, a duke's castle, and a lake whose beauty hides a ruined past. Ebers writes the wonder tale in a storyteller's voice. Readers get a short fantasy of lakes, castles, and vanished splendor, told for listeners who love old tales.
5715-the-campaign-of-chancellorsville:
Theodore Dodge recounts the Civil War campaign of Chancellorsville in a detailed military history dedicated to the Military Historical Society of Massachusetts. Dodge, writing from the society's researches, follows armies, commanders, and movements through one of the war's most studied battles. His account favors maps, numbers, and the sequence of orders over personal anecdote.

Readers who want to understand how Chancellorsville was fought will find careful attention to terrain, timing, and command decisions. The book suits students of the Civil War and readers of battle history, since it explains why plans succeeded or failed on the ground. It remains a solid, old-fashioned staff study of a campaign still debated today.
5716-memoirs-vieux-souvenirs-of-the-prin:
The Prince de Joinville recalls a long life at the center of French history in his Memoirs, translated from the French by Lady Mary Loyd. He opens by noting his birth at Neuilly-sur-Seine, near Paris. He was born on the fourteenth of August, 1818, just after the fall of Napoleon. The narrative then follows courts, navies, and revolutions through the nineteenth century. The memoir moves in clear chapters from childhood onward.

It offers a firsthand view of royal France, naval service, and political upheaval, told by a prince who watched events from inside. The tone is candid and anecdotal rather than grand, with portraits of people met along the way. Historians and general readers alike will value a witness account that mixes personal memory with the public drama of a changing France.
5755-the-fool-errant-being-the-memoirs-o:
The Fool Errant presents itself as the memoirs of Francis Anthony Strelle, a young man adrift in a world of manners, money, and honor. Its exordium reflects that honor is but a garment, money but a walking stick, and fine trappings far more powerful than sober folk admit. Later chapters bring Aurelia and the doctor, as a beautiful lady, only a year the narrator's junior, tries to act as mother to an exile cast upon her hands.

The story follows a picaresque life of folly, charm, and hard lessons, told in elegant, ironic prose. The memoir form lets Strelle confess and excuse himself in the same breath, which is much of the comedy. Lovers of eighteenth-century pastiche and rogue memoirs will enjoy a hero who learns slowly, laughs at himself rarely, and keeps wandering into fresh trouble.
5777-life-s-handicap-being-stories-of-mi:
Rudyard Kipling gathers stories of his own people in Life's Handicap, with a preface set in northern India at a monastery called the Chubara of Dhunni Bhagat. Kipling notes that no one remembered who Dhunni Bhagat had been, only that he had lived his life, mad or saintly, and left a place behind. The stories that follow draw on soldiers, natives, and Anglo-Indians of the Raj years, 1887 to 1889.

Readers meet India through Kipling's sharp, unsentimental tales, where handicap means the limits of birth, rank, and fortune. The collection mixes humor, pathos, and irony, with soldiers' talk carrying much of the truth. Fans of Kipling will find early work of lasting power, while modern readers should note its imperial viewpoint as part of its historical character.
5849-the-philosophy-of-style:
Herbert Spencer examines the force of language in The Philosophy of Style, in two parts on the economy of mental energies. Part one opens with Tristram Shandy wondering at his father's argumentative powers beside his ignorance of formal logic, and Spencer builds from that incongruity toward a principle of economy. Good style, he argues, saves the reader's attention for meaning itself.

This gives a classic Victorian essay on writing, still useful for anyone who wants prose to work harder with fewer words. Spencer's examples favor clarity, order, and the avoidance of needless effort, even when his own sentences grow long. The essay suits writers, students of rhetoric, and readers curious about how style became a subject of science.
5963-mr-bingle:
George Barr McCutcheon introduces Thomas S. Bingle in a modest New York apartment west of Fifth Avenue, not far from Washington Square. A coal fire crackles in the grate as the story opens on the five little Sykeses, an odd relation, and the death of Uncle Joe. Family claims and searches follow.

Later chapters bring the affairs of Amy and Dick, a man called Hinman, thoughts of becoming an angel, trouble upon trouble, and the law's last word. Two Christmas Eves frame the close. McCutcheon mixes humor with sentiment, letting a plain man's household absorb one surprise after another.
5971-jane-cable:
George Barr McCutcheon introduces Jane Cable driving her trap on a bright, clear afternoon in late fall, waiting with growing impatience. A severe little pucker settles on her brow as her eyes turn again and again toward the place she expects someone. The opening gives a smart young woman in a hurry.

The chapters that follow run through the Cables and the Bansemers, a foundling, a crash, and a proposal. Debts, a sea wall tragedy, and a chase in the Philippines ending in a convent fight widen the tale. McCutcheon blends society romance with adventure abroad. Jane's drive proves only the first step in a much longer journey.
6038-the-great-doctrines-of-the-bible:
William Evans gathers his classroom lectures on the great doctrines of the Bible into permanent form at his students' request. The contents run from God, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit through man and salvation, with repentance, faith, regeneration, justification, adoption, sanctification, and prayer.

Later sections treat the church, the scriptures, angels, Satan, and the last things, including the second coming, resurrection, judgment, and the destinies of wicked and righteous. Evans writes from a biblical rather than dogmatic standpoint, primarily for students, but with wider readers in mind. He keeps each doctrine brief, clear, and scriptural.
6142-a-girl-of-the-people:
Meade opens A Girl of the People with girls urging Bet to come along. They insist she won't funk it, and that Joe Wilkins waits round the corner with Sam, Jimmy, and Hester Wright. Hester, they promise, will sing tip-top, a new song from a London music hall.

A dancing newspaper girl teases Bet as a mammy's girl tied to apron strings, and the others join the laugh, while Bet stands stolid and straight, flushing angrily. Meade follows a working girl among London street girls, where peer pressure, song, and loyalty test her. Bet's stand opens the tale.
6218-at-the-sign-of-the-eagle:
At the Sign of the Eagle opens with Sir Duke Lawless asking his wife Molly what she thinks of a big man and a little one talking to Lord Hampstead. The little man seems affected, gauche, and servile, the big one picturesque and superior in a raw way, wishing to be rude but disappointed by Hampstead's politeness.

A dangerous person in a drawing room, yet interesting, Duke admits, and business lies behind it: railways, mines, and Hampstead's nephew going to the States fortune-hunting. Lady Lawless lifts her eyebrows at status for dollars, quoting Hamlet on base uses. Parker mixes society talk with transatlantic dealing.
6352-dora-deane-or-the-east-india-uncle:
Poor little Dora Deane crouches before a scanty fire in a small, low, poorly furnished room high in a crazy old building, warming worn flannel to wrap her sick mother's feet. Tears burst afresh whenever she looks on her pale mother and thinks how soon she will be gone. One small window looks only on roofs and spires of a great city whose dull roar is almost the only sound she has ever known.

Mrs. Mary J. Holmes, author of Tempest and Sunshine and Meadow Brook, writes Dora's story from that garret outward. Country glimpses, a nurse named Leah, and a household where Ella is left alone and begs for something from the kitchen follow. The East India uncle of the subtitle promises rescue and fortune, but the opening earns its feeling first, in cold, hunger, and a daughter's love.
6378-victory-an-island-tale:
Joseph Conrad notes that the last word of this novel was written on May 29, 1914, and that last word was its title, in times of peace. Victory, shining and tragic goal of noble effort, seemed too great and august for a mere novel's head, yet it stayed. The book is an island tale in four parts, with notes to the first edition and an author's note, moving through chapters that the contents list without naming their scenes.

A later scene shows Schomberg meeting Mr. Jones, who proposes a modest bank in a music shed, a dozen candles or so, for clients who bet on ecarte with a fair, baby faced man. Jones fears Martin would take objection badly, and counts on calls for drinks. Conrad writes his island world through such talk, where gambling, menace, and hospitality mix, and a title written in peace turns tragic.
6573-the-boy-ranchers-on-the-trail-or-th:
Willard Baker sends his boy ranchers out on the trail after cattle rustlers who have struck the Diamond X ranch. A round-up opens the tale, then a scratched safe, a broken bottle, and missing steers point to theft on a bold scale. Bud, Nort, and their friends must learn to rope, watch, and ride as real ranch hands.

A watch tower, a signal, a big raid, and a chase through wild country test their nerve at each step. Baker keeps the action clean and the lessons plain: pluck, fair play, and care for the herd. The Boy Ranchers on the Trail is a brisk western for boys, full of dust, danger, and loyal friendship.
6692-the-swiss-family-robinson-told-in-w:
Mary Godolphin retells The Swiss Family Robinson in words of one syllable, for young readers just learning to read. She opens by vowing to be brief. Then she plunges into six days of storm. Masts lie in splints, a leak beats every pump, and the ship feels like a mere hulk. A father tells his four sons to trust God, side by side, as the sea sprays over them.

The family that follows must build, hunt, and keep faith on a strange shore, all in short, plain words. Godolphin's feat is to keep the tale vivid while keeping the language tiny. This version is a charming, useful first step into a great adventure tale.
6743-colonel-carter-of-cartersville:
F. Hopkinson Smith dedicates Colonel Carter of Cartersville to his mother, a delightful storyteller whose early life passed near the colonel's porch. Stories laughed over together with her, he says, remain among his pleasantest memories. The book is dated New York, May 1891, and its contents list the colonel's house, a garden spot seeking the sea, and an old family servant.

Colonel Carter himself, a true Southern gentleman of the old school, holds court with tales, pride, and charm, while his servant Chad dishes the dinner. Smith writes with affection for a vanishing Virginia world. Colonel Carter of Cartersville is a warm, humorous Southern sketch, full of character and talk.
6824-mary-anerley-a-yorkshire-tale:
R. D. Blackmore opens Mary Anerley on a dreary moor, where an unfenced road descends to a rapid river at Seven Corpse Ford. A party of farmers rode home from Middleton on a foggy evening after heavy rain. They laughed at a warning about the water's power and spurred in. Seven of eight, all large farmers who knew land well, never came upon it alive again. Their bodies, cast up on a ridge, gave the ford its dismal name.

Mary Anerley herself, headstrong and headlong, grows from that grim ground into a Yorkshire heroine of love and peril. Blackmore writes with a moorlander's love of place. Mary Anerley is a strong, romantic tale of Yorkshire folk, full of water, wind, and will.
6928-who-wrote-the-bible-a-book-for-the-:
Washington Gladden asks who wrote the Bible, and sets out in compact popular form what scholars then agreed on its literary history. His contents move from a look into the Hebrew Bible and the question of what Moses wrote, through sources of the Pentateuch, early histories, prophecies, and poetical books. Later chapters treat the earlier New Testament writings, the origin of the Gospels, and the canon.

Gladden states plainly that doctrines and claims of supernatural origin are not his main inquiry. He concerns himself chiefly with natural and human agencies behind the books, and he closes by asking how the books were written and how much the Bible is worth. The book aims at intelligent readers with no special training.
6936-robinson-crusoe-in-words-of-one-syl:
Mary Godolphin retells Defoe's Robinson Crusoe for the youngest readers, using words of one syllable throughout. Her preface says the task needs little excuse, since the title explains itself, and the chief work lay in reducing plain language to single beats. Proper names form the main exception, since a boy like Xury cannot be renamed to fit the rule.

Godolphin claims no novelty in the story matter, but holds the scope and build of the book to be quite new. The one syllable books of the day gave only short, unconnected lines, mostly in spelling books. Here the deep interest young minds always find in Crusoe carries a whole tale told in the simplest words.
6982-hawthorne-and-his-circle:
Julian Hawthorne writes of his father Nathaniel Hawthorne and his circle, opening with the inheritance of friendships and his own good fortune. His father stands as the central figure, and Julian asks what his gift cost the giver, recalling a revelation in Colorado and the lights and shadows of memory. The contents value dates, his aunt Lizzie's efforts, his mother's strong box, and the spirit of The Scarlet Letter.

Later notes recall the strain of imaginative composition, his grandmother Hawthorne's death, children's plays and books, and the house on Mall Street. Scarlet fever, a study on the third floor, a haunted mahogany desk with secret drawers, and a flowered writing gown all bring the writer home to life. Julian tells an informal, affectionate memoir.
6985-a-prefect-s-uncle:
Wodehouse's A Prefect's Uncle opens with term beginning at Beckford College, where Marriott hurls his portmanteau onto the senior day room table. William, a mix of butler and bootboy for Leicester's House, comes in with a pail of water from cleaning up. The contents soon introduce an unusual uncle, who makes himself at home, while Pringle makes a sporting offer and Farnie gets into trouble and stays there.

The bishop goes for a ride, the MCC match is played, and the bishop finishes his ride, as poetry meets stump cricket and a disputed authorship stirs the house. Leicester's house team goes into a second edition, Norris takes a short holiday, and the winter term brings the bishop's scoring turn. Wodehouse keeps the school tale bright and brisk.
7088-the-pilgrim-s-progress-in-words-of-:
Mary Godolphin retells Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress in words of one syllable, for adult beginners no less than for children. Her preface notes a large class who begin reading late in life, for whom such a book is peculiarly fit. Some may object that short words can still prove hard, and that longer words might explain better, but Godolphin says she avoided hard and technical terms as far as possible.

Brevity itself, she argues, attracts beginners of all ages, and her method spares pupils the labor of dividing and accenting words. The pilgrim's road, slough, and celestial city thus open to readers who stumble over long words. Like her Robinson Crusoe, the book proves a classic can live in the simplest speech.
7096-the-babylonian-story-of-the-deluge-:
E A Wallis Budge tells the Babylonian story of the deluge as Assyrian tablets from Nineveh record it. Layard excavated the ruins in 1845 to 1847 and again in 1849 to 1851, on the east bank of the Tigris opposite Mosul. At first he placed Nineveh at Nimrud, twenty miles downstream, but Christian, Roman, and Muhammadan tradition left no doubt of the true site, always known to local memory.

The tablets, found with Rassam and Smith, carry a flood tale older than Genesis in its written form, with a hero, a boat, and a deluge sent by gods. Budge sets the discovery in its place, quoting Jonah on the great city with more than sixteen thousand who cannot tell right hand from left. The book gives the tablets a plain English voice.
7177-my-tropic-isle:
E. J. Banfield, author of The Confessions of a Beachcomber, writes of island life off the coast of North Queensland in this book of sketches. Much of it first ran in the North Queensland Register as Rural Homilies. Banfield thanks that paper's editor for giving up his rights so the pieces could be gathered here. He dedicates the book to his wife.

The sketches keep a quiet, watchful pace, noting weather, work, and the small events of a remote home rather than chasing grand adventure. Banfield treats the island as a place to live in, not a scene to exploit, and his prose favours plain detail over show. Readers get a slow portrait of tropic days far from city noise.
7294-battle-studies-ancient-and-modern-b:
Colonel Ardant du Picq's Battle Studies, translated from the eighth French edition by Colonel John N. Greely and Major Robert C. Cotton, opens with a letter from Marshal Foch praising du Picq as the exponent of moral force. Foch's note to Major General Greely, dated at Malsherbe in October 1920, frames the book as a soldier's study of what truly decides battle.

Du Picq argues that men, fear, cohesion, and will matter more than weapons alone, drawing on ancient and modern fighting alike. The American translators bring his French classic to English readers with a soldier's care for exact terms. The book remains a founding text of combat psychology and leadership under fire.
7357-j-cole:
Emma Gellibrand's J. Cole opens with a boy's letter, spelled as he spells it, answering an advertisement for a page boy: J. Cole is over thirteen, can clean plate, wait, clean windows and boots, and asks eight shillings, all found, or seven if his washing is done. His brother, under a butler, taught him, and Cole adds that he is not very tall but growing, sharp, and able to read, write, and add figures.

The mistress who advertised takes up the tale in chapter one, and the novel follows a page boy's life in service, with its comedy, snobbery, and small kindnesses. Gellibrand writes in a warm, observant voice, letting Cole's own letter set the book's charm. Readers meet a household from below stairs, through a boy's eager eyes.
7482-stories-of-the-prophets-before-the-:
Isaac Landman retells the Hebrew prophets for young readers. This volume was prepared for the Commission on Jewish Education of the Union of American Hebrew Congregations and the Central Conference of American Rabbis. The stories cover the prophets before the exile, when Judah still stood but its doom was gathering. Landman dedicates the book to his parents, who first introduced him to the prophets.

The chapters follow the last days of the kingdom. They tell of Baruch's first venture, the king hearing and acting, and the beginning of the end. Then come the first deportation, and life in exile and in the homeland. Lamentations, vain hope, cowardice, and treachery all have their place. The retellings aim to make ancient voices vivid for a new generation, without losing their moral urgency.
751-the-autocrat-of-the-breakfast-table:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote this series of talks by the Autocrat, a witty Boston gentleman who holds forth at a boarding-house breakfast table. He discourses on books, science, human nature, and city life, while the other boarders chime in, tease, and tell their own tales. The talk ranges wide and never stays dull.

Holmes mixes essay, poem, and anecdote, with humour that is warm rather than biting. The Autocrat's table became a beloved fixture of American letters, and the book made Holmes famous. It still reads as a model of the familiar essay: learned, funny, and humane, in the voice of a man who loves talk for its own sake.
782-the-travels-of-sir-john-mandeville:
A traveller calling himself Sir John Mandeville told this famous account of the East in the fourteenth century, in the Cotton manuscript version here given in modern spelling. He claims to have journeyed to Jerusalem, Egypt, India, and Cathay, describing holy sites, strange beasts, and peoples of every custom.

Much of the book borrows from other writers, and its marvels, from dog-headed men to rivers of gems, are fables rather than facts. Yet it shaped how Europe imagined Asia for two hundred years. The volume, with three tales from Hakluyt added, is a key text of medieval travel lore, valued for its wonder and its influence.
7820-monitress-merle:
Angela Brazil's Monitress Merle continues the school adventures of Mavis and Merle, written for readers who asked for more. Chapters run from a last bathe and a school ballot to the new monitress, Chagmouth folk, Miss Mitchell, fisher maidens, musical stars, Yuletide, and facing the footlights.

Later come the mumps, Bamberton Ferry, fifth-form justice, the Kittiwake, a haunted tree, leave-takings, the Tadpole Club, the Fourth of July, and love-in-a-mist. September sun over Chagmouth roofs and harbor opens a warm, busy school story of friendship, duty, and fun, with a heroine learning to lead.
7940-the-native-born-or-the-rajah-s-peop:
I. A. R. Wylie published this novel in 1910, calling it her first serious literary effort in the preface. Its scenes are set in India under British rule, and its chapter headings name both English residents, such as Archibald Travers, and Indian figures, such as Nehal Singh. The two books of the story move from a tense prologue toward a cathedral-building project and a reckoning between peoples.

The opening finds two women waiting in fear through a moonlit night, dreading what will happen when a light goes out. From there the novel follows divided loyalties, love, and the clash between British authority and Indian life. Wylie wrote it as a work of imagination, not history, and it reads today as a period portrait of empire told through personal lives caught in a larger conflict.
7958-the-napoleon-of-the-people:
Honoré de Balzac's short tale of Napoleon comes from his novel The Country Doctor, where an old soldier named Goguelat tells it to a group of peasants. Translated here by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell, it opens in Corsica, the French island warmed by the Italian sun, where Napoleon was born. And follows his rise as his listeners understand it: a story of glory, hardship, and loyalty told around a fire. It later joined a collection of folk tales about Napoleon.

The tale matters because it shows Napoleon as the common people imagined him, not as historians judged him. Goguelat's voice is warm, boastful, and moving, and Balzac lets the peasants' wonder carry the story. Short and stirring, it is a fine sample of Balzac's power to make history live through a single speaker.
8417-what-led-to-the-discovery-of-the-so:
John Hanning Speke wrote this account of what led him to the source of the Nile, a question that obsessed Victorian geography. The volume, merged from two Gutenberg submissions, follows Speke's reasoning and travels toward Lake Victoria. He claimed the lake as the Nile's head, in rivalry with other explorers and amid fierce debate back in London.

Speke's story is part travel narrative, part argument: he must persuade readers that his lake, not another, feeds the great river. Readers meet African guides, porters, and rulers without whom no expedition moved, though Speke tells the tale in his own voice. The book remains a key document of exploration, and of how exploration claims were made and fought.
8438-the-nicomachean-ethics-of-aristotle:
Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, introduced by J. A. Smith, asks what a good life is and how character is formed. Smith's introduction notes that the Ethics is one half of a single treatise, with the Politics as the other half, both dealing with what Aristotle calls the philosophy of human affairs. The ten books move from happiness to virtue, friendship, and pleasure.

Aristotle argues that virtue is a habit, found as a mean between excess and defect, and that friendship and contemplation crown a life. Readers meet the most influential moral philosophy of the ancient world, in a translation made for students. The book rewards slow reading, and its ideas still shape how people talk about character.
8647-afloat-and-ashore-a-sea-tale:
James Fenimore Cooper calls this a sea tale and teases readers in his preface about how much of it is truth and how much fiction. He refuses to say, leaving each reader to believe as much or as little as suits their knowledge of the world. Dares anyone to swear they know just where Clawbonny is, or that they knew old Mr Hardinge and heard him preach. The game sets the tone for a long, rolling narrative.

Afloat and ashore, the hero moves between land and sea, through voyages, wrecks, and the discipline of shipboard life that Cooper knew firsthand. Cooper's sea fiction helped invent the American nautical novel, and this tale shows his strengths: weather, seamanship, and the moral tests of men at sea. Readers who enjoy long nineteenth-century adventures will find plenty of salt water here, with a sly author winking from the quarterdeck.
9387-theresa-marchmont-or-the-maid-of-ho:
Mrs. Charles Gore wrote this tale in 1824, set first on a gloomy autumn evening in 1676. Driving blasts sweep from the sea upon Greville Cross, a dreary mansion on the Lancashire coast, promising a stormy night. The house, once a Benedictine monastery, passed at the Reformation to Sir Ralph de Greville, ancestor of its present lord.

Theresa Marchmont, maid of honour, moves through court intrigue in a world La Bruyère called marble: men hard, yet polished. Macbeth's words front the tale, on shapes that shake firm nerves. Gore's novel remains a spirited Restoration romance, gothic, courtly, and full of storm.
944-the-voyage-of-the-beagle:
Charles Darwin wrote this journal of his voyage round the world aboard HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836. He states in his preface that the work grew from his notes on the voyage and from the zoology of the expedition. He tells of lands from South America to Australia and the Galápagos Isles.

Darwin describes animals, plants, rocks, and peoples with a naturalist's keen eye, noting finches, fossils, and earthquakes as he goes. The voyage shaped the theory he would later publish, and the journal shows that theory forming. The book remains a classic of travel and science, vivid, curious, and full of wonder.
9440-the-further-adventures-of-jimmie-da:
Frank Packard wrote these further adventures of Jimmie Dale in 1919, picking up the Gray Seal's double life. Chapters bear titles such as Smarlinghue, The Warning, and Death to the Gray Seal. A diamond pendant, a bond robbery, and a chase through the underworld follow, with a secret room and a last card played.

Jimmie Dale, gentleman by day and masked avenger by night, outwits police and crooks alike. Packard keeps the pulp pace breathless. The book remains a classic of the masked-hero tale, and a favorite of early crime fiction readers.
9650-independent-bohemia-an-account-of-t:
Vladimir Nosek, secretary to the Czecho-Slovak Legation in London, wrote Independent Bohemia in 1918, an account of the Czecho-Slovak struggle for liberty. Nosek opens by asking what Austria-Hungary is, then traces Czech parties, wartime terror, and monster trials. Deputies jailed, presses crushed, and civilians interned fill the dark chapters. At home, Czechs aided the Allies; abroad, they fought and pled.

Later chapters follow the Czech declaration of May 1917, brave Reichsrat speeches, and the amnesty, toward a free republic. Masaryk's portrait fronts the book. A reader gets a wartime brief for a new nation, written from inside its London legation.
9762-calderon-the-courtier-a-tale:
Edward Bulwer Lytton wrote Calderon, the Courtier, a tale of Spanish court intrigue under Philip III. The king, weak and superstitious, leaves rule to the Duke of Lerma, who in turn yields power to Roderigo Calderon. Chapters trace an antechamber, a lover and confidant, a rival, and webs of plot. Civil ambition and church power tangle through the tale.

Later chapters follow an escape, a counterplot, and a harvest of sown deeds, as rivers run to the ocean's judgment. Lytton writes with polished irony on favor, corruption, and fall. A reader gets a compact court romance, rich in Spanish history and in the price of borrowed power.
9784-thomas-carlyle:
John Nichol wrote Thomas Carlyle in 1904, a life and estimate of the Scots prophet of letters. Nichol draws on renewed study of Carlyle's work, slight personal impressions, and earlier narrators' tales. Chapters trace Ecclefechan and Edinburgh, then Carlyle's political philosophy, ethics, and influence. An appendix weighs his religion.

Nichol judges Carlyle's genius with candor, praising his force while noting his faults. The life moves from humble Annandale roots to London fame. A reader gets a compact, scholarly Carlyle, fit for those who want the man and his thought in one short book.
9844-w-a-g-s-tale:
Margaret Turnbull edited W.A.G.'s Tale, a child's own story with Zobzee pictures by the author. Contents follow Uncle Burt's Billy, a house, a next-door neighbor, and a towpath on the Delaware. George, a white tent, and a turn at Turner's fill the middle acts. The author, a child narrator, draws his own Zobzees for the tale.

Pictures show a boy on a bridge, a rope pulled boat, and cats chasing a man to a white stone house. The tale favors a child's voice and fancy. A reader gets a charming, old-style children's book, where a young author's words and drawings share one playful world.
9878-the-survey-of-cornwall-and-an-epist:
Richard Carew of Antony wrote this survey of Cornwall in the reign of Elizabeth, and it remains the classic description of the county. Carew, a Cornish gentleman, describes the land, its people, customs, tin mines, and towns, with the pride of a man writing about home.

Bound with the survey is his epistle on the excellencies of the English tongue, praising his own language against Latin and French, plus a life of the author. Readers get Tudor Cornwall in rich detail, and an early argument for English as a language fit for learning and literature.
9999-harriet-the-moses-of-her-people:
Sarah H. Bradford's 1886 biography tells the life of Harriet Tubman, the escaped slave who returned south again and again to lead others to freedom. Bradford calls her the Moses of her people, and quotes the songs Tubman sang on the road, including farewells to old masters and hymns of trust.

The book draws on Tubman's own accounts and on letters, including one from Susan B. Anthony dated January 1903. It follows her from slavery through escapes, rescues, and war work. Readers meet one of America's great figures in a warm, direct narrative written while her deeds were still fresh.
a-brief-account-of-the-rise-and-progress: William Penn gives a brief account of the rise and progress of the people called Quakers. He sets out their fundamental principle, doctrines, worship, ministry, and discipline in plain terms. An opening survey traces earlier dispensations of God in the world as an introduction. Penn writes for readers who wish to know what Quakers believe and how they came to be.
a-dog-s-tale:
Mark Twain lets a dog tell her own story, beginning with her parentage: her father was a St. Bernard, her mother a collie, but she is a Presbyterian, as her mother told her. The mother, who picked up grand words at the dining-room door and Sunday school, taught her pup the uses of fine language. The family serves a kind master and his children.

Three chapters carry the dog from puppyhood to motherhood, through a fire she helps fight and a nursery she guards. Then human cruelty, dressed as science, strikes her own pup, and her loyalty meets a world that does not deserve it. Twain wrote the tale against cruelty to animals, and its plain pathos still lands.
a-girl-of-the-people:
A Girl of the People, by L T Meade, opens in a street crowd tugging at one girl's resolve. Meade's Bet stands stolid and straight while her companions chant that she is funking it, afraid to join their outing where Joe Wilkins, Sam, Jimmy, and Hester Wright wait round the corner. A dancing newspaper girl shakes a dirty hand in her face and calls her a mammy's girl, tied to her mother's apron strings, while the whole group laughs.

Bet flushes, pales, bites her lips, and answers with money instead of surrender: she tosses her share, a shilling, onto the pavement and marches home. That refusal sets the novel's terms. Meade follows a working class heroine. Her pleasures are real and her wages matter. Self respect costs her something every time she keeps it. Her friends spend theirs freely.
a-hoosier-chronicle: Meredith Nicholson writes a Hoosier chronicle of Indiana life and politics. Its chapters introduce Sylvia, a small dinner at Mrs. Owen's, Daniel Harwood, and the home life of Hoosier statesmen. Sylvia at Lake Waupegan and a lady of the constellations fill the story. Nicholson writes a novel of ambition, society, and the Middle West.
a-horse-s-tale:
Mark Twain tells a story in the voice of Soldier Boy, a horse who belongs to Buffalo Bill and serves with the army in the West. The title page of this edition, published in October 1907 with pictures by Lucius Hitchcock, shows the horse taken to an Indian camp. Soldier Boy is proud of his breeding and eager to explain horse society.

The tale mixes the horse's own chapters with letters from General Alison, his mother, and young Cathy, the girl Soldier Boy loves. Talk among horses, army life, a scout ride, and a bullfight scene fill the middle. Twain uses the animal's honest voice to mock human pride and cruelty.
a-jacobite-exile:
A Jacobite Exile is an 1894 adventure novel by G A Henty. Sir Marmaduke Carstairs is a Jacobite, a supporter of the exiled Stuart cause, and he is denounced as a plotter against King William. He and his son Charlie flee England for Sweden, where a very different war is being fought under King Charles the Twelfth.

Charlie joins the foreign legion in Swedish service and wins honor in several campaigns against the Poles and Russians. Henty folds the boy's exile into the great northern wars of the age, mixing real battles with a young soldier's rise. The novel gives readers both a Jacobite's grievance and a tour of Charles the Twelfth's battlefields.
a-modest-proposal-for-preventing-the-chi:
Jonathan Swift published his pamphlet in 1729, as its title page states, and it opens with a grim sight: beggar mothers in Ireland followed by ragged children with no food. The speaker then offers his modest proposal in the calm tone of a man of business. Poor parents, he says, should sell their infants as meat for rich tables.

He supports the plan with numbers, prices, and recipes, and lists its benefits for landlords, parents, and the kingdom. The horror builds because the voice never wavers or jokes. Swift meant the piece as an attack on English policy and cold economic thinking that treated Irish people as cattle.
a-mummer-s-tale: Anatole France follows the actress Felicie Nanteuil through the Paris theatre world in this novel, opening in her dressing room at the Odeon as she prepares for the stage. Translated by Charles Roche, the story traces her career among dressers, physicians, and fellow players, where applause, rivalry, and private feeling mix behind the curtain. Its comedy comes from the contrast between the glamour of performance and the workaday life of a company.
a-prefect-s-uncle:
P. G. Wodehouse dates his school novel 1903 on the title page and opens as term begins at Beckford College, where Marriott hurls his portmanteau onto the senior day-room table. The contents promise an unusual uncle in chapter two, and the uncle making himself at home in chapter three. He is the Bishop, uncle to a prefect, and a cricketer of alarming energy.

Chapters follow the bishop's ride, the M.C.C. match, stump cricket and poetry, house matches, and a disputed authorship, through the winter term to the bishop scoring at last. Wodehouse, fresh from school himself, writes the world of houses, prefects, and games with perfect recall and rising comic control. It is his second novel, and the school stories' high spirits are already his.
afloat-and-ashore-a-sea-tale: James Fenimore Cooper tells a sea tale of a young sailor's life afloat and ashore, from his home port to long voyages and hard service at sea. The novel follows ships, storms, ports, and the discipline of maritime life, with the author's first-hand feeling for rigging, weather, and command. It stands as a classic American sea story, rich in nautical detail and steady adventure.
alfgar-the-dane-or-the-second-chronicle-: Augustine David Crake continues his chronicle of Aescendune with Alfgar the Dane, a tale set in the days of Edmund Ironside. The story opens with the diary of Father Cuthbert and follows Alfgar through the night of St. Brice, the Danes in Wessex, and forest tracks toward suffering and glory. Aimed at young readers, it mixes history with adventure and Christian courage.
alice-in-wonderland-retold-in-words-of-o: Lewis Carroll's Alice returns here retold entirely in words of one syllable, so that the youngest readers can follow her strange adventures. The familiar scenes of Wonderland are kept, but the language is pared to short, plain words, with full illustrations to help along the way. The retelling shows how a classic can be made open to children just learning to read.
almoran-and-hamet-an-oriental-tale: John Hawkesworth tells an oriental tale of Almoran and Hamet, two princes whose rivalry unfolds in an imagined Eastern court. The story moves through ambition, love, and moral choice, using Eastern colour to carry lessons on power and virtue. First published in 1761, it belongs to the age of the philosophical tale, where fiction served instruction.
among-the-farmyard-people: Clara Dillingham Pierson writes for children among the farmyard people, telling the doings of hens, ducks, cows, and other animals in simple stories. Dedicated to the children themselves, the book gives each creature a voice and a small adventure. Its gentle lessons in kindness and observation suited the youngest readers.
an-enemy-of-the-people:
Henrik Ibsen sets his five-act play in a coastal town in southern Norway, in R. Farquharson Sharp's translation. The cast list names Dr. Thomas Stockmann, medical officer of the municipal baths, and his elder brother Peter, mayor of the town and chairman of the baths committee. The doctor has found the town's healing waters poisoned by pollution.

Stockmann expects praise and gets ruin: the mayor, the press, and the town meeting turn on him to protect the baths' income. His daughter Petra stands by him, and Captain Horster offers his house for the famous meeting scene. Alone at the end, Stockmann calls the strongest man the one who stands by himself. The play still serves as the model drama of truth against the crowd.
an-original-belle:
E. P. Roe's An Original Belle opens with a preface on power, which Roe calls the measure of character. The greatest power, he argues, belongs to trained intelligence and moral quality. His heroine Marian begins commonplace enough, a belle of ordinary homage. Circumstances school her to stay honest to her nature and her conscience.

The story culminates in the summer of 1863, Roe's preface says, amid the critical period of the Civil War. Willard Merwyn and Captain Lane stand as the contrasting men of the contents. A scheme of life, a chained will, and a father's forethought shape Marian's probation. Roe sought fairness to the South's motives, he tells its readers directly. The novel uses invasion and battle to test character, not the reverse. Marian's originality is her refusal of the belle's trade: she will be valued for herself, or not at all.
armadale:
Wilkie Collins dedicates his long sensation novel to John Forster. In his preface he warns readers plainly. The story oversteps the limits some critics set for modern fiction, and he is not afraid of his design. Two young men bear the same name, Allan Armadale, bound by a deathbed letter and a shared, guilty inheritance.

The plot runs through a wreck, a Swiss sanatorium, a yachting trip, and London lodgings, driven by Lydia Gwilt, a brilliant and dangerous woman with a forged past. Forged letters, hidden identities, and a plan built on the two Allans' sameness keep the suspense high. Collins sustains the huge machine of coincidence with great skill.
around-the-tea-table: Thomas De Witt Talmage invites readers to an evening tea table where friends trade chat, tales, and short papers. Chapters range from a growler soothed and an old pair of scissors to a lie viewed through zoology and a breath of English air. The pieces are brief, genial, and often comic, with a moral tucked inside the talk. Talmage writes as host, and the book reads like an evening spent among good company.
at-the-sign-of-the-eagle:
At the Sign of the Eagle, by Gilbert Parker, opens at a London dinner where two Americans are being weighed. Parker gives the first judgment to Molly, Lady Lawless. Her husband Duke asks what she thinks of their guests. The little man, she says, is affected and servile. The big one strikes her as commanding and rough edged. He looks dangerous in a drawing room, and the more interesting for it.

Business hides behind the invitation. Railways and mines are in play. Lord Hampstead's nephew means to hunt a fortune in the States. Status for dollars is the bargain on the table.
