Lady Lawless quotes Hamlet at her husband for proposing it. Parker sets American money against English rank in his most social novel. The eagle of the title is the American bird. It has come to roost in Mayfair, and the drawing room must decide what it is worth.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-at-millville:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this volume in 1908. Uncle John buys a farm near the village of Millville, and the nieces descend on it with Major Doyle for a summer stay. Millville hears exciting news, the agent Peggy McNutt presents his bill, and Ethel the school-ma'am prepares for the nabobs' arrival.

Louise scents a mystery: a man in hiding, a locked cupboard, and Joe's tale of the great trouble deepen it chapter by chapter. The girls turn amateur detectives, bait Peggy, and set a trap that catches its quarry. Farm comedy runs alongside, as when Beth gravely condemns making a hen hatch duck eggs as treachery toward the hen. Mr. West explains all before Peggy takes his revenge.
b09-sachs-fastnachtspiele:
Hans Sachs, the Nuremberg shoemaker and master singer, wrote plays for Shrove Tuesday, the carnival before Lent. Four of his Fastnachtspiele, carnival plays, are gathered here in German, from about 1550. The best known of them, Der fahrende Schüler im Paradies, sends a wandering scholar through a comic Paradise.

Carnival plays were short, rowdy, and played by tradesmen for their neighbors in the street. Sachs fills his with sharp talk, mistaken hopes, and fools who get what they earn. The humor is broad, but the craft is real: tight scenes and quick, singing verse. Together the four plays show popular theatre at the height of the Reformation age.
battle-studies-ancient-and-modern-battle:
Colonel Ardant du Picq's Battle Studies examines ancient and modern battle, translated from the eighth French edition by Colonel John N. Greely and Major Robert C. Cotton. Foch's prefatory letter calls Du Picq the champion of moral force, the army's strongest element.

Du Picq argues that moral force preponderates in the outcome of battles, and Foch says American experience in 1918 amply verified his conclusions. The studies draw on ancient warfare and on modern campaigns alike, seeking what actually breaks men in combat. Soldiers and military historians will find Du Picq's analysis of fear, cohesion and leadership still bracing.
bob-son-of-battle:
Alfred Ollivant wrote the great sheepdog novel in this story of Bob, the gray dog of Kenmuir. The book is laid out in six parts, from The Coming of the Tailless Tyke to the final contest for the Shepherds' Trophy. Bob's master is James Moore of Kenmuir, and the dog's rival is Red Wull, the tailless terror owned by the dour Adam McAdam.

Ollivant tells the feud of the two dogs and their masters across years of trials on the Cumberland fells. A sheep-killing mystery hangs over the flock, and suspicion falls where it can do most harm. Chapters of dialect talk among the shepherds carry much of the humour and the grief. The trophy competition decides the rivalry in public, but the black killer plot must be settled first, in darkness.
bob-the-castaway-or-the-wreck-of-the-eag:
Frank V Webster wrote Bob the Castaway, a boys' sea novel published by Cupples and Leon of New York in 1909. Webster centers the tale on Bob Henderson, a prank-loving boy sent to sea in hope the trip will sober him. Nervous Mr Tarbill sails with him on the Eagle.

Bob's jokes go wrong on land and at sea, and a storm settles the score. The Eagle wrecks, boats drift apart, and Bob lands on an island where he finds Tarbill alive. More castaways reach shore, hope fades, and at last a sail home ends the wait. Bob grows up through the ordeal. He ends as a ship's captain in the making. The tale sells steadiness to boys who love pranks and the sea.
born-in-exile:
George Gissing's Born in Exile follows Godwin Peak, a clever boy born to a struggling shopkeeper's family. The story opens at Whitelaw College on a summer day in 1874. Peak's father kept a small cottage household on two pounds a week. The boy's militant egoism, his hunger to rise, grows with his schooling.

Peak wins scholarships yet feels exiled among gentlemen by his birth. He falls in love with Sidwell Warricombe, a clergyman's daughter of sincere faith. To win her world he feigns religious belief he does not hold. His friend Earwaker watches the deception with unease. Gissing writes a pitiless study of class shame and intellectual pride. Peak's exile is self-made, and the novel asks whether a man can lie his way into belonging.
britannica-1911-abbeville:
Abbeville receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The French town on the Somme, capital of its arrondissement, stands part on an island and part on both banks. Narrow streets and gabled wooden houses fill a fertile valley near Amiens.

St Vulfran's church, flamboyant Gothic with twin towers, dominates the town though its nave stayed short. A thirteenth-century belfry crowns the town hall. Cloth is the old trade; hemp, sugar, ships, and locks add work, and grain moves in trade. Ponthieu's chief town passed from St Riquier's abbey to counts, Castille, and Edward the First of England by marriage. France and England held it by turns till Burgundy took it in 1435, and Louis the Eleventh annexed it in 1477.
britannica-1911-aberfoyle:
Aberfoyle receives a parish entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Perthshire village sits at Craigmore's base on the Laggan, a head-water of the Forth, with 1,052 parish folk in 1901. The duke of Montrose's road of 1885 made it the other gate to the Trossachs.

Loch Ard lies two miles west, three miles long with the green isle Eilean Gorm near its west end. Ledard falls drop by its north-west shore. Loch Chon beyond drains by the Avon Dhu into Ard, and Ard by the Laggan to the Forth. Walkers bound for Loch Katrine pass through the village since the road came. Slate quarries on Craigmore stand as the parish's only industry, the entry notes, in a landscape sold on rest.
britannica-1911-abstract-of-title:
Abstract of title, in English law, names the summary drawn up when land changes hands. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, it explains a term from conveyancing, the branch of law that handles sales and mortgages of estates. The abstract sets out, in shortened form, the deeds and events through which a seller claims the right to sell.

Contents stay close to practice. A competent person prepares the abstract for the buyer or the lender taking a mortgage. The buyer's solicitor then checks it line by line against the original deeds. Readers meet a working safeguard: before money moves, the paper chain behind a title must be shown and verified.
britannica-1911-acireale:
Acireale is a town and episcopal see in the Sicilian province of Catania, nine miles north of the city of Catania, with more than thirty-five thousand people in 1901. It has some importance as a thermal station, a resort for its hot springs, which the Romans themselves used. A river gives the town its name and carries a Greek love story with it.

Legend fills the close. Acis, lover of the sea nymph Galatea, was slain by the Cyclops Polyphemus and changed into the river Acis. The rocks Polyphemus hurled at Ulysses are identified with the seven great sea stacks, the Scogli de' Ciclopi, standing a little south of the town, still shown to visitors.
britannica-1911-adam-or-adan-de-le-hale:
Adam de le Hale (died about 1288) was a French trouvere. He was born at Arras, son of a noted citizen. Contemporaries called him Adam le Bossu, the hunchback. He studied grammar, theology, and music. The Cistercian abbey of Vaucelles trained him. The church was his intended career. He renounced it and married Marie instead. She figures in many of his songs.

Service took him across the Mediterranean world. He joined the household of Robert of Artois. Then he followed Charles of Anjou's fortunes. Egypt, Syria, Palestine, and Italy all hosted him. At Naples he wrote his most famous work. The Jeu de Robin et Marion is a pastoral play with music. It is cited as France's earliest secular play with music.
britannica-1911-adam-s-apple:
Adam's apple is the projection at the front of the throat. The thyroid cartilage of the larynx forms it. It moves when a person swallows or speaks. Males show it more prominently than females. The 1911 Britannica entry explains the name by legend. A piece of the forbidden fruit lodged in Adam's throat. That story fixed the name in common speech.

One practical note closes the short entry. The Adam's apple is a target point in jiu-jitsu. That Japanese system of self-defence attacks it deliberately. A blow there can disable an opponent quickly. Readers get anatomy, folklore, and martial use together. Few throat features carry so much story. The entry keeps all three in a few lines.
britannica-1911-aiguille:
Aiguille, a French word meaning needle, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a mountain form. An aiguille is one of the sharp, jagged points that stand above the snow-line on a mountain massif, the main bulk of a range. Frost does the shaping. It splits the rock along joints or planes of cleavage, the natural cracks and layers in the stone.

The sides left behind are too steep for snow to rest on them. So the snow-line passes below bare, pointed rock. Aiguilles are what remains when high ridges with a house-roof structure are split apart into detached pinnacles. The short entry is a piece of physical geography, explaining a landform by the process that made it rather than by any single famous peak.
britannica-1911-aisle:
Aisle, an architecture term, is given its own article within the hosted text of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Latin ala, a wing, and first meant the wing of a house. In building it names the side divisions of a church or large hall. Colonnades or arcades divide the aisles from the nave, the central area.

The basilica of Trajan offered an early example, with double aisles on each side. Old St Peter's at Rome, the Bethlehem basilica, and the Holy Sepulchre church had the same arrangement. Aisles can also flank the transept or choir, and aisles carried round a rounded choir to reach chapels form a chevet. Britain usually keeps one aisle per side, Chichester and Elgin excepted. Antwerp Cathedral has three per side, and German hall churches raise their aisles to the nave's full height.
britannica-1911-aisse-mademoiselle:
Mademoiselle Aïssé (about 1694–1733) was carried off as a small child and ended as a famed French writer of letters. Her name twists the name Haidée. Turks looted her father's palace when she was four; she, a Circassian chief's daughter, was sold to the Comte de Ferriol, France's envoy at Constantinople.

Ferriol's sister-in-law brought her up in Paris beside her own sons. Beauty and a strange past made Aïssé the talk of society, yet she found the will to turn down the regent's offers. Her lasting bond was with the Chevalier d'Aydie, who fathered her daughter. Letters to Madame Calandrini give news of noted figures such as Madame du Deffand and Madame de Tencin. Most of all they reveal her own warmth and loyalty. Voltaire later brought them out in print.
britannica-1911-ale:
Ale, an old word for fermented liquor made chiefly from malt, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In England ale is nowadays practically the same thing as beer. That was not always so. Before hops reached England from Flanders in the sixteenth century, ale named malt liquor brewed without them, while beer described liquor brewed with an infusion of hops.

The distinction survives only in fragments, since ale is never used for stout, porter, or lager. Varieties such as mild ale, a full, sweetish, dark beer with little hop, and pale ale are distinguished. Old Welsh and Scots laws priced common and spiced ales against mead by the cask. The article also traces ale in social life. Whitsun-ales, church-ales, and clerk-ales were parish festivals. Bid-ales were benefit feasts where guests contributed. The word bridal itself is really bride-ale, the wedding feast.
britannica-1911-alecsandri-vasile:
Alecsandri, Vasile, a Rumanian lyric poet of 1821 to 1890, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bacau in Moldavia in July 1821, he was educated first at Jassy and then in Paris from 1834 to 1839. A long trip over the Carpathian Mountains in 1839 changed his work. He became the first collector of Rumanian popular songs, following Western examples.

His collection first appeared in 1844, and his own lyrical poems, Doine si Lacrimioare, came out at Paris in 1852, followed by a fuller gathering of ballads and songs at Jassy. He adapted French plays for the new Rumanian theatre and wrote original pieces too. His link with the revolutionary movement of 1848 drove him to shelter in western Europe, including England. Later came the lighter Pastele and his serious dramas, culminating in Ovid. In later life he entered politics and served as minister for foreign affairs from 1859.
britannica-1911-angle:
What an angle really is split the ancient writers. Proclus said it must be a quality, a quantity, or a relationship. Eudemus took it as a bend away from a straight line, while Carpus of Antioch took it as the space between lines that cross. Euclid chose the relationship view, though his tests for right, acute, and obtuse angles rest on size.

Euclid's own wording calls a plane angle the tilt toward each other of two lines in a plane that meet without lying straight. The term itself comes from Latin angulus, a corner, tied to roots for bending or squeezing. A curious list of Greek-derived names for curve shapes, among them biconvex and biconcave forms, rounds off the entry.
britannica-1911-anglo-saxon-chronicle:
Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a name that misleads slightly, the entry begins. There are really four Anglo-Saxon Chronicles, not one. All four grow from a common stock. They sometimes share material, as many groups of medieval chronicles do. Each still deserves treatment as an independent work. Seven manuscripts survive. They are lettered A through G in the standard list.

One manuscript, G, is now a mere fragment. It was a transcript of A. Manuscript F gives its entries in both Saxon and Latin. It marks a stage in the shift from vernacular to Latin chronicle-writing. Manuscripts B and C share an original as far as they run. The relationships among the four true chronicles vary greatly in different parts. Neglecting that fact has produced serious error. Editions and translations close the article. Stevenson's Church Historians of England version is among them.
britannica-1911-ankle: Ankle, also spelled ancle, is the joint connecting the foot with the leg. The word appears in various forms across the Teutonic languages. Its origin probably connects with the Latin angulus, meaning an angle. A Greek word for bent may also stand behind it. Beyond that etymology, the entry adds nothing of its own. It simply points the reader to the article on joints for the anatomy of the ankle.
britannica-1911-axile: Axile, or axial, is a science term meaning related to the axis. In botany, an embryo is called axile when it runs in the same direction as the axis of the seed that holds it. The very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives that one technical use, tying the word to the line of the seed and the young plant's line within it.
britannica-1911-axle:
Axle, in Middle English axel-tre, from Old Norwegian for an axle-tree, names the pin or spindle on which a wheel turns. Its roots reach to Sanskrit aksha, Greek axon, and Latin axis, one word family for the turning bar.

On carriages the axle-tree is the bar carrying the wheels, while the axles strictly are its thinner rounded ends, on which the wheels actually turn. Pins through those ends keep the wheels from slipping off. Such pins are called axle-pins or linch-pins, linch being a worn form of the Old English word for axle itself, confused in speech with link. The short entry thus covers build, strict usage, and word history together.
britannica-1911-bairnsdale:
Bairnsdale is a town in Tanjil county, Victoria, Australia. It stands on the Mitchell river. Melbourne lies 171 miles west by rail. The town counted 3,074 people in 1901. It sits near the head of Lake King lagoon. That lagoon opens to the sea.

Water travel links Bairnsdale with Melbourne regularly. The district around is chiefly pastoral. Several goldfields lie within it. Both alluvial and reef mining go on there. Tanneries work in the town itself. Cheese and butter factories stand there too. Ships carry maize and other grain to Melbourne. Hops, fruit, and dairy produce join the trade. Pasture, gold, and shipping fill this short colonial town entry.
britannica-1911-bale:
Bale is a word with several old senses, and the 1911 Britannica entry sets them out one by one. The first sense, shared across Teutonic tongues, means evil or suffering. That use was already dated by 1911, kept alive mostly in poetry and in the form baleful, where early verse often set it against bliss.

A second sense, from Old English bael, means a blazing fire or funeral pyre, still heard in the north of England in bale-fire. A third names a bundle of goods such as cotton, wool, or hay, packed for transport. A fourth, properly bail, means to scoop water out of a boat with a bucket.
britannica-1911-ballycastle:
Ballycastle is a seaport and watering place on the north coast of County Antrim, Ireland, facing Rathlin Island across a bay of the same name. Its population in 1901 was 1,481. A light railway linked the town with Ballymoney, and its two parts, a quarter mile apart, were joined by a fine avenue.

In the late 1700s Hugh Boyd took the estate and poured money into the town, starting manufactures, charities, and churches. More than £150,000, the entry says, went on pier and harbour, but the sea wrecked the pier and sand choked the harbour. East of the town stand the remains of Bonamargy Abbey, burial place of many of the MacDonnell family.
britannica-1911-balmoral-castle:
Balmoral Castle is a private home of the British sovereign in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. It stands in the parish of Crathie and Braemar, on the right bank of the Dee, nine miles west of Ballater and 900 feet above the sea. The estate once belonged to the Farquharsons of Inverey and passed through Sir Robert Gordon's hands.

The Prince Consort took the lease in 1848, bought the whole estate in 1852, and left it to Queen Victoria. The 1911 Britannica entry describes a granite castle in the Scots baronial style, with an eastern tower 100 feet high. Views run to Ballochbuie, Glen Gairn, and Lochnagar. Memorial cairns to royal family members crown Craig Gowan nearby.
britannica-1911-banderole:
Banderole, French for a little banner, is a small flag or streamer. Knights carried such streamers on their lances. Ships flew them from the masthead in battle. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the word in three fields, and it is a short entry throughout.

In heraldry, a banderole is a streamer hanging below the crook of a bishop's crosier and folding over the staff. In the building arts, it names a carved band of the Renaissance period used to bear an inscription. A close cousin, bannerol, means much the same, but it is the term used for the square banners carried at the funerals of great men and then placed over their tombs.
britannica-1911-banganapalle:
Banganapalle was a state of southern India, ringed by the Madras district of Kurnool. It covered 255 square miles and held 32,264 people in 1901, a drop of nine per cent in ten years. Its estimated revenue was £6,400, much of it granted away to junior branches of the ruling family, and it paid no tribute.

Overspending by the nawab, Syed Fateh Ali Khan, and slack administration worried the government of India. In February 1905 he was removed from the running of the state for a time. The 1911 Britannica entry adds one line on the town itself: it lies not far from the Southern Mahratta railway branch running from Guntakal to Bezwada.
britannica-1911-barnacle:
Barnacle is a name for crustaceans of the division Cirripedia. At first it belonged to the stalked barnacles, which fix themselves in crowds to driftwood and floating objects and are a chief cause of the fouling of ships' bottoms on long voyages. The sessile barnacles, or acorn-shells, crust the rocks between tide marks on all coasts in millions.

The stranger half of the entry is a myth. Medieval natural history, from the 1100s at least, told that the barnacle goose hatched from a shell-like fruit of a tree by the sea, since its Arctic nesting places were unknown. The 1911 Britannica entry shows how that fable moved the goose's name onto these shellfish, and it figures several kinds, from Scalpellum to the whale barnacle.
britannica-1911-barnard-castle:
Barnard Castle is a market town in Durham, England, seventeen miles west of Darlington by rail, with 4,421 people in 1901. It stands in beauty on the steep left bank of the Tees. An octagonal town hall of 1747, a few picturesque old houses, and a fragment of an Augustinian convent are noted among its buildings.

The castle that gives the town its name holds the chief interest: its remains cover more than six acres, and it is the principal scene of Scott's Rokeby. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the Bowes Mansion and Museum, bequeathed to the town in 1874 and rich in works of art. Nearby stand Egglestone Abbey and Raby Castle. Shoe-thread making and an important corn market lead the town's trade.
britannica-1911-barnstable:
Barnstable is a seaport township in Massachusetts, in the United States, and the county seat of Barnstable county. It stretches across Cape Cod, between Cape Cod Bay to the north and Nantucket Sound to the south. Its population was 4,364 in 1900 and 4,676 in 1910, and the New York, New Haven and Hartford railway serves it.

Unlike much of the county, its soil suits farming well, and its chief industry is growing vegetables and supplying milk and poultry to its villages, nearly all of them summer resorts. Cranberries are raised in large amounts, with oyster and shell fisheries besides. The 1911 Britannica entry recalls that mackerel and whale fisheries once ruled its economy, and that the town was settled and incorporated in 1639.
britannica-1911-barnstaple:
Barnstaple is a seaport, market town, and municipal borough in Devonshire, England, on the river Taw near the north coast. Its population in 1901 was 14,137. Three railways serve it, and the Taw is crossed by a stone bridge of sixteen arches, said to date from the 12th or 13th century.

Lace, gloves, sail-cloth, and fishing nets are made in the town, with potteries, tanneries, sawmills, and foundries, and shipbuilding besides, though the harbour takes only small coasting vessels. The poet John Gay was born nearby and schooled at the free grammar school, founded in the 14th century. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses the borough's age: it ranks among the most ancient royal boroughs, named several times in Domesday Book.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-auguste-marse:
Auguste Marseille Barthélemy (1796–1867), a French satirical poet born at Marseilles, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name, the entry says, can hardly be parted from that of his friend Joseph Méry. The two worked so closely that their shares in joint works cannot be told apart. After local fame as a poet, Barthélemy went to Paris, where Le Sacre de Charles X in 1825 first won him the favour of the court.

Satire for the opposition soon replaced court favour. La Villéliade ran through fifteen editions in a year, and Napoléon en Égypte through nearly a dozen. A poem on Napoleon's son brought Barthélemy prison and a fine in 1829, while the weekly verse satires of Némésis attacked Louis Philippe's ministers from 1831. Suspected of being paid into silence and later pensioned, he lost his influence, and his later work passed unnoticed.
britannica-1911-bastille:
Bastille, from a French word for building, was at first any fortified building in a system of defence, as the long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article explains. The name settled on the castle of Saint Antoine in Paris. About 1369 Hugues Aubriot, for Charles V, made the Saint Antoine gate a regular fort. He added six massive towers to its two, ringed by thick walls and a ditch twenty-five feet wide.

Fortress turned prison fills the history. The Bastille changed hands in the wars of the 1400s, held Henry IV's treasure, and fell to the Fronde in 1649 after a short cannonade. As the royal state prison its records later told much of its own story. At the outbreak of the Revolution Parisians attacked it, and after vigorous resistance it was taken and razed on 14 July 1789. Only seven prisoners were found inside. A bronze column now marks the site.
britannica-1911-bauble:
Bauble is a word whose mixed birth and mixed uses are set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is thought to be a blend of two unlike words: an old French baubel, a child's plaything, and an old English babyll, a thing swinging to and fro. From those roots it was used for a stick with a weight fixed to it, for weighing, and for a child's toy.

Most of the entry belongs to the fool. Above all, bauble names the mock symbol of office carried by a court jester: a baton, a short staff, ending in a figure of Folly with cap and bells. A bladder was sometimes tied to the other end. Because the stick stood for his foolish office, the word slid into wider use. It came to mean any trifle, any showy thing of no real worth, or any childish folly in act or speech.
britannica-1911-bell-alexander-melville:
Alexander Melville Bell (1819–1905) was an American educationalist born at Edinburgh, father of Alexander Graham Bell. He trained under his own father, an expert on phonetics and faulty speech, and became his chief assistant. From 1843 he lectured on elocution at Edinburgh, and later at the university of London.

In 1870 Bell settled in Canada as a lecturer at Queen’s College, Kingston, and in 1881 he moved to Washington. There he taught deaf mutes by his “visible speech” method, whose letters picture the positions of the speech organs. His many books run from Steno-Phonography in 1852 to The Science of Speech in 1897.
britannica-1911-bench-table: Bench table, in French banc and Italian sedile, is the stone seat that runs around the walls of large churches. It sometimes runs around the piers, the great posts that hold up the roof, as well. Church porches very often have one too. The whole entry is that single placing note: what the feature is, the names it carries in three tongues, and where in a church a visitor should look for it.
britannica-1911-bennett-sir-william-ster:
Sir William Sterndale Bennett (1816–1875) was an English composer born at Sheffield, son of an organist. Orphaned early, he was raised at Cambridge by his grandfather, who gave him his first music lessons. He sang in King’s College choir from 1824 and entered the Royal Academy of Music in 1826 for ten years of study.

Trips to Germany between 1836 and 1842 brought Bennett face to face with the new music there. At Düsseldorf he met Mendelssohn, and at a Leipzig Gewandhaus concert he played his third piano concerto to great applause. Schumann called him the most musical of Englishmen. He later headed the Royal Academy, and a scholarship there keeps his name; he died in London in 1875.
britannica-1911-bicycle:
Bicycle names a two-wheeled machine built from the older velocipede. The 1911 Britannica article opens with its working parts. Two wheels stand one behind the other on a frame with a saddle. A crank axle between the wheels carries the pedals. A chain carries the drive to the rear wheel. Some models use a shaft and bevel wheels instead of a chain. A free-wheel lets the rear wheel spin on its own momentum.

The article then works through frame, gears, brakes, tyres, and steering in fine detail. A variable speed gear lets the rider change the drive ratio at will. Ball bearings carry the steering tube in its socket. The long closing section turns to motor bicycles. Engine sizes, twin and four-cylinder layouts, side-cars, and trailers are all covered there.
britannica-1911-bill-of-sale:
Bill of sale, in law, is a document that assigns personal property to a buyer. It is still used for transfers of ships, the 1911 Britannica article notes. The term now also covers mortgages of goods. A bill of sale may show a sale or a loan security over chattels. In both cases the goods stay in the giver's hands, not the buyer's. That gap between paper ownership and possession drives the whole law here.

The first English statute on the subject came in 1854. Its preamble says secret bills let debtors look rich while creditors lost out. Unregistered bills were made void against execution creditors. Later acts of 1866, 1878, and 1882 rebuilt the registration system in full. The article sets out forms, fees, and stamp duties in close detail. Publishing a registration usually destroys the giver's credit, it warns at the close.
britannica-1911-binnacle:
Binnacle is the name of a case fixed on the deck of a ship. It generally stands in front of the steersman, the sailor at the wheel. Inside the case is kept the ship's compass. A light is fitted with it, so the compass can be read at night. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single short paragraph on the word and the object. It traces the word's path through several languages to its Latin root.

Before the 18th century the English form was bittacle. That came through the Spanish bitácula, the entry explains. Behind the Spanish stands the Latin habitaculum, meaning a little dwelling. The name fits the case as a small house for the compass on deck. No maker, date, or ship is named in the text. The entry stays with the word's history and the case's plain use at the helm.
britannica-1911-biquintile: Biquintile is an astrology term for one of the aspects, or angles, between two planets. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single sentence. It breaks the word down from Latin parts. Bi- means twice, and quintilis means fifth. The measure follows from those parts. The planets stand apart by twice the fifth part of a great circle. That distance is 144 degrees. The entry adds one more fact: Kepler introduced the biquintile among his new aspects.
britannica-1911-bishop-s-castle:
Bishop's Castle is a market town and borough in southern Shropshire, England. It is the terminus of the Bishop's Castle light railway from Craven Arms. Its population in 1901 was 1,378. The town climbs a hill east of Clun Forest, in pleasant country. Only the slightest fragments remain of the bishops of Hereford's castle. That castle gave the town its name. A mayor, four aldermen, and twelve councillors govern it.

The town began inside the manor of Lydbury, held by Hereford church before the Conquest. A bishop built Lydbury Castle between 1085 and 1154 to guard the manor from the Welsh. The town that grew round it took the Bishop's Castle name in the 13th century. Elizabeth's charter of 1572 is its earliest incorporation charter. From 1584 it sent two members to parliament. That right ended with disfranchisement in 1832. Some farm trade supports the town today.
bulfinch-s-mythology-the-age-of-fable:
Thomas Bulfinch wrote The Age of Fable to retell the myths of Greece and Rome for general readers, and the Reverend E E Hale revised this edition. Bulfinch aimed at readers who met mythological names in poetry and art without knowing the stories. Greek and Roman gods stand at the center. Their Latin and Greek names are explained as the tales proceed.

Early chapters cover creation, the golden age, Prometheus, and Pandora. Stories follow Apollo and Daphne, Pyramus and Thisbe, and Phaeton driving the sun's chariot. Midas, Baucis and Philemon, Cupid and Psyche, and the founding of Thebes come later. Bulfinch retells each tale in clear, calm prose and links many to later poems. Readers get the classic nineteenth-century doorway into classical myth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-font:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Fontenelle, or the Abbey of Saint Wandrille, describes a Benedictine monastery in Normandy near Caudebec. St. Wandrille came of Austrasia's royal family and stood high at Dagobert the First's court. He retired to Montfaucon in 629, spent time at Bobbio and Romainmôtier, and returned to Normandy to found his monastery in 648.

He built a great St. Peter's basilica almost three hundred feet in length, consecrated by St. Ouen in 657. Fire destroyed it in 756, Abbot Ansegisus rebuilt it with narthex and tower, and Danish pirates wrecked it about 862, scattering the monks for over a century through Chartres, Boulogne and St. Omer. The entry follows the community's long exile and eventual return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-patri:
Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, first appears as orphanotrophos, the dignitary entrusted with the care of orphans in the church of Constantinople. That post carried high rank and curial influence, and he made the most of it. Suidas describes a striking personality: engaging magnificence of manner, openhanded, suave yet noble in bearing, courtly in speech, and fond of ecclesiastical display. When Patriarch Gennadius died in 471, he succeeded him.

For five or six years his episcopate was uneventful. Change came when the usurping Emperor Basiliscus, won over to Eutychian teaching by Timotheus Aelurus, issued an encyclical rejecting the Council of Chalcedon. Acacius at first hesitated over adding his name to the new course. He died in 489, and his schism outlived him some thirty years, ending only with Emperor Justin's return to unity under Pope Hormisdas in 519.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aci-reale:
Aci-Reale, or Jaca Regalis, is a Sicilian diocese over fourteen communes in Catania's civil province, immediately subject to Rome. Gregory XVI created it in 1844; Monsignor Gerlando Maria Genuardi of the Oratory became its first bishop only in 1872. The episcopal city stands picturesquely at Mount Etna's foot, amid rich orange and almond gardens.

The diocese counts 18 parishes and 305 churches, served by 330 secular priests and 70 regulars, among 150,219 inhabitants. The entry cites Cappelletti, Gams, Vigo, and Pirri, and notes the controversy over the cult of St. Expedite, treated in Civilta Cattolica and the Analecta Bollandiana.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrianople:
Adrianople is a city of Turkey in Europe, said by legend to have been built by Orestes, son of Agamemnon, at the meeting of the Tonsus and Ardiscus with the Hebrus. Emperor Hadrian developed and adorned it with monuments, renaming Orestias as Hadrianopolis, and made it capital of Haemimont, or Thrace. Constantine defeated Licinius there in 323, and Valens was killed by the Goths there in 378.

Theodore of Epirus seized it in 1227 during the Latin Empire, and Asen of Bulgaria killed him there two years later. Murad I captured it in 1360, and it served as Turkish capital from 1362 to 1453. Russians occupied it in 1829 and again in 1878, in wars for Greek and Bulgarian independence. Today it heads a vilayet of about 960,000 people, trading in woven stuffs, silks, carpets, and farm products, and it holds the grand mosque of Selim II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-affinity-in-t:
Scripture treats affinity as a bar to wedlock, evident from Leviticus 18 and 20. Unlike church affinity, which arises from lawful and unlawful intercourse alike, biblical affinity springs from betrothal only, which among Hebrews scarcely differed from ratified marriage. The Leviticus texts bar direct-line marriage with a stepmother, stepdaughter, grand-stepdaughter, mother-in-law, and daughter-in-law.

In the collateral line they bar marriage with a paternal uncle's wife, with a sister-in-law except where the levirate law applies, and with a wife's sister while the former wife lives. Jews held the wife's relation to her husband's family closer than the husband's to his wife's. Leviticus 20 sanctions these rules: death threatens direct-line transgressors, while childlessness threatens collateral ones, meaning offspring counted illegitimate or assigned to the dead uncle or brother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aisle:
Aisle, from Latin ala and Old French aile, is in architecture one of a church's lateral divisions, separated from the nave by piers, pillars, or columns in rows. Sometimes a church has only one side aisle. Often the aisle continues around the apse. Occasionally aisles stop at the transepts. Very large churches' transepts may have three aisles.

Gothic architecture's rule puts aisle roofs well below the nave roof, admitting light through clerestory windows. In most Romanesque churches aisle roofs are but little lower than the nave's. The aisle generally has one story, though occasionally an upper one, sometimes used as a gallery. Chichester, Milan, and Amiens have five, Antwerp and Paris seven, and Cordova cathedral in Spain nineteen. Aisles existed in Roman basilicas and in most Christian churches of all periods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-de-l-is:
Alain de l'Isle, also Alain of Lille, Alanus ab Insulis, or de Insulis, was a monk, poet, preacher, theologian, and eclectic philosopher, born about 1128, probably at Lille, whence his name. He died at Citeaux in 1203. He is believed to have studied and taught in Paris for some time before joining the Third Council of the Lateran in 1179.

In his day Alain won extraordinary celebrity as teacher and learned man, called Alain the Great and the Universal Doctor. Legend tells of a scholar crying that his dialectical opponent was either Alain or the devil. His principal work, Ars Fidei Catholicae, dedicated to Clement III, refutes with rational argument the errors of Mohammedans, Jews, and heretics. He also wrote Tractatus Contra Haereticos and Theologicae Regulae. He also wrote two poems, De Planctu Naturae and Anticlaudianus. His theology blends rationalism with mysticism, and he ranks among medieval writers who influenced Dante.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-cas:
Albert of Castile was a Dominican historian born about 1460 and dead in 1522. He joined the Dominican order young at the Venice house of Sts. John and Paul and became skilled in nearly every branch of learning of his day, with history as his chief study. His own works include catalogues of the illustrious men and the saints of his order, both printed at Venice in 1501.

His short chronicle of the order, printed in 1504, traces the popes, the Dominican generals, and the order's notable men from its foundation, drawing chiefly on Giacomo de Luzato. Castile also edited a Latin Bible with full apparatus printed at Venice in 1506. He re-edited it fifteen years later with a concordance, an index to the words of both Testaments. He also edited the order's constitutions and other liturgical books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-de-toc:
Alexis de Tocqueville was a French writer and statesman, born at Verneuil in July 1805 and dead at Cannes in April 1859. His great-grandfather was Malesherbes, who defended Louis XVI. While judging at Versailles in 1830 he befriended Gustave de Beaumont, and the two travelled to America, where Tocqueville studied the penitentiary system and democracy.

Two books came from the journey: a joint work on the American penitentiary system. Tocqueville's own Democracy in America appeared in two volumes, in 1835 and 1840. The book won him seats in the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences in 1838 and the French Academy in 1841. As deputy for Valognes he sat with the opposition. He served the Second Republic as vice-president of the Legislative Assembly and foreign minister in 1849. Under the Empire he wrote The Old Regime and the Revolution, whose first part appeared in 1856.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-stole: The altar stole was a medieval ornament shaped like the ends of a stole and fixed to the altar's front. It borrowed the stole's form for display rather than wear, marking the altar itself with a priestly emblem. Medieval altars thus carried a familiar vestment shape as pure ornament alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-lisle:
Ambrose Lisle March Phillipps de Lisle was born 17 March 1809 and died 5 March 1878, son of Charles March Phillipps of Garendon Park and Harriet Ducarel of Huguenot descent. He took the de Lisle name in 1862 on inheriting the family's estates at his father's death. Brought up Anglican, he met the émigré Abbé Giraud at school, whose holy life clashed with what he had heard of Catholics. A Paris visit in 1823 introduced him to Catholic liturgy.

He persuaded his Anglican rector to set a cross on the communion table, promptly suppressed by Peterborough's bishop as savouring of Popery. He later devoted persistent energy and faith to Catholicism's spread, through material help and spiritual means he valued more strongly. The rest of his life passed without special incident, though he stayed active in public affairs touching the Church's fortunes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amende-honora:
The amende honorable was an obsolete French church form of honorary satisfaction, lasting into the seventeenth century. The name itself marks the act: honourable amends offered openly, not privately. Performed at the ecclesiastical judge's bidding within his court's precinct, it could once be enforced at the church door or another public place. It fell ordinarily only on condemned criminals, who came stripped to the shirt, barefoot and bareheaded, candle in hand, begging pardon of God, the king, and justice.

Its public, barefoot, candle-lit form made the penance itself the satisfaction, performed where justice sat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amiel-weeks-w:
Amiel Weeks Whipple, military engineer and soldier, was born at Greenwich, Massachusetts, in 1818 and died at Washington in 1863. Son of David and Abigail Pepper Whipple, he studied at Amherst, graduated West Point in 1841, and surveyed the Patapsco, New Orleans approaches, and Portsmouth Harbour. He later fixed parts of the Canadian and Mexican boundaries, and in 1853 led Pacific railroad explorations near the 35th parallel.

Becoming Catholic around 1857 in Detroit lighthouse service, he engineered under McDowell and McClellan, his maps serving many Virginian battlefields. As brigadier-general of volunteers in 1862 he defended Washington's Virginia side and fought gallantly at Antietam and Fredericksburg. He was mortally wounded by a sharpshooter at Chancellorsville, receiving the last rites on the field. Breveted brigadier-general on 4 May, major-general of volunteers on 6 May, and major-general by brevet on 7 May, he died hours later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancren-riwle:
Ancren Riwle is a thirteenth-century rule for anchoresses. In Middle English ancren meant solitaries of either sex. This rule speaks only to ladies who left the world for a secluded religious life. Several copies survive. One, at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, bears the title Ancren Wisse. Some take it for an abridgment of Simon of Ghent's Latin tract. Simon was Bishop of Salisbury from 1297 to 1315.

The British Museum holds five copies. Three served Morton's Camden Society edition of 1852. Morton rejects the idea that the English text translates Simon of Ghent. He judges Cotton Cleopatra C vi the English original. The rule orders a day given mostly to prayer, with Litany and Office for the Dead. Its author admits the life, with the ten old Commandments, is hard. Yet he adds that nothing is so hard that love does not make it tender, soft, and sweet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animals-in-th:
The Bible makes no pretensions to science, so it holds no elaborate classification. The sacred books were composed by and for a pastoral people in constant communication with nature. To such a people, references to animals are natural, and the more animals abounded, the more frequent they are. In fact, over a hundred and twenty species are named in the Scriptures.

How animal references are introduced, their frequency, and their documents' dates may show the country's conditions at different stages of its history. The article proceeds species by species, weighing Hebrew names against Palestine's fauna. Entries run from the camel, reckoned unclean among the Jews, to the camelopardalus of Deuteronomy, combining camel and leopard for the giraffe. This translation is doubtless erroneous, since neither giraffe nor chamois lived in Palestine. Further entries cover the cankerworm, the locust in its larva state, and the cat, mentioned only once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-teril:
Anthony Terill, born Bonville, was an English theologian from Canford, born in 1623 and died at Liège in 1676. His Catholic mother and faith-estranged father raised him in heresy until fifteen, when he converted and left England as Terill. He studied about three years at Saint Omer's English College, then began priesthood studies at Rome's English College.

Two months after ordination he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Saint Andrea. After his noviceship he served as penitentiary at Loreto, professor at Florence and Parma, then theology and mathematics professor at Liège, and rector there for three years. He wrote Conclusiones philosophicæ (1657), Problema mathematico-philosophicum (1660), Fundamentum totius theologiæ moralis (1668), and Regula morum (1677, posthumous). The last two made him a moral theologian: the Fundamentum defends probabilism, and the Regula morum answers objections from Concina, Elizalde, and other Rigorists. Amort calls him eruditissimum et probabilistarum antsignanum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-perre:
Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, a statesman cardinal born in 1517, served two Habsburg emperors across a long career. Son of Charles the Fifth's chief minister, he studied at Padua and Louvain and became bishop of Arras at twenty-one. He spoke for the emperor at the Council of Trent and helped settle the Peace of Crepy and the marriage of Philip the Second to Mary Tudor.

Under Philip Philip raised him to Mechlin's archbishopric in 1559, and to the cardinalate two years later, guiding the Netherlands as chief counsellor to Margaret of Parma. Unpopular with local nobles, he left Brussels, yet his vast correspondence, edited in many volumes, still records Habsburg policy in detail. The entry portrays a tireless minister whose pen shaped an empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apsidiole: An apsidiole, also written absidiale, is a small or secondary apse. It is one of the apses flanking the main apse in a three-apse church. It may also be an apse chapel projecting outside the church, above all when the projection itself resembles an apse in shape. Bond, writing on Gothic architecture in England, notes that the Norman plan of the eastern limb brought to England at the Conquest held a central apse flanked by apsidioles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aristotle:
Aristotle, called here the greatest of pagan philosophers, was born at Stagira, a Greek colony in Chalcidice, in 384 BC and died at Chalcis in Euboea in 322 BC. His father Nicomachus served as court physician to King Amyntas of Macedonia, a post his ancestors had held, so medicine ran in the family. That background likely shaped the young Aristotle's turn toward investigating natural phenomena when, at eighteen, he went to Athens.

From eighteen to thirty-seven he stayed at Athens as Plato's pupil, distinguished among those who gathered in the Grove of Academus near Plato's house. Legends about teacher and pupil abound, many painting Aristotle in a harsh light. The article sets those tales beside the record of a mind that ranged over logic, nature, ethics, and politics. Readers get the life that underlies the system later Christians both used and debated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armidale:
Armidale is a diocese in New South Wales, Australia, with Armidale's cathedral, 335 miles north of Sydney, and one of six suffragan sees in the Sydney province. Its borders run from Queensland in the north to Lismore diocese in the east, Wilcannia ten miles beyond Walgett in the west, and Maitland and Bathurst in the south. They cover about 85,000 square miles. Armidale became a municipality only in 1863.

Ten years earlier, in 1853, Timothy McCarthy became its first resident priest, in a thinly settled farming and grazing district where Catholics lived few and far apart. McCarthy made Armidale his headquarters, and his missionary district, Cardinal Moran says, stretched to the Queensland border and the Pacific Ocean. His tours lasted three months, from the Tweed down to the Richmond, then to the Clarence, on to Walcha, and across the Liverpool ranges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astronomy-in-:
Astronomy in the Bible begins from a negative: Jews made no systematic observations of heavenly bodies. Astral worship was rife in Palestine, and close attention to its objects risked yielding to its seductions. Astronomy therefore stayed inseparable from star worship, and prophets' anathemas against it were not careless. As the Almighty's most glorious works, celestial lights are celebrated in scripture in passages thrilling with rapture, but practical appeal to them shrank to a minimum.

Even regulating times and seasons stayed largely empirical. Jews used a lunar year, beginning for religious purposes with the new moon following the spring equinox, normally twelve months or 354 days. Since festivals were partly agricultural, the calendar also depended on the sun's course, and some adjustment was needed to fit lunar months to solar seasons. The entry follows that calendar problem through biblical texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auriesville:
Auriesville is the site of the Mohawk village in Montgomery County, New York, where Father Isaac Jogues and his companions Goupil and Lalande were killed for the faith. It stands on the south bank of the Mohawk, about forty miles west of Albany. The name comes from Auries, the last Mohawk there, while the Indians called the village Ossernenon, also Gandawaga. Jogues and Goupil were brought there as prisoners in 1642, and Jogues returned with Lalande in 1646.

Bressani was tortured there in 1644, and after Le Moyne's peace embassy a permanent mission rose in 1667. Fathers such as Lamberville, Fremin, and Bruyas labored there until the mission was destroyed in 1684. The Indian girl Tegakwitha was born at the village and later escaped to Canada. Pilgrims still gather in summer, often four or five thousand strong, fasting and receiving Communion at the shrine. The buildings are temporary, pending the Church's judgment on the martyrdoms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-authenticity-:
The authenticity of the Bible, this short entry argues, is twofold, because its authorship is twofold. First, the books of the Bible are authentic in the human sense: they enjoy all the natural authority due to their respective human authors. That first kind of authenticity must be weighed book by book, and the entry sends readers to the articles on the several books of Scripture for those cases.

Second, the books hold a higher authenticity, because a divine, supernatural authority clothes them through divine authorship. They are, in the entry's terms, the inspired word of God. That second sense springs from biblical inspiration itself, and the entry points to the article on Inspiration for its full defense. The piece is thus a brief map of a larger argument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barocco-style:
Barocco, French baroque, is a debased application of Renaissance features to architecture. The term also marks bad taste in design and ornament generally. Carlo Maderna, Bernini, and Borromini rank among its most famous practitioners. Leading examples are Maderna's Santa Maria della Vittoria and Borromini's Santa Agnese, both at Rome.

Naples is full of baroque churches, though a few, like the Gesù Nuovo, are dignified and creditable designs. Longhena's domical Santa Maria della Salute at Venice stands majestic and in excellent style. Three Venetian churches, San Barnaba, San Basso, and San Moise, show three different baroque types. The style ruled church architecture for nearly two centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belleville:
Belleville is a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covering the southern Illinois diocese created in 1887. Its territory runs across the southern counties of the state, carved out of the older Diocese of Alton after its bishop died. John Janssen, once vicar-general at Alton, became its first bishop in 1888.

Statistics anchor the entry, listing parishes, clergy, schools, and church buildings at the diocese's founding and in its later years. Growth in priests, parishes, and Catholic schools shows a young diocese filling out its map. The piece reads as a snapshot of church organization on the American prairie.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury, was the last Plantagenet of her line to fall to Henry VIII. She was executed in 1541 after her son Reginald denounced the king's divorce. Born in 1473, she was the daughter of George, Duke of Clarence. She married Richard Pole, was widowed in 1505, and was restored by Henry VIII as countess and governess to Princess Mary.

Her favor ended when Reginald, then in exile, sent Henry his treatise defending church unity and attacking the divorce. Though Margaret and her eldest son rebuked Reginald, Henry struck at the family in England. Two sons were arrested for treason in 1538, and Margaret herself was put to death on Tower Green on 27 May 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brownsville:
Brownsville, a vicariate apostolic erected in 1874, covers 22,391 square miles of lower Texas along the Rio Grande. Before that date all Texas lay under Galveston. The state then split into Galveston north of the Colorado, San Antonio between the Colorado and Nueces, and Brownsville southward. Brownsville took Cameron, Hidalgo, Starr, Zapata, and Webb counties with others north of the Nueces.

Its chief towns are Laredo with 12,000 people, Brownsville with 8,000, and Corpus Christi with 7,000, amid a total of about 110,000, including 79,000 Catholics, mostly Mexican, and 3,000 English-speaking Catholics. Indians held the land less than sixty years before. Brownsville began with Major Brown in the Mexican War, and its church rose in 1852. Oblate fathers, settled in 1852, mission from San Ignacio to the river's mouth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burchard-of-b:
Burchard of Basle, an eleventh-century bishop and loyal partisan of Henry IV, fought the pope's cause with sword and council. Born to the counts of Neuenburg about mid-century, he became Bishop of Basle in 1072 through Henry's favor and served as a foremost royal adviser. He aided Henry against the Saxons in 1073 and 1075, then joined the Worms assembly of January 1076 that proclaimed Gregory VII deposed and wrote him an insulting letter.

With Huzmann of Speyer he won Lombard bishops at Piacenza to renounce Gregory, earning excommunication and deposition at the Lenten synod of 1076. He walked with Henry to Canossa in January 1077 and regained his office. In the civil war against Rudolf of Swabia he fought repeatedly, suffered crushing defeat in 1078 and barely escaped, then ravaged Swabia with cruel soldiery until Rudolf fell dead in 1080. Henry rewarded him with land, and he died on 12 April 1107.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canticle:
Canticle is the English Catholic Bible's word for the Vulgate's canticum when it means a sacred song. Other uses of the same Latin word appear simply as song. The distinction matters because the Authorized Version translates from Hebrew and Greek and calls everything song. It does not mark the sacred cases apart.

Seven Old Testament canticles from the Breviary serve at Lauds through the week. Sundays use the Canticle of the Three Children, and Saturdays use the Canticle of Moses. New Testament canticles join them, including Zachary's at Lauds. The entry also notes English usage, where the Prayer Book restricts the word to the Benedicite. Its calendar applies Canticles to the Song of Solomon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-captain-in-th:
Captain in the Douay Bible stands for several different Hebrew and Latin words covering both civil and military officers. The entry warns that the rendering follows no fixed rule. The same Hebrew or Latin term may appear as captain in one place and under another word elsewhere. That holds for the Vulgate as well as for the Hebrew and Greek texts.

Civil uses are rare and reserved for the highest offices, such as captain of my people. Military uses run through every grade, from captains of the host and of thousands to captains of hundreds, fifties, and tens. Chariot captains, cavalry commanders, and bodyguard chiefs complete the range. In the New Testament the word occurs only once, in Matthew's quotation of Micah's promise of a captain to rule Israel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlisle:
Carlisle was an ancient English diocese, smaller than the present Anglican diocese enlarged in 1856. Its territory first became a political unit under William Rufus. He made it the Earldom of Carlisle from most of Cumberland and Westmoreland. Under Henry I the earldom became a bishopric, after belonging to Durham with a strong Celtic element looking to Glasgow.

Henry secured his former confessor Æthelwulf, an Augustinian prior, as first bishop in 1133, and Æthelwulf ruled until 1156, building a Norman minster whose transepts and nave survive in part. His Augustinian canons served the cathedral, an arrangement unusual in England. The entry closes with a plundered diocese, a single archdeaconry, and a cathedral first dedicated to the Virgin and later, at the Reformation, to the Holy Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-epis:
The Catholic Epistles are the letter of St. James, the letter of St. Jude, two letters of St. Peter, and the first three letters of St. John. They carry the name Catholic because, unlike the letters of St. Paul, they were written not to one person or church but to the faithful in general, in the manner of an encyclical letter.

The name reaches a little further than the address alone would suggest. The other two letters of St. John, though written to particular persons, also carry the name Catholic, since they have always been shelved with the letters bearing it. The entry is short, but it fixes the meaning of a term readers meet throughout the New Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-saint:
An entry on Charles Sainte-Claire Deville, a French geologist who studied volcanoes and built France's weather service. Born at St. Thomas in the West Indies in 1814, he trained at the Paris School of Mines and began with explorations in the Antilles, studying earthquakes and eruptions. Visits to Vesuvius and Stromboli in the late 1850s fed his theory that eruptions come from sea water entering cracks in the earth's crust and meeting hot rock.

Deville joined the Academy of Sciences in 1857, assisted Elie de Beaumont at the Collège de France, succeeding him as professor in 1875. As inspector general of the Meteorological Service from 1872, he set up a chain of weather stations across France and Algeria and became first president of the Montsouris observatory. He also worked in chemistry, analysing minerals and studying molecular physics, before his death in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chasuble:
An entry on the chasuble, the chief and most visible vestment worn by a priest at Mass, covering all the rest. In Latin it is called casula or planeta. Liturgical dress grew from ordinary Roman clothing, with garments set aside, newer and cleaner, for sacred use. The chasuble itself began as the common outer cloak of the lower orders, a square or round cloth with a hole for the head.

Its name means little house, since like a small cottage it covers the whole person. Over time the garment narrowed, and the French type grew less ample and often stiff, with a cross on the back. Medieval crosses often took a Y shape for reasons of cut rather than symbol. Before use the chasuble is blessed, and at ordination the bishop calls it the priestly vestment signifying charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chile:
A wide-ranging entry on Chile, the narrow strip of South American coast between the Pacific and the Andes. It runs some 2,500 miles from latitude 17 degrees south to Cape Horn, varying from 185 to 100 miles in width. Peaks rise over 22,000 feet, more than forty volcanoes dot the range, and the north is arid while the south is cold and timbered, with glaciers reaching the sea. Its minerals include gold, silver, copper, iron, nitrates, and coal.

Church life forms one part of the survey. Chile makes a single ecclesiastical province, with the Archdiocese of Santiago and the sees of Concepción, Ancud, and Serena, plus the vicariates of Tarapacá and Antofagasta. Indian missions in the south are run by Franciscans, Capuchins, and Salesians, religious orders staff many schools and colleges, and religious teaching is compulsory even in public schools. The entry also traces the country's peoples and history from before 1535.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronicon-pas:
An entry on the Chronicon Paschale, the Paschal Chronicle, a valuable Byzantine world chronicle of the seventh century. It takes its name from its system of Christian chronology, built on the paschal canon, the cycle for fixing Easter. It is also called the Alexandrine, Antiochene, Casaubonian, Constantinopolitan chronicle, or the Sicilian Fasti.

Its anonymous author titled it an epitome spanning Adam, the first man, to the twentieth year of the emperor Heraclius and the nineteenth consulship of his son Constantine. Like other Byzantine chronicles it follows Eusebius, beginning with Creation and running to its own day. Written in the plain but ornate idiom of common life, it mixes church history with anecdotes, portraits, earthquakes, and comets for monks and ordinary readers of the Eastern Empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commentaries-:
Cornelius Aherne's vast survey admits at the start that a full history of exegesis would fill many volumes. Even Dante, a recent writer, had drawn thirteen hundred commentaries by 1900. So Aherne gives only the barest outline, with a bibliography to lead readers further. He touches the high points of Jewish, patristic, medieval, and modern commentaries, both Catholic and non-Catholic. Jewish writing comes first, since it leads naturally into Christian exegesis.

That Jewish section runs through Philo, the Targums, the Mishna and Talmuds, and the Midrashim. Hillel and Shammai, the last of the paired teachers, anchor the Mishna tradition, while later rabbis debated its text for generations. Patristic, medieval, and modern writers follow in turn, each age reading Scripture through its own tools. The entry serves as a map: a reader can grasp the whole field's shape, then follow its bibliography into any period or school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordances-:
John Francis Fenlon's entry defines Bible concordances as verbal indexes: lists of Bible words in alphabetical order, pointing to every passage where each word occurs. A good concordance quotes enough of each passage to jog the memory of one who knows it. Subject indexes exist too, but English usage means a verbal concordance, a text-finder. It helps every Bible student locate a half-remembered text from a single important word. Fenlon calls it useful, indeed indispensable.

Verbal concordances began with Dominican friars for Latin. Hebrew's first came from Mordecai or Isaac Nathan, worked on from 1438 to 1448. Greek Septuagint concordances start with Kircher in 1607 and Tromm in 1718. Greek New Testament pioneers include Betulius in 1546, Estienne in 1594, and Schmid in 1638. Syriac rests on Schaaf's Lexicon of 1709. English concordances arose in the mid-sixteenth century. No concordance to the English Catholic Bible then existed, save for deutero-canonical books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantinopl:
Siméon Vailhé's entry follows Constantinople, city of Constantine, Byzantine, now Ottoman, capital. The modern city holds one of the world's finest sites, joining Europe with Asia. It links the Black Sea and Southern Russia with greater Europe and Asia. Water surrounds it except on the west, guarded by walls. Its sea front runs about eight miles, air generally pure, climate very temperate.

A special district in three sections, two European and one Asian, frames the city. Stamboul borders the Sea of Marmora, while Galata and Pera form European quarters. The Bosporus, about eighteen miles long, separates Europe from Asia. Early history traces Byzantium's founding; the Christian city took the name Constantinople by 324. Constantine chose it as the Empire's new capital, though wars kept him away. Church prosperity matched political grandeur, with rich churches and court luxury exciting covetousness. Heresy and schism follow, Photius leading the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ba:
The Council of Basle, convoked by Martin V in 1431 and closed at Lausanne in 1449, grew from the wounds of the Avignon papacy and the Great Western Schism. Rival claimants for St Peter's throne had shaken faith in monarchical church government. Reformers looked to a council for remedy. Reform of the Church in head and members, peace among nations, and settlement of the Hussite wars stood as its purposes.

Quarrels with Eugene IV over presidency and dissolution split the assembly, which declared a council superior to a pope, deposed Eugene, and elected the antipope Felix V. The rump at Basle faded into schism while the council's ideas lived on, feeding Gallicanism in France through the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges and preparing German minds for severance from Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-cons:
A biographical entry presents Cuthbert Constable, formerly Tunstall, who died on 27 March 1746. Son of Francis Tunstall of Wycliffe Hall, he inherited the Burton Constable estates in 1718 on his uncle's death and changed his surname to Constable. Educated at Douai, he studied medicine at Montpellier and took a doctorate.

At Burton Constable he built a large collection of books and manuscripts and became a steady patron of Catholic letters. He lent documents to Bishop Challoner for his Memoirs of Missionary Priests and helped fund Dodd's History of the Church of England. His papers hold correspondence with Oxford scholars, above all on Abraham Woodhead, whom he revered. His only publication was a life of Woodhead prefixed to an edition of Woodhead's work in 1736.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-noble:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Noble, a Manchester physician born in 1810 and dead in 1885. Son of a Preston Catholic family, he was apprenticed to a surgeon. He joined the Royal College of Surgeons, and began practice in Manchester in 1834. There he soon developed the keen interest in mental disease that marked his career.

His first work, an essay on estimating human character, made him president of the Manchester Phrenological Society. Later books covered manufactures and health, the brain and its physiology, and psychological medicine, including a study of insanity. He married in 1840, fathered eight children, one the novelist Frances Noble, and became a fellow of the College of Physicians in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desert-in-the:
An entry on the Hebrew words that the Douay Bible renders as desert or wilderness, and why they differ from the English idea. No Sahara-like waste is meant: these tracts gave pasture for flocks and sheltered nomads, not settled towns. Four words carry the sense, each with its own shade, and the entry works through them one by one.

Midbar, the most general term, comes from a root meaning to lead cattle to pasture. Arabah names an arid steppe plain, Horbah a place lying waste, and Jeshimon a waterless waste. Chief biblical deserts follow, from the Exodus tract to Sin, Sinai, Cades, and Pharan, and the temptation of Christ is placed, tentatively, in the Arabah west of the Jordan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-disciple:
Disciple most often means one who learns an art or science from a master. The word comes from the Latin discipulus, though the English sense is narrower, setting disciple against master as scholar stands to teacher. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the Old Testament uses the word only once, in Isaiah. Yet the idea appears when writers speak of sons of the prophets and of children in the wisdom books.

The New Testament uses disciple far more freely, first for pupils of a teacher and then for converts and believers, men and women alike. Even the half-taught folk Saint Paul found at Ephesus bear the name. The entry thus maps a word that grew from the classroom into the very title of the Christian believer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domicile:
Domicile, in canon law, is the right of dwelling or residence, borrowed from Roman law and refined by the Church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that canon law holds no home-grown theory of domicile. Both canon law and modern civil codes took the Roman doctrine, while canon law added the notion of quasi-domicile, a second home with legal weight.

For centuries church law made no special rule on domicile, bending to Roman and barbarian custom. Only in the thirteenth century, after Bologna revived Roman law study, did legists and canonists bring the Roman theory into the schools and then into practice. The entry traces that reception and its bearing on marriage, benefices, and church courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donatus-of-fi:
Donatus of Fiesole was an Irish teacher, poet, and bishop who ruled from about 829 to 876. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry draws on an old collection of lives of the fathers, copied in the eleventh century at Florence. Irish-born of a noble house, Donatus visited the apostles' tombs at Rome about 816. Journeying north, providence led him to Fiesole as the people prayed for a bishop.

Raised by popular acclaim to the see, he revived piety and learning in his church and taught the art of metrical composition himself. He also wrote verse praising his homeland and its people, and an epitaph recalling his Irish birth, his service to the princes of Italy, and his teaching of grammar and poetry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-douay-bible:
The Douay Bible is the English Catholic version on which nearly all later English Catholic Bibles still rest. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces it to the religious wars of the sixteenth century, when Protestant versions, used as weapons of debate, showed signs of controversial bias in their renderings. English Catholics needed a translation of their own, exact and fit to appeal to in argument.

The English College at Douai in Flanders took up the task; William Allen had founded it in 1568. Doctor Gregory Martin carried the chief share. Challoner's revision of 1749 became the standard text in most later editions, while Archbishop Kenrick's independent revision served America from 1849 to 1859. The entry thus tells the birth of the English Catholic Bible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-droit-de-rega:
Droit de regale, the right of regality, first meant all rights belonging to the king alone. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry splits them into greater rights, essential to sovereignty such as royal authority, and lesser rights, such as hunting, fishing, and mining. By abuse, rulers of the Middle Ages and later claimed the income of vacant sees and imperial abbeys, and the phrase narrowed to that seized right.

On what ground rulers claimed the income is disputed, whether from sovereignty itself, from investiture, or from feudal tenure. The entry weighs these views and points to the long quarrel with the papacy, above all under Innocent the Eleventh and Louis the Fourteenth. It cites Stutz, Michelet, and Mention among the scholars of the dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-editions-of-t:
Editions of the Bible, in this entry, means the printed reproductions of its original texts. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets aside both manuscript copies of the originals and printed or written versions, which have their own articles. Since the original text was written in Hebrew or Greek, with small Aramaic portions counted with the Hebrew, the study follows the printed Hebrew and Greek texts from their first presses onward.

The entry explains the critical marks and symbols by which Bible codices are denoted, a system set out more fully under Biblical Criticism. It closes with the great modern editors, from Gregory's Text Criticism to Von Soden's writings on the oldest reachable form of the New Testament. For students of the Bible's text, it is a map of print after centuries of hand copying.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eduard-von-st:
Eduard von Steinle was an Austrian historical painter of the Romantic school, born at Vienna in 1810 and dead at Frankfurt in 1886. He learned from Kupelwieser, Overbeck, and Cornelius, and took in the new German manner formed at Rome, though he chose to work in Germany. Early commissions took him to Rheineck Castle chapel and to Frankfurt's Hall of Emperors, where he painted Albert I and Ferdinand III.

From 1850 he taught historical painting at Frankfurt's Stadel Institute. He left more than a hundred religious panel pictures and cartoons for church windows, and he painted great fresco cycles at Klein-Heubach, Munster, Aachen, and Cologne Cathedral. Critics praised his detail but felt his wall work lacked the broad, monumental sweep such painting needs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphanius-of:
Epiphanius of Constantinople was Patriarch of that city from 520 until his death in 535. He followed John II at a turning point: the reaction against Monophysitism that came with the accession of the Catholic emperor Justin I in 518. Justin let the Henotikon of Zeno quietly drop, and a synod of forty bishops under John II proclaimed Chalcedon across the empire and deposed Monophysite bishops.

That synod also reopened talks with Rome after the Acacian schism of 484 to 519. On Easter Day, 24 March 519, reunion was proclaimed, and Monophysite leaders fled to Egypt. When John died in 520, Epiphanius succeeded him with papal authority to reconcile schismatics who retracted and signed Pope Hormisdas's formula. He signed it himself first, and four of his letters to Hormisdas survive, with the pope's replies, showing his eagerness for communion with Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euphemius-of-:
Euphemius was Patriarch of Constantinople from 490 to 496, during the Acacian schism that split East and West for thirty-five years. The breach began when Emperor Zeno's Henotikon of 482 tried to please both sides. It held to Nicaea and Constantinople while passing over Chalcedon and its teaching on Christ's two natures. Euphemius, who followed Acacius and his successor, set out to heal the wound.

He recognized Chalcedon, put the pope's name back in the diptychs, the lists read aloud in the liturgy, and broke with Peter Mongus of Alexandria. Yet he would not strike the names of Acacius and his own predecessor from those lists, and Rome refused communion on any other terms. Later he made Emperor Anastasius sign a Catholic profession of faith. The emperor turned on him, had him accused of treason, deposed him in 496, and sent him into exile, where he died at Ancyra in 515.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fiesole:
Fiesole is a Tuscan diocese, suffragan of the archdiocese of Florence. Of ancient Etruscan origin, it once outdid Florence in power in the valley below. Sulla colonised it, and the Florentines sacked it in 1010 and 1025. Its cathedral of St Romulus, built in 1028, holds notable sculptures by Mino da Fiesole.

St Donatus, an Irish monk and bishop from 826, advised the emperors Louis the Pious and Lothair. St Andrew Corsini, bishop from 1352, won fame as a peacemaker between individuals and states. Fra Angelico, called da Fiesole, trained in its Dominican house of San Domenico. The diocese counted 254 parishes and some 155,800 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-council:
The First Council of Constantinople met in May 381, called by Emperor Theodosius. Its aims were a Catholic line at Constantinople, the Nicene faith, and an end to Macedonian heresy. Some 150 Catholic and 36 dissenting bishops attended, first under Meletius of Antioch. After Meletius died, Gregory Nazianzen and then Nectarius presided in turn.

The council confirmed Gregory as bishop and issued the famous Constantinopolitan creed. That creed, likely a Jerusalem form of words from 369 to 373, stressed the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Its first canon condemned Arianism, Macedonianism, and Apollinarianism in all their shades. Its third canon gave Constantinople honour second only to Old Rome, a rank Rome long resisted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fourth-counci:
The Fourth Council of Constantinople, counted as the Eighth General Council, opened on 5 October 869 in the cathedral of Hagia Sophia under legates of Pope Adrian II. It grew out of a decade of turmoil in which Photius had displaced Patriarch Ignatius and tried to depose Pope Nicholas I. When the emperor Basil the Macedonian took power in 867, Photius was confined to a monastery, Ignatius was recalled, and both emperor and patriarch asked Rome for a general council.

Never more than 102 bishops attended. The council made them sign the formula of Pope Hormisdas, pledging to follow the Apostolic See of Rome. It reconciled bishops who had sided with Photius, heard Photius himself in silence or brief answers, renewed his excommunication, and banished him to a monastery on the Bosporus. Its twenty-seven canons also condemned the last traces of iconoclasm and interference by civil rulers in church affairs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-vata:
Francois Vatable, better called Watebled and also written Gastebled or Ouateble, was a French Hellenist and Hebraist born at Gamaches in Picardy, probably late in the fifteenth century. He died at Paris on 16 March 1547.

He is rightly regarded as the restorer of Hebrew scholarship in France, and his Paris lectures drew large audiences, even Jews among them, yet he published nothing in his lifetime. From notes taken by his pupils Robert Estienne drew scholia for his edition of Leo of Juda's new Latin Bible. But Zurich Protestants shamefully garbled those notes, the Sorbonne condemned their Lutheran tendencies, and Vatable himself disowned them, though they remain a model of clear scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galle:
Galle, a diocese in Ceylon created by Leo XIII in August 1893, covers the Southern and Sabaragamuwa provinces, some 4,000 square miles. Of about 900,000 people, only 10,160 were Catholics in 1909, scattered among Sinhalese, Moors, and Tamils, Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and Protestants. Racial and religious variety makes conversion and teaching slow work.

Leo XIII gave the new see to Belgian Jesuits, with Joseph Van Reeth as first bishop, consecrated at Antwerp in March 1895. He arrived with three priests and a lay brother that November. Progress ran slow but steady: confessions rose from 6,381 in 1897 to 27,956 in 1908, schools grew from fourteen to thirty-nine, and Saint Aloysius College opened in 1901. Sisters' lace even won gold at Saint Louis in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genealogy-in-:
Genealogy in the Bible treats the lists that open with the words these are the generations, a phrase the article reads as simply this is the history.
