The word genealogy itself appears only twice in the New Testament and rarely in the Old, yet lists crowd the early books. Primitive history, the entry argues, was genealogy dressed with anecdotes.

The article first untangles the heading, noting that heaven and earth have no posterity and that the Flood story follows the formula in Genesis. It then names the chief lists: Adam to Noah, Noah's sons as peoples, Shem to Abraham, Thare's line, Nahor's, Ishmael's, Jacob's sons, Esau's princes, and Jacob's house entering Egypt. Sources, weight, and gaps of each list follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-d:
Geoffrey of Dunstable, also called Geoffrey of Gorham, ruled Saint Albans Abbey wisely for twenty-six years. A scholar from Maine in Normandy, he was invited to lead the abbey school, found the post filled on arrival, and opened his own school at Dunstable instead. After borrowing copes for a miracle play, he lost house and all in a fire the night after the show.

To repay God and the saint for the copes, Geoffrey became a monk of Saint Albans, rose to prior, and was elected abbot in 1119. He built an infirmary with chapel and spent lavishly on a new shrine for Saint Alban's body, translated in August 1129. He endowed Sopwell nunnery, founded Markyate for Christina the recluse, and opened a leper hospital. He even saved the abbey in Stephen's civil war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-d-an:
Giuseppe D'Annibale was a cardinal and theologian born at Borbona in the diocese of Rieti on 22 September 1815, who died at the same place on 18 July 1892. He taught at the seminary of Rieti and later served as vicar-general of the diocese. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a moral theologian of two valued works.

Leo XIII made him titular Bishop of Caryste in 1881 and created him Cardinal-Priest of Saints Boniface and Alexis in 1889. He became Prefect of the Congregation of Indulgences. His treatise on moral theology, the Summula theologiae moralis, appeared at Milan from 1881 to 1883. His commentary on the constitution Apostolicae Sedis, published at Rieti in 1880, is also valued by theologians and canonists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gremiale:
Within Catholic ceremonial dress, the gremiale is a square or oblong cloth that a bishop wears over his lap while seated on his throne. The entry lists its moments of use: the choir's singing of the Kyrie, Gloria, and Credo, the giving out of blessed candles, palms, or ashes, and anointings at ordinations. It never appears at pontifical Vespers.

Its plain job is to keep other vestments, above all the chasuble, clean. Silk serves for pontifical Mass, marked with a central cross and silk embroidery in the chasuble's colour, while linen serves at other functions so it can be washed. First noted about 1311, it is not blessed and carries no symbolic meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grenoble:
Grenoble's entry covers a French diocese now made up of the Isère department and the canton of Villeurbanne, tracing its bishops from Domninus, present at Aquileia in 381, through reforming St. Hugh, restorer Pierre Scarron, and charity organizer Cardinal Le Camus. A second part treats the older Archbishopric of Vienne and the legends around its first bishops.

Monastic life fills much of the story, from early Benedictine and Augustinian priories to the Carthusians founded by St. Bruno in 1084, alongside the Waldenses, the wars of religion, and the passages of Popes Pius VI and Pius VII through the city. Readers get both a diocesan survey and a critical look at Vienne's forged early claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-del:
Paris mapmaker Guillaume Delisle, born in 1675, remade cartography by building maps on measured astronomy instead of copied guesswork. His father Claude taught geography and drew maps. The son's Map of the World and Map of the Continents of 1700, followed by maps of each land worked out one by one, set a new standard. It won him the new post of First Royal Geographer.

Delisle used French astronomers' scale measurements to fix places and sifted travel books and older maps where star readings ran short. He named his sources on disputed points and kept one fixed scale across neighbouring regions. The entry praises his corrected longitudes, full place lists, and careful spelling of names, and notes his Academy ranks from élève in 1702 to associé in 1718.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hebrew-bible:
The Hebrew Bible holds the whole Old Testament except the seven deuterocanonical books and the added portions of Esther and Daniel. This Jewish tradition never counted in the official Hebrew canon. Protestant versions follow its contents, while its threefold shape, Law, Prophets, and Writings, predates the prologue to Ecclesiasticus and differs sharply from the Septuagint order taken up by the Vulgate.

Law gives the five books of Moses in fixed order. Prophets join Joshua through Kings with Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve Minor Prophets as one book. Writings gather Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five festival Rolls, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles. Scribes first wrote bare consonants, then added word spacing, verse marks, and Massoretic helps, counting every letter, before Christian chapter numbers entered printed Hebrew Bibles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-seus:
Tyrolese Dominican Heinrich Seuse Denifle, born at Imst in 1844, was paleographer, historian, and Vatican archive keeper whose work reshaped the study of mystic thought and medieval seats of learning. A village schoolmaster's son, he entered the Dominicans at Graz in 1861, taught philosophy and theology there for a decade, and preached apologetic sermons printed in 1872.

His harvest of 2,500 fourteenth-century mystical texts in 1873, his exposure of the Gottesfreund as a myth. His proof that Catholic mystic thought rests on scholastic theology made his name. As archive keeper from 1883 he hunted Thomas Aquinas manuscripts across Europe and wrote the first volume of a university history in 1885. It showed these schools did not generally grow from cathedral schools and at first often taught no theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-etienne:
Chemist Henri-Etienne Sainte-Claire Deville, born at St. Thomas in the West Indies in 1818, made aluminium a commercial metal and discovered dissociation. After eight years in a self-built Paris laboratory without teachers or pupils, he organized Besançon's science faculty in 1844. He taught at the École Normale from 1851 and succeeded Dumas at the Sorbonne in 1859.

His mineral chemistry ranks him among the century's great chemists. Dissociation from 1857, nitrogen pentoxide, and a sodium process for aluminium, first found by Wöhler in 1827, let Napoleon III admire the silver of clay. With Debray he worked platinum metallurgy and pushed petroleum and heavy oils as steam fuel, publishing widely in the Comptes rendus and Annales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-chichel:
Henry Chichele, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1414, rose from a yeoman's family at Higham Ferrers through Winchester College and New College, Oxford, to many livings and legal offices. A skilled canon lawyer, he served Henry IV on missions to popes and to the King of France, attended the Council of Pisa, and was consecrated Bishop of St. David's in 1408 before the king nominated him to Canterbury. There he became Henry V's trusted councillor.

Chichele pursued the Lollards vigorously and defended ecclesiastical liberties against the statutes of Provisors and Praemunire. Martin V twice passed him over for the cardinalate and suspended his legatine office for weakness in pressing repeal. His lasting monuments are charitable and academic: a college and hospital at Higham Ferrers, and at Oxford the College of All Souls, whose modern history chair still bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-cole:
Henry Cole, a confessor of the faith born about 1500, studied at Winchester and New College, Oxford. There he became a perpetual fellow in 1523, then spent seven years in Italy, chiefly at Padua. He accumulated preferments, including the wardenship of New College, before returning to the Catholic faith about 1547 and resigning them all. Under Mary he rose again as Archdeacon of Ely, canon of Westminster, vicar-general to Cardinal Pole, and debater against Cranmer, Ridley, and Latimer at Oxford.

Elizabeth's reign brought the reverse: fined 500 marks, deprived of every preferment, committed to the Tower in May 1560 and then to the Fleet. There he remained nearly twenty years until his death in 1579 or 1580. Cole's writings survive largely inside other men's books. Disputations and sermons printed in Foxe's Acts and Monuments, answers to Protestant propositions in Burnet, and letters from Padua and Paris all trace a scholar caught between two religious settlements.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hexham-and-ne:
Hexham and Newcastle is the English diocese whose roots run back to an abbey founded in 674 by St. Wilfrid of York on land Queen St. Etheldreda gave. When York's diocese was divided in 678, Hexham became a bishopric for the land between the Aln and the Tees. Of the eleven bishops who followed the first bishop, St. Eata, six were saints, including St. John of Beverley and St. Acca, to whom Bede dedicated several works.

The ancient line ended with Tidfert about 821. Danish devastation brought disorder until Hexham monastery rose again in 1113 as a priory of Austin Canons, flourishing until its dissolution under Henry VIII. The bishopric meanwhile merged into Lindisfarne, removed to Chester-le-Street and then to Durham. The entry carries the story from those early saints through the priory years to the modern diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-carb:
Ignatius Carbonnelle was a Belgian professor of mathematics and science, born at Tournai in 1829 and dead at Brussels in 1889. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1844, gave himself to mathematical study, and contributed papers to the Royal Academy of Belgium's bulletins. After ordination, Calcutta claimed six years of his teaching, 1861 to 1867.

At Calcutta he became first editor of the Indo-European Correspondence from 1865 to 1867. Returning to Europe, he taught mathematics and astronomy at Louvain, then joined the staffs of Études, the Revue Catholique, and Brussels scientific annals and reviews. The Scientific Society of Brussels dates to his founding in 1875; he served as its secretary from 1877 and edited its annals and review until his death. Some essays were reprinted as Les Confins de la Science et de la Philosophie.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-inspiration-o:
Four questions drive this theology entry. Why do Catholics hold that certain books carry God's word? What does that inspiration mean? How far does it reach? How do Protestant views differ? Belief in sacred books runs as old as Hebrew literature itself, the entry notes. Moses and the prophets wrote down part of the message they were sent to deliver to Israel.

Prophets counted as authorized speakers of God's thoughts and wishes. They were called men of God and men of the Spirit. After the exile, the Temple and the Book anchored the people's religious and national renewal. Philo, writing around the turn of the era, already spoke of sacred books and most holy scripture. The entry builds from that Jewish ground toward the Catholic doctrine and its Protestant critics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-and-j:
Jacques de Lamberville was a Jesuit missionary born at Rouen in 1641. He died at Quebec in 1710. He joined the Society in 1661. He sailed to Canada in 1675. He labored almost without break on the Iroquois missions until death. At Onondaga he recognized a saint's soul in the Algonquin captive Catherine Tegakwitha. He instructed and baptized her.

He helped his brother Jean pacify Iroquois angered by Governor de la Barre's ill-timed campaign. After respite at Quebec and Montreal, he returned to Onondaga at native request. He left in 1709 through Abraham Schuyler's intrigues. He lived among the Iroquois while French and English rivalry for their alliance endangered missioners' lives. Charlevoix called him one of New France's holiest missionaries. The Indians called him the divine man. Jean's parallel career frames the same frontier story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-delil:
French abbé and man of letters Jacques Delille was born at Aigueperse on 22 June 1738. He died at Paris on 1 May 1813. He was educated at Paris' Collège de Lisieux. He became an instructor at the Collège de la Marche in Paris. His verse translation of Virgil's Georgics appeared in 1770. It won very great success and later gained him a seat in the French Academy.

He was then named to the poetry chair at the Collège de France. Through Count d'Artois' patronage he received the abbey of Saint-Séverin as a benefice, though he took only minor orders. In 1786 he accompanied Count de Choiseul to Constantinople and visited Greece. The Revolution stripped him of post and benefice. In 1794 he left France for exile in Switzerland, Germany, and England. He later returned to France. The entry follows a fashionable verse translator through revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-warren-:
Irish bishop James Warren Doyle was born near New Ross, County Wexford, in 1786. He died at Carlow in 1834. He belonged to a respectable but poor family. He was educated at Clonleigh, Rathconrogue, and later at New Ross' Augustinian college. Shortly after 1800 he joined the Augustinian order and was sent to Coimbra, Portugal. There at university he first showed great intellectual powers. In the university library he read everything, Voltaire and Rousseau among others.

As a consequence his faith became unsettled, but his vigorous intellect soon reasserted itself. Afterwards he became a fearless champion of the Church of his birth. During the French invasion he did sentry duty at Coimbra and accompanied the English to Lisbon as interpreter. He so impressed the Portuguese court that high employment was offered him. He declined it and returned to Ireland. The entry presents a bishop famed as Ireland's fearless controversialist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Corneille, a French painter and engraver born in Paris about 1646 and dead there in 1695, learned his craft from his father Michel. Called the younger Corneille, he took academy prizes in 1664 and 1668, studied in Rome, and entered the Royal Academy in 1675 with a scene of Hercules punishing Busiris.

Corneille painted for Paris churches, Notre-Dame, and the Tuileries, and became academy professor in 1692. His manner followed the Desiderosi school, a touch below his brother Michel in design and drawing. He also etched plates after his own pictures and after the Carracci, with a spirited hand that showed full command of line and acid.

Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, sieur de Bienville, Louisiana's French governor and the founder of New Orleans, was born at Montreal in 1680 and died in Paris in 1767. His father settled in Canada in 1640, and his brothers Iberville, Sérigny, and Chateauguay all helped shape early Louisiana.

Sailing with Iberville in 1698, Bienville helped found Biloxi, became its commandant in 1700, and governor after his brother's death in 1706. He fought the Natchez, finished Fort Rosalie, and under shifting companies held the colony through lean years. His lasting act came in 1718, when he laid out New Orleans, the city that grew into Louisiana's heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-chapeauv:
Jean Chapeauville, a Belgian theologian and historian born at Liège in 1551 and dead there in 1617, served his city church for a lifetime. After philosophy at Cologne and Louvain and a theology licentiate, he became synodal examiner in 1578, parish priest of Saint Michael's in 1579, and later provost of Saint Peter's.

Chapeauville also held posts as penitentiary canon, archdeacon of Famenne, inquisitor, and vicar-general under two bishops of Liège. He won praise for nursing the sick in the 1581 plague, for piety, and for teaching theology in Liège monasteries. He pressed Trent's reforms at home, above all a clerical seminary and open contests for parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-haute:
Jean de Hautefeuille, a French physicist born at Orléans in 1647 and dead there in 1724. He was a baker's son lifted by the Duchess of Bouillon, who funded his studies, took him through England and Italy, and left him a pension. Entering the Church, he held benefices from her gift.

Hautefeuille turned an inventive mind to clocks, proposing a coiled spring and balance wheel to replace the pendulum, a notion Huygens and Hooke also claimed. He studied speaking trumpets and echoes, improved lenses, sought to lift water by gunpowder blasts, and built a tide gauge he called a thalassameter. Genius he had, but rarely the patience to finish what he began.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-mande:
Jean de Mandeville, supposed author of a medieval book of travels much read in his age, is said to have died in 1372. The writer calls himself an English knight born at Saint Albans who left in 1322. He fought as a mercenary in Egypt, crossed Palestine, India, inner Asia, and China, and served the Great Khan for fifteen months.

After thirty-four years abroad he returned in 1356 and, with a physician met in Egypt, wrote his account at Liège. Later study showed the true author was Jean de Bourgoigne, a Liège physician who had seen only Egypt and stitched his book from other travellers' tales. Its wide reading and lively telling still made it a medieval bestseller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-paul-med:
Jean-Paul Médaille, a French Jesuit missionary born at Carcassonne in 1618 and dead at Auch in 1689. He joined the Society in 1640, taught college courses for years, including six years of philosophy, and then preached for eighteen years as his life's work.

Formed in the school of Saint Francis Régis, Médaille evangelised Velay, Auvergne, Languedoc, and Aveyron, founding fervent sodalities of men and women wherever he preached. Those groups taught children, visited the sick, and aided the poor, carrying his missions' fruits onward. Age and austerity at last turned him to directing sodalities and hearing confessions, above all of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-sire-de-:
Jean, Sire de Joinville, seneschal of Champagne and historian, was born in 1225 and died at Joinville in 1317. His family held high feudal rank in Champagne, and his father Simon defended Troyes in 1230 before dying in 1233, leaving Jean to his mother Beatrix of Burgundy.

Joinville took the cross in 1248, following Saint Louis yet refusing the king's oath since he was not his man. Funding two bannerets and ten knights himself, he sailed from Marseilles, joined Louis at Cyprus, fought in Egypt. He faced grave danger at Mansourah in 1250, fell ill, and was captured with the king. Freed that May, he followed Louis to Acre and later wrote the life of the saint-king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk Schelble was a German musician remembered as the founder of Frankfurt's Society of St. Cecilia. Born in the Black Forest in 1789, he sang at the Stuttgart court and opera, studied composition there, and went to Vienna in 1814, where he met Beethoven. In 1818 he became first tenor at Frankfurt, the city where he spent the rest of his life.

Starting with weekly musical evenings in his own house, Schelble built the Cacilienverein from twenty-one members in 1818 to about a hundred within a few years. Its concerts brought Mozart, Handel, Haydn, Beethoven, and after 1828 Bach to Frankfurt audiences, alongside older masters such as Palestrina. When illness forced him home in 1836, Felix Mendelssohn took his place, and friends praised Schelble's character as warmly as his art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-c-drumgo:
John C. Drumgoole was an Irish-born priest whose Mission of the Immaculate Virgin sheltered thousands of homeless New York children. Born at Granard in 1816, he emigrated to New York in 1824, worked as a shoemaker to support his widowed mother, and became sexton of St. Mary's in 1844. Running a small bookshop to fund his studies, he entered the seminary in 1865 and was ordained in 1869.

Put in charge of a languishing boys' lodging-house of the St. Vincent de Paul Society, he revived it, founded St. Joseph's Union to support it worldwide, and in 1881 opened an imposing Mission building on Great Jones Street. A Staten Island farm, Mount Loretto, followed, with trade schools run by Franciscan sisters, housing two thousand destitute children a year. At his death in 1888 he left the whole enterprise free of debt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-constabl:
John Constable, writing as Clerophilus Alethes, was an English Jesuit controversialist who defended Catholic orders against Anglican claims. Born in Lincolnshire in 1676 or 1678, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1695. He served the Fitzherbert family at Swinnerton for many years, where he is buried.

His chief opponents were the Abbe Courayer, who championed Anglican ordinations after coming to England in 1728, and Charles Dodd, who wrote with prejudice against Jesuits. Constable answered Courayer's defense of English ordinations with remarks proving their invalidity. He mocked him as a sham defender writing only for booty. He wrote on the ancient doctrine of the Eucharist and on amendments to Dodd's Church History of England, dying in 1743.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-doyle:
John Doyle was an English portrait painter and caricaturist whose signed drawings, H.B., charted the politics of his age. Born in Dublin in 1797, he studied under Gabrielli and the miniature painter Comerford. He came to London in 1821 as a portrait painter and turned to caricature in 1827. He formed his signature from his initials, the letters J and D placed one above the other.

From 1829 to 1851 he produced a famous series of drawings in brilliant style on every political movement of the day. Unlike Rowlandson and Gillray, his work is marked by reticence, courtesy, and good breeding, clever and at times stinging in epigram, though Thackeray underrated it as merely genteel. Some six hundred drawings in the British Museum form a graphic history of England's politics. Doyle kept his incognito to the last, retiring seventeen years before his death in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-machale:
John MacHale was the Irish Archbishop of Tuam whose long life spanned the hedge schools, the Famine, and the struggle for Catholic freedom. Born at Tubbernavine in County Mayo in 1791, so feeble at birth that he was baptized at home, he ran barefoot to the hedge school. He listened to saints' lives, national songs, and tales of the French Revolution from his uncle, and watched French troops march to Castlebar in 1798.

At sixteen he won a bursarship to Maynooth, where emigre French priests taught him French, Latin, Greek, Italian, German, and Hebrew, plus the English classics. After seven years he was appointed lecturer in theology in 1814 while still a subdeacon. He was ordained at twenty-four and became professor in 1820. Students esteemed him for a zeal and earnestness that marked his whole career as priest, bishop, and champion of his people until his death in 1881.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-haute:
John of Hauteville was a twelfth-century moralist and satirical poet, author of the Latin poem Archithrenius. Little is known of his life: he was probably not English-born and not a Benedictine, and he flourished about 1184. His one certain work, eight cantos named for its hero, the Prince of Lamentations, follows the hero's search for a remedy for human woes.

In a prose prologue Archithrenius deplores men's miseries and sets out for Nature. He passes through Venus's palace, the land of belly-worshippers, and Paris. There a eulogy of the city contrasts with the wretchedness of its students, valuable evidence for the early university. He climbs the mountains of Ambition and Presumption and meets the monster Cupidity and the greed of prelates. He hears Greek sages declaim against vice at Thule, and at last finds Nature, who prescribes marriage with Moderation as his cure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-joseph-v:
Karl Joseph von Hefele was Bishop of Rottenburg, born at Unterkochen in Württemberg in 1809 and dead at Rottenburg in 1893. The son of a royal furnace superintendent, he studied at Ellwangen, Ehingen, and Tübingen, and was ordained in 1833. He succeeded Möhler in Tübingen's church history chair in 1836 and held it until his election as bishop in 1869. Following Möhler, he joined historical accuracy to a firm grasp of facts and a great power of exposition.

His lectures drew hundreds of students, and later manuals by Knöpfler and Funk rested on his teaching. Besides some 150 Kirchenlexikon articles, his standard work was the seven-volume Conciliengeschichte, reaching to the fifteenth century. At the Vatican Council he stood among the bishops opposing papal infallibility, publishing his reasons in Causa Honorii Papae and voting Non placet on 13 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-rochelle:
La Rochelle is a French diocese, suffragan of Bordeaux, covering the whole department of Charente-Inferieure. The see of Maillezais moved there on 7 May 1648, and at the Concordat the old sees of Saintes and Lucon were added, though Lucon regained its own see in 1821.

St. Louis of France titles its cathedral, and St. Eutropius, Saintes's first bishop, is the diocese's chief patron, with martyrs and abbots like St. Gemme and St. Martin of Saintes also honoured. From 1534 the city was a Calvinist centre and chief Huguenot fortress, holding out against the Duke of Anjou in 1573. The great siege of 1627 to 1628 cut its people from 18,000 to 5,000 and ended Protestant political claims in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-neale:
Leonard Neale (1746-1817) was the second Archbishop of Baltimore, born near Port Tobacco, Maryland, a descendant of Maryland settler Captain James Neale. At twelve he was sent to St. Omers's Jesuit College. He then went to Bruges and Liege, where he was ordained priest. On the suppression of the Society he worked four years in England. He then asked for a mission and laboured at Demarara in British Guiana from 1779 to 1783.

Discouraged by slow progress and broken health, he sailed for America in January 1783. He joined his brethren, among them John Carroll. During Philadelphia's yellow fever epidemic of 1793 he replaced the stricken priests. He stayed six years as vicar-general to Carroll and caught the fever in 1797-98. In 1798 Carroll called him to head Georgetown College, which grew from academy to college in 1801. Consecrated coadjutor in 1800, he succeeded Carroll in 1815. He received the pallium from Pius VII the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lille:
Lille, the ancient capital of Flanders, is now the Nord department's chief town. A religious centre since the eleventh century, Lille grew in the nineteenth into a great industrial centre. Its population stood at 12,818 in 1789, 24,300 in 1821, 140,000 in 1860, and 211,000 in 1905. The legend that Lideric killed the giant Finard in the seventh century and founded the counts of Flanders dates from the thirteenth century.

Baldwin of the Iron Arm was the first Count of Flanders in the ninth century, and Lille's earlier history is wholly uncertain. The city was founded by Count Baldwin V, and in 1054 Henry III dared not besiege it.  St. Peter's was served by forty canons and had prosperous schools by 1100.  Another teacher was Gautier de Chatillon, author of the Alexandreis, a Latin epic about Alexander read instead of Virgil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-braille:
Louis Braille was the French inventor of the raised-dot writing that bears his name, born at Coupvray in 1809 and dead in 1852. Blinded at three, he entered the Paris Institution for the Blind at thirteen, shone in study and music, and stayed on as a teacher.

Before him, Hauy printed raised letters and Barbier built a sound-based dot code, but Barbier's signs missed punctuation and figures. Braille kept the dots and made them alphabetic: six-dot patterns for letters, punctuation, and even music. Set out in his 1829 manual, the system, though later revised in America and England, still grounds most blind education today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louisville:
Louisville is a Kentucky diocese covering the state west of the Kentucky River, some 22,714 square miles. First called Bardstown, it once held all Kentucky, a territory now split into over twenty-eight dioceses, five of them archdioceses.

Maryland Catholics and Irish immigrants settled Harrod's Fort from 1775, yet no priest came until Father Whelan in 1787. Badin, Nerinckx, who built ten churches and founded the Sisters of Loretto, and Trappist and Dominican pioneers followed. Later bishops, schools, and parishes fill the survey, which traces a frontier mission's growth into a settled diocese with its own colleges and convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maniple:
Maniple was an ornamental vestment worn on the left arm at Mass. It was a band-shaped vestment, just over a yard long and two to four inches wide. Silk or half-silk formed its material. Two strings, an elastic band, or a loop fastened it to the arm.

Older names such as mappula, sudarium, and mantile hint at its origin. It began at Rome, most likely as a folded cloth. In the Middle Ages it gained many symbolic readings. The Greek Rite matches it with the epigonation, a diamond-shaped vestment. A near cousin, the subcinctorium, belonged to the pope alone. Its form, material, use, name, age, manner of wearing, and symbolism are all treated in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuscripts-o:
Manuscripts of the Bible are handwritten copies of the original text or a version, whole or in part, as opposed to printed books. This vast entry works through them language by language. Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Coptic manuscripts each get detailed treatment, while other versions are set aside as less weighty.

Materials come first, with papyrus and vellum, and palimpsests whose older writing lies beneath a newer text. Hebrew manuscripts divide into pre-Massoretic and Massoretic, the latter from the tenth century onward, with some 3,400 rolls and codices counted. Greek copies split into uncials in large letters and later minuscules, with Septuagint families and New Testament witnesses by the thousand. Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Coptic sections follow the same pattern, from 8,000 Vulgate copies to Armenian manuscripts dating from A.D. 887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-marguer:
Marie-Marguerite d'Youville founded the Grey Nuns, or Sisters of Charity, born at Varennes near Montreal in 1701 and dead in 1771. She was daughter of Christophe Dufrost de Lajemmerais and Renee de Varennes, sister of La Verendrye, discoverer of the Rockies. 

She married in 1722 a husband who treated her coldly and left her widowed, indebted, with three children in 1730. She traded on a small scale to pay her debts and helped the needy from her own poverty. In 1747 the General Hospital passed to her, already begun with companions under a provisional rule. She opened it to soldiers, aged, insane, incurable, foundlings, and orphans, took on its whole debt of 49,000 livres, and earned revenue making clothes for royal stores and upper-country traders. Her institute spread across Canada, and her beatification cause opened in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-masolino-da-p:
Masolino da Panicale, son of Cristoforo Fini, was born at Panicale di Valdese near Florence in 1383 and died about 1440. In 1427 he served in Hungary under Florentine adventurer Filippo Scolari, called Pippo Spano.

Between 1428 and 1435 he painted at Castiglione d'Olona near Varese, in baptistery and collegiate church, works found forty years ago. He died four or five years later at fifty-seven, not thirty-seven as Vasari claimed. His glory lies in collaborating at the Carmine, where he painted only three compositions. They were the Temptation of Adam and Eve on an entrance pillar. In the chapel came the Preaching and Miracles of St Peter, best of all, joining the Cure of the Paralytic and Resurrection of Tabitha. Masaccio treated the same subjects with grandeur, while Masolino offered a familiar study full of springlike youth, lively beauty, and delicate architecture and landscape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miracle:
Miracle comes from the Latin miraculum, from mirari, to wonder, and in general use it denotes a marvellous thing, the sense it carried in classical Latin. In a specific sense the Latin Vulgate uses miracula for wonders of a peculiar kind. The Greek text puts them more clearly as terata, dynameis, and semeia, wonders worked by supernatural power as signs of a special mission or gift, and ascribed to God.

These terms appear habitually in the New Testament and fix the meaning of miraculum. Thus St. Peter in his first sermon speaks of Christ as approved of God by miracles, wonders, and signs. The article examines the nature of miracle and errors about it. These range from Babbage's mechanical view to Spinoza's unknown law, and cover antecedent improbability, criticism, and the place and value of miracles in the Christian view of the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monreale:
Monreale, in the province of Palermo, Sicily, sits on the slopes of Mount Caputo above the port of Palermo. It began as a pleasure resort of the Norman kings. In 1167 William II raised there the church of Santa Maria Nuova. He added a Benedictine monastery from Cava dei Tirreni, a house famed for its cloister and graceful Moorish colonnade.

The church, now the cathedral, is called the noblest in Sicily. Its bronze doors by Bonanno of Pisa date from 1186. Three naves stand on Egyptian marble columns, each capital different. Apse and walls are covered in mosaics from Old and New Testament scenes. Tombs of William I and William II stand in a side chapel. The high altar wears seventeenth-century worked silver, and an 1811 fire left the restored roof with its rafters bare.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moritz-von-ab:
Moritz von Aberle, born at Rottum near Biberach on 25 April 1819, was a Catholic theologian. He died at Tubingen on 3 November 1875. He taught at Ehingen, directed the Wilhelmstift from 1848, and held the Tubingen chair of moral theology and New Testament exegesis from 1850 until his death. He gathered many pupils in both fields but gave himself above all to Scripture.

He stressed the active part played by the human bearers of revelation, without reducing it to a merely natural process. He published his findings in the Tubingen theological quarterly from 1851 to 1872. Paul Schanz later gathered his main thoughts as an Introduction to the New Testament. His view of the Gospels and Acts as apologetic writings answering needs of apostolic times is judged unsustainable. His newspaper campaign for church liberty in Wurttemberg forced the state to settle church affairs on tolerable terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nashville:
Nashville is a diocese comprising the entire state of Tennessee. From its inland site and peculiar civil history, it gained little from immigration, so its Catholic growth came chiefly from its own internal work. No important history of the Tennessee church then existed, and the diocese long stood in an embryo state, with would-be historians lacking time and opportunity.

The Diocese of Nashville was established on 28 July 1837, separated from Bardstown, now Louisville, and its first bishop was Richard Pius Miles, consecrated at Bardstown on 16 September 1838. Before that date no authentic record shows missionary work in Tennessee beyond sporadic efforts. The earliest records are two 1799 letters in Baltimore's archives, from Father Badin to Bishop Carroll, about an offer from John Sevier, Tennessee's first governor. The entry follows the diocese's parishes, schools and growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neville:
Several English Jesuits of the penal times share the name Neville, and this entry groups them. Edmund Neville, known as Sales, was born at Hopcut, Lancashire, in 1605 and died in 1647. Saint Omer schooled him, and he joined the English College at Rome in 1621, winning notice in philosophy. He became a Jesuit in 1626, worked at Ghent, London, Oxford, and South Wales, and fell into Commonwealth hands, though he soon walked free.

His pen gave the world the Palm of Christian Fortitude, a story of the Japanese persecutions. A Life of Saint Augustine and Second Thoughts never saw print. His uncle Edmund Neville, called Elijah Nelson, born about 1563 and dead in 1648, stands as de jure seventh Earl of Northumberland. Scarisbrick kin in large numbers likewise took Neville as a Jesuit alias, Edward Scarisbrick, born 1639, among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newbattle:
Newbattle, or Neubotle, new dwelling, stands in the ancient Diocese of Saint Andrews about seven miles from Edinburgh. It was founded about 1140 as the second of six Cistercian monasteries established by Saint David, King of Scotland. It was a filiation of Melrose, itself Clairvaux's daughter, set in a beautiful valley along the South Esk, as Cistercian custom required.

Rudolph, its first abbot, kept the rule strictly and severely and threw himself into raising fitting buildings. Its cruciform church ran 240 feet long, other buildings in proportion, for the community once counted eighty monks and seventy lay brothers. The abbey soon prospered, famed for its members' regularity, several becoming well-known bishops. Scotland's kings loved it dearly, scarcely one failing to visit, always generous benefactors. Coal mines, among Scotland's first, formed a principal income.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oracle:
An oracle, in the ancient world, was a divine message given at a set place through appointed persons, and also the place itself. Babylonian baru priests, servants of Shamash and Adad, rose before dawn, bathed, anointed themselves, and donned sacred dress to receive the barutu, or oracle lore.

Hereditary office, freedom from blemish, and long initiation marked the priest, as with Aaron's sons in Israel. The entry moves from Babylon and Assyria through Egypt, Greece, and Rome to Israel's prophets, weighing true and false divination and the church's judgment on seeking the future.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-candl:
The paschal candle, a column of wax of unusual size in a great candlestick, is blessed on Holy Saturday by the deacon in white dalmatic. During the long Exultet chant he adorns it with five grains of incense and lights it from the newly blessed fire. Later, at the font blessing, he dips it three times in the water, praying that the Holy Spirit's power descend into the fountain's fullness.

From Holy Saturday to Ascension Day the candle stands in the sanctuary on the Gospel side, lit at high Mass and solemn Vespers on Sundays. It goes out after the Gospel on Ascension Day and is removed. Research points to high antiquity for the candle, and Dom Morin defended Jerome's letter to Presidius, in which the saint answers a plea to compose a paschal chant, against Duchesne's doubts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pectorale:
Pectorale, or crux pectoralis, is the cross worn by pope, cardinals, bishops, abbots, and other prelates. It hangs on the breast from a chain or silken cord, green, violet, or black by the wearer's dignity. Made of precious metal, ornamented with diamonds or pearls, it holds a saint's relics or a particle of the Holy Cross. It is worn above the alb at liturgical functions.

Before putting it on, the prelate should kiss it and say the prayer Munire me digneris. Of medieval origin, it begs God's protection and constant memory of the Lord's Passion and confessors' triumphs. The pontifical cross differs from the simple cross often allowed to cathedral chapter members. Canons so privileged wear it at choir service only, not over the alb unless specially allowed. No episcopal ornament came later than the pectoral, though breast crosses date to ancient time among bishops, priests, and laity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-photius-of-co:
Photius of Constantinople was the scholar-patriarch at the heart of the great East-West schism, born about 815. His family, kin to Patriarch Tarasius, had suffered under Iconoclast emperors, and Photius himself won praise for mastery of grammar, poetry, rhetoric, philosophy, medicine, and law. A passing monastic inclination gave way to a worldly career. When Ignatius was deposed and banished in 857, the pliant Photius was rushed through holy orders in six days to the patriarchate.

Pope Nicholas I protested, and in 867 Photius struck back, excommunicating the pope and his Latins over Saturday fasting and other Latin customs. The council of 869, recognized as the Eighth General Council, tried and confirmed his deposition, but a rival synod of 879 restored him. His Bibliotheca, notes on 280 books he had read, remains a treasure of lost antiquity. He probably died on 6 February 897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-andre-:
Pierre André Latreille was a French priest who founded modern entomology, born at Brives in 1762. Left destitute in 1778, he found benefactors in Paris, was adopted by the mineralogist Abbé Haüy, studied theology, and was ordained in 1786. Back at Brives he spent leisure on insects, returning to Paris in 1788 until the Revolution drove him out. Arrested as a priest in 1792, he faced transportation to Bordeaux.

A fellow prisoner's rare beetle, Necrobia ruficollis, brought him to the naturalist Bory de Saint-Vincent, who won his release. Arrested again as an émigré in 1797, friends saved him once more. In 1799 he took charge of entomology at Paris's Museum of Natural History, joined the Academy in 1814, and succeeded Lamarck as entomology professor in 1829. His Précis of 1795 and Genera of 1806 to 1809 ordered insects and crustaceans anew. He died at Paris in 1833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cornei:
Pierre Corneille was France's great classical dramatist, born at Rouen on 6 June 1606. Son of the king's advocate, he studied at Rouen's Jesuit college and law at Caen, joined the bar in 1624, and became advocate to the Admiralty in 1628. His first comedy, Mélite of 1629, succeeded so well that he resolved to write for the stage.

Richelieu enrolled him among the five authors in 1633, then dismissed him in 1635. Le Cid of 1636 opened a new epoch in French drama, and the Academy, at Richelieu's command, criticized it, though Paris admired it. Horace and Cinna followed in 1640, then masterpieces to 1651 including Polyeucte, Le Menteur, and Nicomède. Elected to the Academy in 1647, he later translated the Imitation of Christ and wrote declining later plays. A true Christian and churchwarden at Rouen, he showed men heroic and self-sacrificing. He died at Paris in 1684.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-ber:
Pierre de Bérulle was a French cardinal and founder of the French Oratory, born at Cérilly in Champagne on 4 February 1575. From a family of magistrates, he gave himself even before ordination to converting Protestants. As priest and chaplain to Henry IV, he laboured with Cardinal du Perron and St. Francis de Sales for the Huguenots' conversion.

With Madame Acarie he brought Teresa's reformed Carmelites into France, and in 1611 he founded the French Congregation of the Oratory on St. Philip Neri's Roman model. From it sprang France's seventeenth-century clergy reform; the Jesuit Coton called it necessary to the Church. He also arranged Charles I's marriage to Henrietta of France, and Urban VIII made him cardinal in 1627. His Discours on Jesus' state and grandeurs of 1623 and Vie de Jésus of 1629 aim to make Christ better known and loved. He died in October 1629.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-bra:
Pierre de Bourdeille, seigneur de Brantôme, was a famous French memoir writer, born in Périgord in 1539 or a little later. Son of a nobleman, raised at the Queen of Navarre's court, he studied at Paris and Poitiers and returned to court by 1556. In 1557 he received the Abbey of Brantôme, whose name he took. Seven peacetime journeys abroad took him to Italy, Scotland, England, Spain, Portugal, Malta, La Goulette, and Greece.

He sailed with Mary Stuart to Scotland, fought in the civil war of 1562, and haunted Catherine de' Medici's court, whose flying squadron of ladies he called paradise on earth. His Mémoires, first printed imperfectly in 1655, preserve details of Renaissance court life and portraits of Marguerite of Navarre and Mary Stuart. An uneven, uncritical witness who admired bravery above morality, he fathered the scandal chroniclers Tallemant and Bussy-Rabutin. He died on 15 July 1614.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-le-moy:
Pierre Le Moyne, Sieur d'Iberville, was a Canadian-born French sailor and soldier who founded the colony of Louisiana. He was born at Ville-Marie, Montreal, in 1661, the third son of Charles Le Moyne. He went to sea young and fought the English in Hudson Bay. In 1697 he won a famous single-ship fight against three English vessels.

Chosen by the French minister of marine to find the mouth of the Mississippi, he sailed from Brest in 1698. He reached the Gulf Coast early in 1699. With his brother Bienville he located the river's mouth on 2 March of that year. The entry traces his Hudson Bay campaigns, his Gulf exploration, and the beginnings of Louisiana before his death at Havana in 1706.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-nicole:
Pierre Nicole was a French theologian and writer linked to Port-Royal, the centre of the Jansenist movement. Jansenism was a strict school of Catholic thought on grace. Nicole was born at Chartres in 1625, studied at Paris, and taught in the Port-Royal schools. He became the close ally of Antoine Arnauld.

He translated Pascal's Provincial Letters into Latin under a pen name. He defended Jansenist positions in print and produced some eighty-eight works in all. With Pascal he helped shape clear French prose. Refused ordination beyond the tonsure and exiled from Paris for a letter to the pope, he was later allowed to return and died in 1695.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-della-:
Pietro della Valle, Italian traveller in the Orient, was born at Rome on 2 April 1586 and died there on 21 April 1652. Of noble family and excellent education, he was as a young man a poet, orator, soldier in papal service, and member of the Roman Academy of the Umoristi. In 1611 he campaigned against the Barbary States. An unfortunate love affair led to a pilgrimage lasting eleven years.

Starting from Venice on 8 June 1614, he spent a year at Constantinople learning Turkish and Arabic. He went on to Alexandria, Cairo, Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo, and Baghdad, where he married the Syrian Christian Maani. He explored Persia, was received by Shah Abbas the Great, and spent two years in India before returning to Rome on 28 March 1626. His Viaggi, in fifty-four familiar letters, appeared at Rome in 1650 to 1653.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pius-zingerle:
Pius Zingerle was a Tyrolese Benedictine Orientalist, a scholar of Eastern languages, famed for bringing Saint Ephraem's Syriac writings into German. He was born at Meran in 1801 and joined the Benedictines at Marienberg in 1820. He was ordained in 1824 and taught for years at the Meran gymnasium, becoming its director in 1852.

Called to Rome in 1862 by Pius IX, he taught Oriental languages at the Sapienza and advised the Propaganda on Eastern affairs. He also worked in the Vatican Library, but the climate drove him back to Marienberg in 1865. There he continued his translations of Ephraem, his Syriac reader and dictionary, and studies of Syriac verse until his death in 1881.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-placide-louis:
Placide-Louis Chapelle was a French-born archbishop of New Orleans who served as the pope's diplomat in Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines. He was born at Ruynes in 1842 and studied at Mende, Enghien, and Saint Mary's Seminary in Baltimore. He was ordained in 1865 and rose through parishes in Maryland and Washington to become bishop of Santa Fe in 1894.

Transferred to New Orleans in 1897, he was sent as apostolic delegate, the pope's envoy, to Cuba and Puerto Rico in 1898 and to the Philippines in 1899. In Paris he secured a treaty clause protecting church property under the new American rule. In Manila he freed priests held by Aguinaldo's forces and helped pacify the islands before returning to Louisiana, where he died in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plants-in-the:
Plants in the Bible surveys the flora of the Holy Land, a country Moses praised as a land of wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, and olives. The entry shows how, within less than two hundred miles, altitude falls from Lebanon's ten-thousand-foot peaks to the Dead Sea shore, more than a thousand feet below the Mediterranean. That range lets Alpine, Mediterranean, steppe, and subtropical plants grow side by side.

More than three thousand species are known in Palestine, yet today's land gives only a faint picture of biblical times. Then cedar forests crowned Lebanon, pine woods covered Hermon and Gilead, oak forests marked Bashan, and palm groves enriched the Jordan Valley. Soil, climate, and the ruin of ancient woodlands all shape the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontificale:
The Pontificale is the liturgical book holding the rites for episcopal functions, such as confirmation and Holy Orders, apart from Mass and the Divine Office. It is, in effect, a bishop's ritual, gathering formularies and rubrics that once lived in old sacramentaries and Roman ordines into one volume for the officiating bishop's convenience.

Earlier collections bore names such as Liber Sacramentorum, Liber Officialis, and Benedictional. The most ancient and important for study is the Pontifical of Egbert, Archbishop of York from 732 to 736. The first printed edition appeared in 1485 under Innocent VIII. Clement VIII made a corrected official edition obligatory in 1596. Urban VIII, Benedict XIV, and Leo XIII revised it further, Leo's typical edition coming in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precious-ston:
Precious stones are stones prized for colour, sheen, or rarity, held in high esteem in all ages, above all in the East. Scripture shows Orientals of old decking rings, bracelets, and necklaces with them, and setting kings' crowns and robes with them. Solomon even sent a fleet that came back from Ophir laden with precious stones.

The Bible's stones matter most in three places: the high priest's breastplate, the King of Tyre's treasure, and the New Jerusalem's foundations. The breastplate held twelve stones, with two more on the shoulder ornaments, and Jews seem to have seen them as tribal marks. The entry then weighs stone by stone, as with the chrysolite. The Hebrew word gives no hint of its kind. But the Septuagint renders it chrysolithos, the Vulgate follows, and Aquila, Josephus, and Epiphanius agree, so the old chrysolite, our topaz, is safely meant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefecture-ap:
The Prefecture Apostolic of the Delta of the Nile lies in north Egypt and covers four of the six provinces of Lower Egypt: Gharbieh, Charkieb, Menufieh, and Kalyiubieh. Ere the prefecture rose, the four provinces held 1,000 Catholics of varied rites. Propaganda raised the prefecture on 17 March 1887. In 1888 Augustin Duret of the Lyons Society for African Missions was named first prefect apostolic, and the prefecture was given to that society.

At first it held but two mission posts, at Tantah and Zagazig. A post rose at Zifteh in 1887 and one at Mahalla-el-Kebir in 1891. As Cairo spilled north past its old bounds, crowded quarters grew inside the prefecture. For resident Catholics a Latin parish rose in Choubra in 1894, and one at Zeïtoun in 1896. The 1897 census gave the four provinces 3,282,457 folk, with 73,365 schismatics of varied rites, 3,091 Catholics of varied rites, and 241 Protestants.

Welle prefecture lies in the far north of the Belgian Congo. On 12 May 1898 Propaganda cut it from the Congo Free State's Vicariate Apostolic and gave it to the Premonstratensian Canons Regular of Tongerloo, Belgium. Its bounds ran north to the Vicariate of Central Africa or Sudan, and east to Northern Nyanza. West ran a line from the Uelle-Ubanghi junction to the Itimbri-Congo meeting. South ran the watershed of the Itimbri's south tributaries to 30° east longitude.

Its folk number 1,500,000, mostly fetishists, with 922 Catholics and 1,951 catechumens. The staff counts 11 priests, 9 lay brothers, 65 catechists, and 8 nuns in 2 houses of Berlaer's Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Mary. Three chief stations, Imbembo, Amadi, and Gambari, head 41 lesser posts. Three schools hold 445 pupils, a catechist school at Imbembo holds 100, two orphanages hold 380 orphans, and 15 workshops hold 109 pupils. The first and present prefect apostolic is Leo Derikx.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ranulf-de-gla:
Ranulf de Glanville, Chief Justiciar of England, was born at Stratford in Suffolk, though the year is unknown, and died before Acre in Palestine in 1190. This encyclopedia entry traces a baronial house named from Glanville in Normandy, holding land in Norfolk and Suffolk. Ranulf was a younger son of William de Glanville, but on an elder brother's death he inherited the family estates and honours.

Before and after reaching the judicial bench, he served as sheriff of various counties. He held Yorkshire from 1163 until Henry the Second's death, save a short break, and took Lancashire in 1173. That year saw the rebellion of Henry's sons, backed by William the Lion of Scotland and the French king. The legal treatise bearing Glanville's name was more likely written by his nephew and secretary, Hubert Walter, the entry notes. Ranulf founded Butley Abbey in 1171, Leiston Abbey in 1183, and a leper hospital at Somerton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rationale:
The rationale is an episcopal humeral, a shoulder vestment matching the pallium and worn over the chasuble. This encyclopedia entry notes that only the Bishops of Eichstätt, Paderborn, Toul and Cracow use it. As worn at Eichstätt, Paderborn and Toul, it takes the form of a humeral collar, ornamented with appendages. The Cracow form uses two bands crossing the shoulder, joined at breast and back, looking like a disc joined by medallions.

In the Middle Ages many German bishops used the rationale, from Würzburg, Ratisbon and Naumburg to Halberstadt, Minden, Speier, Metz, Augsburg, Prague and Olmutz. Liège and Toul, whose dioceses then belonged to the German Empire, used it too. No full account of the vestment survives from the early centuries. It grew out of tenth-century episcopal splendour, named for the breast ornament worn by the Jewish high priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reginald-card:
Reginald Pole, cardinal and kinsman of Henry the Eighth, was born at Stourton Castle in Staffordshire in March 1500 and died at Lambeth Palace on 17 November 1558. Third son of Sir Richard Pole and Margaret, daughter of George, Duke of Clarence, he stood close to the throne from boyhood. Henry favoured him and made his widowed mother Countess of Salisbury in 1513, then governess to Princess Mary in 1516. The boy learned for five years at the Charterhouse at Sheen, then went to Oxford at twelve or thirteen.

Later favour turned to danger. A mission to Francis the First failed, both French and Spaniards rebuffed him, and he took refuge with the Cardinal Bishop of Liège. Recalled to Rome, he attended the 1538 meeting of Charles the Fifth and Francis at Nice. Meanwhile his brothers were arrested in England, and hired killers threatened his life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-:
La Louvesc in France, beside the tomb of Saint John Francis Regis, saw the Society of Our Lady of the Cenacle founded in 1826. Its founders were Jean-Pierre-Etienne Terme, a Diocese of Viviers missionary priest of great zeal, and Marie-Victoire-Therese Couderc, a woman of twenty mature in courage, energy, and faith. They hoped to draw pilgrims to the tomb and lead them to recollect themselves in solitude, prayer, and meditation.

They opened houses where women could follow the exercises of a retreat, the first at La Louvesc. Terme died in 1834, leaving his religious family in Jesuit hands. Episcopal encouragement and Pope Gregory the Sixteenth favoured the work. Retreats, associations, and every office of spiritual charity extending God's kingdom in souls belong to its work. All is done in the spirit of the Cenacle, for love of Christ and the Blessed Virgin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-robert-c:
René-Robert-Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, explorer, was born at Rouen in 1643 and died in Texas in 1687. As a youth he showed unusual precocity in mathematics and a love of natural science, with a somewhat puritanical outlook. He may have been schooled for the Society of Jesus. He joined some religious order afterwards, since that fact cost him his estates, but he abandoned a church career for Canada.

A grant of land at La Chine on the Saint Lawrence from the Sulpicians, lords of Montreal, brought him to Canada as adventurer and trader in 1666. An elder brother in the order there may have helped. For three years he lived on his estate, mastering Indian dialects and pondering a southwest passage. His plans outran his generation, yet France followed his projected lines through the eighteenth century until the English overthrew her in the French and Indian Wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-doyle:
Richard Doyle, an English artist and caricaturist of the Victorian age, drew with a light, playful hand from childhood. Born in London in 1824, the son of the artist John Doyle, he filled a teenage journal with small pen-and-ink sketches now kept in the British Museum. Joining Punch in 1843, he drew cartoons for the magazine and designed its famous cover, which stayed in use for decades afterward.

Faith ended his Punch career in 1850, when he left over the paper's attacks on Catholic claims. He then turned to book illustration and watercolour painting, supplying pictures for works such as The Newcomes and The King of the Golden River. His drawings, praised for grace, humour, and gentle fancy rather than biting force, also appear in the Fitzwilliam Museum at Cambridge. Readers who enjoy Victorian illustration will find here a compact life of a gifted draughtsman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-rolle:
Richard Rolle of Hampole was a fourteenth-century hermit whose writings on the spiritual life were read across England for two hundred years. Born at Thornton in Yorkshire about 1300, he was sent to Oxford at the expense of a Durham archdeacon. At nineteen he left the university, refusing to join any order, and set out to live as a hermit. A former fellow student, John de Dalton, gave him a cell and support.

At Dalton he described his growth in prayer through three stages, which he named heat, song, and sweetness. He later wandered, visited the anchoress Margaret Kyrkby, and finally settled at Hampole near a Cistercian nunnery. After his death his tomb drew pilgrims seeking miracles, and a canonization cause was prepared but never pursued. The Lollards tampered with his texts, adding passages to suit their views, so the Hampole nuns guarded genuine copies of his works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-ciboul:
Robert Ciboule was a French theologian and moralist who served church and crown in the fifteenth century. Born in the department of Eure near the close of the fourteenth century, he became chancellor of Notre-Dame in Paris. He later served as dean of Evreux and chamberlain to Pope Nicholas V. He died in 1458.

In 1437 Charles VII consulted him, with other theologians, on the rehabilitation of Joan of Arc, and his judgment was favourable. The king then dispatched him to the Council of Basle, naming him ambassador to Pope Eugene IV at Florence in 1439. He wrote many devotional works, all left in manuscript. His Sainte meditation de l'homme sur soi-meme was printed at Paris in 1510 and reprinted several times. Several sermons survive in the National Library of France, and his opinion on Joan appears in the published rehabilitation proceedings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rococo-style:
Rococo is a style of decoration that flourished in France during the regency after Louis XIV's death, roughly 1715 to 1750. Its name came in the nineteenth century from French emigres. They used it whimsically for the old shellwork manner, style rocaille, then seen as old Frankish against simpler styles that followed. It might be called the climax or degeneration of the Baroque, joined to French grace, turning grotesques into curves, lines, and bands under Jean Berain.

It touched building less than decoration, dissolving interior forms such as pilasters and architraves in free ornament, and shaping space, facades, portals, doors, and windows. Germany took it up with still more arbitrary fancy until 1770 or later, while England gave it no welcome. To a taste grown weary of heavy Baroque, the small and light pleased most. Walls, ceilings, furniture, metal, and porcelain joined in one ensemble, with shell curves and hidden construction under stucco.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-sebasti:
Roman Sebastian Zangerle was Prince-Bishop of Seekau in Styria. Born near Ulm in 1771, he studied humanities with the Benedictines at Wiblingen, entered the novitiate in 1788, took vows in 1792, and was ordained priest in 1793. From 1794 he studied Oriental languages at Zwiefalten, then taught Scripture at Wiblingen, Mehrerau, Salzburg, Cracow, Prague, and Vienna in turn.

In 1824, fifteen years after his monastery was suppressed, he took dispensation from his vows to accept a canonry at Vienna. That April he became Prince-Bishop of Seekau and administrator of Leoben. The two dioceses, with 800,000 people, had lacked a bishop for twelve years. Despite official opposition he renewed both dioceses, reformed monasteries, and brought in Redemptorists, Jesuits, Carmelites, and Vincentian Sisters. He founded School Sisters in 1843 and built a boys' seminary at Leoben.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sale:
Sale, a diocese in Victoria, Australia, covers the whole of Gippsland, a region first crossed in 1840 by the Polish scientist Count Strzelecki with the young Irishman James Riley. They found a fertile land of forests, ranges, and swift rivers, long dismissed as trackless waste yet now called the Garden of Australia. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tells how a wild corner became a settled see.

Colonisation came slowly, since settlers feared the native inhabitants and battled dense bush and rough country, but Gippsland grew rich in pasture, timber, and minerals still only partly worked. The town of Sale became the seat of a bishopric erected in 1887 at the request of a plenary synod, with James Francis Corbett of Limerick as first bishop. The entry gives tourists and historians alike a portrait of a young Australian church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scruple:
Scruple, Latin scrupulus, a small sharp stone, means in a transferred sense an uneasiness of mind: an unfounded fear that something is a sin when in fact it is not. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia treats it less as a single act than as a habitual state, the scrupulous conscience known to directors of souls.

Alphonsus describes it as a state where trifling reasons, without solid ground, often make a person fear sin where none lies. The anxiety may concern what is to be done now or what has already been done. Some suppose scrupulosity itself a spiritual benefit, but the entry calls that a great error. God's providence can draw good from it as from other evils, yet apart from that it is a bad habit harming body and soul, sometimes grievously, when clung to with obstinacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seattle:
Seattle, a diocese covering the whole state of Washington across 66,680 square miles with over a million people, began on 24 July 1846 as the see of Walla Walla under Pius IX. On 31 May 1850 its name changed to Nesqually, with Vancouver, Washington, as cathedral city, and in September 1907 it became Seattle, with cathedral and bishop's house on Puget Sound. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a frontier church.

A century earlier Washington formed part of the Oregon Country, a rugged wilderness described by the Jesuit De Smet in his Oregon mission accounts. Catholic faith reached Washington and Oregon remarkably, not chiefly through religious orders, but through lay settlers and secular priests. The entry follows missions, parishes, and bishops as a wilderness territory became a settled diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-ral:
Sebastian Rale, also spelled Rasle, missionary and martyr, was born at Pontarlier in the Besançon diocese on 20 January 1654. He was shot by an English force attacking Norridgewock mission in Maine on 23 August 1724. He entered the Jesuit novitiate at Dole in 1675, studied at Carpentras, taught at Nîmes, finished theology at Lyons in 1688, and volunteered for America. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a priest caught between empires.

Sailing in 1689 with Frontenac's party from La Rochelle, he first worked at an Abenaki village near Quebec. Recalled to Quebec in 1691, he spent two years among the Illinois, then reached the Kennebec Abenaki mission in 1694. New England colonists suspected and hated a Frenchman among Indians mostly hostile to England, blaming him for frontier outrages during his long stay. The entry weighs that charge against his missionary record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-second-counci:
The Second Council of Constantinople, the Fifth General Council, met from 5 May to 2 June 553. Emperor Justinian called it, and mostly Eastern bishops attended, with only six Western, African, bishops present. Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, presided. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia presents the council as the last act of a long, violent quarrel.

The quarrel began with Justinian's edict of 543 against Origenism. The emperor believed Nestorianism still drew strength from Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Ibas of Edessa, and from the esteem in which the first two were still held. From January 547 Pope Vigilius was forcibly kept in the capital, having first refused to join condemnation of the Three Chapters. The entry gives the brief account, pointing readers to Vigilius and Three Chapters for the fuller story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seigneur-and-:
Jacques-René de Brisay, Seigneur and Marquis de Denonville, governed New France from 1685 after a career as a colonel of dragoons in France. He had married Catherine Courtin in 1668. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him from La Rochelle to Quebec, where he arrived with his wife and two young daughters on 1 August. He was charged with winning over the native peoples, keeping the peace, and waging war on the Seneca branch of the Iroquois.

Short of troops, Denonville begged France for help. Thomas Dongan, governor of New York, stirred the Iroquois against him. The entry covers the winter of preparation and the arrival of 800 recruits in spring 1687. It follows the campaign that followed, then his recall to France. There the king showed fresh trust by making him assistant tutor to the royal children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seville:
The archdiocese of Seville in Spain, bounded by Badajoz, Cordova, Malaga, Cadiz, and Portugal, is covered here in history, bishops, and buildings. Its city holds some 144,000 people, and its suffragans include Badajoz, Cadiz, the Canaries, Cordova, and Tenerife. In Roman times Seville was capital of Baetica, and the diocese claims roots in apostolic times. Sabinus was bishop by 303, when Saints Justa and Rufina were martyred for refusing to adore the idol Salambo.

Much of the entry walks the great cathedral, rebuilt from 1403 to 1506 on a scale the chapter hoped posterity would call madness. Only the Giralda tower and the Court of Oranges survived from the mosque. Inside stand the vast high-altar reredos, the choir stalls of 1475, and the royal chapel tombs of Saint Ferdinand and Alfonso the Wise. The Alcázar, best preserved of Muslim buildings in Spain, gets a full tour as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
The Sisters of the Temple, fully the Sisters of the Finding of Jesus in the Temple, are a pre-Reformation foundation. A London dean whose name is lost founded them for education at the time of the Crusades. They spread widely in England over following centuries, but the Reformation drove them into exile.

In 1860 Cardinal Wiseman, with generous help from Abbé Roullin, re-established them in the Archdiocese of Westminster, from which they moved to Clifton. Only after a house opened at Vernon, Normandy, did they flourish again, opening six houses in France and Belgium and numbering 170 sisters. They keep a home for invalid priests at Clifton, and their chief work now is nursing among all classes. Their blue habit earns them the name Blue Nuns in England and France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cyril-of-c:
Carmelite history gives Cyril of Constantinople only a thin outline, and this encyclopedia entry explains why his later fame outgrew the facts. He served as prior on Mount Carmel for three years and headed the Carmelites until his death around 1235, with a reputation as a prophet. The entry comes from the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913, which treats him as a saint and doctor of the Church.

Much of the piece sorts out writings wrongly tied to his name. An obscure oracle was said to have reached him from an angel during Mass. It was first noted near 1295 and later read as a comment on the Western Schism. A work on his order came from another hand. He had also been folded into Cyril of Jerusalem and Cyril of Alexandria. His doctor's title was defended by crediting him with a lost treatise on the Holy Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ignatius-o:
Ignatius of Constantinople, patriarch from 847, was made a eunuch to bar him from a throne, then made patriarch anyway. Born about 799 to Emperor Michael I and Procopia, he was first named Nicetas. At fourteen his name changed to Ignatius, when Leo the Armenian deposed his father, castrated him, and shut him in a monastery. There he embraced religious life freely and in time became abbot. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 23 October 877.

Ordained by Basil of Paros, he succeeded to the patriarchate in 847 with Empress Theodora's goodwill, after Methodius's death. Michael III, a youthful profligate, found a companion in his uncle Bardas, who urged the emperor to force Theodora into a convent for undivided power. Ignatius was asked to help that scheme, and his refusal set patriarch against emperor. The entry opens on a eunuch abbot holding the line against a court plot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isidore-of:
Isidore of Seville, archbishop and scholar, mastered three languages in Spain's first cathedral school. Born at Cartagena about 560, he was son of Severianus and Theodora. He followed his elder brother Leander in Seville's metropolitan see. His younger brother Fulgentius held Astigi, and his sister Florentina ruled, so the entry says, forty convents and a thousand religious. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death to 4 April 636.

In Seville's cathedral school, the first of its kind in Spain, Leander's learned circle taught trivium and quadrivium. Isidore mastered Latin, Greek, and Hebrew with remarkable speed. Whether he ever took monastic vows remains open, though he esteemed monks highly and became their protector on elevation. In 619 he pronounced anathema on any cleric who should break faith with his charge. The entry opens on a scholar bishop at Visigothic Spain's centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-bapti:
John Baptist de la Salle, founder of the Christian Brothers, is called father of modern pedagogy. Born at Reims on 30 April 1651, he was eldest child of Louis de la Salle and Nicolle de Moet de Brouillet. He studied at the College des Bons Enfants and took a Master of Arts on 10 July 1669. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Saint-Yon, Rouen, to Good Friday, 7 April 1719.

His family traced itself to Johan Salla, ninth-century commander under Alfonso the Chaste, settling in Champagne about 1350. De la Salle opened free elementary schools at Reims, letting Adrien Nyel share the honours while he laboured for real progress. Daily he visited teachers, urging practical methods for definite results. When teachers faltered, he drew them into community, and from that community grew the Institute of the Brothers of the Christian Schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lawrence-o:
Lawrence O'Toole, archbishop of Dublin's predecessor as Glendalough's abbot, rose from child hostage to canonized confessor. Born about 1128 in present County Kildare to the chief of Hy Murray and a mother of Clan O'Byrne, he was taken at ten as hostage by Dermot McMurrogh, king of Leinster. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Eu in Normandy to 14 November 1180.

In 1140 the boy entered Glendalough's monastic school, studying thirteen years in that valley sanctuary, conspicuous for piety and learning. On Abbot Dunlaing's death early in 1154, the community unanimously called him to preside over St. Kevin's abbey. Dermot, who married Lawrence's sister Mor, was painted darkly by native annalists, yet befriended the Church richly, founding a Dublin nunnery in 1151 and a Cistercian abbey besides. Honorius III canonized Lawrence in 1225.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-leander-of:
Leander of Seville, bishop from 579 to 600, built a school that became orthodoxy's centre in Visigothic Spain. Born at Carthage about 534 to a Roman family, he was son of Severian. Isidore calls Severian simply a citizen, though some claim he was Carthage's duke or governor. The family emigrated to Seville about 554. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Seville to 13 March 600 or 601.

Severian's children show distinguished rearing: Leander and Isidore both became Seville's bishops, Fulgentius held Carthagena, and Florentina, a nun, directed forty convents and a thousand nuns. Wrongly, some made another daughter, Theodosia, wife of King Leovigild. Leander first became a Benedictine monk, then bishop, founding a celebrated school. He helped Princess Ingunthis convert her husband's house, a work the entry follows into Spain's Catholic turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maximus-of:
Maximus the Confessor, born at Constantinople about 580, stands among the chief doctors of the Incarnation and of ascetic mysticism. First secretary to the emperor Heraclius, he left court life for a monastery at Chrysopolis, became its abbot, and later joined Sophronius of Jerusalem in Africa. There he entered the storm over Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had only one will.

His letters and disputations pressed the orthodox claim that Christ, one person in two natures, must have two natural operations and two wills. Exiled and mutilated for his stand, he died on 13 August 662. The entry follows his career, his defence of Rome's primacy, and his vast writings on prayer, the liturgy, and the spiritual life, which shaped Eastern theology for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paul-the-s:
Paul the Simple, a guileless Egyptian farmer, won a place among the desert fathers through sheer obedience. Palladius heard his story from men who had known Anthony. Discovering his wife's infidelity one day, the sixty-year-old husbandman set off to become a monk and knocked at Anthony's cell.

Anthony turned him away as too old for the solitary life, but Paul waited outside four days until fear for his life opened the door. Set to weave palm rope, undo it, and weave it again, he obeyed without complaint. He ate only when Anthony ate, prayed long graces, and learned the monastic rule by doing. The entry preserves a charming tale of persistence from the desert fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-philip-the:
Philip the Apostle, a native of Bethsaida like Peter and Andrew, was called by Jesus with the words Follow me. He stood among those around the Baptist when John pointed out Jesus as the Lamb of God, and soon after his call he brought Nathanael as a new disciple. His name stands fifth in the three apostolic lists of the Twelve.

John's Gospel gives him three scenes. He questions the cost of bread before the feeding of the multitude. He reports that Greeks in Jerusalem wish to see Jesus. At the Last Supper he pleads, Show us the Father. Later ecclesiastical traditions send him preaching in Phrygia and dying at Hierapolis. The entry separates Gospel fact from legend for a quiet apostle often overshadowed by his namesake the deacon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-simon-the-:
Simon the Apostle, called the Cananaean and the Zealot, remains one of the least known of the Twelve. His name appears in every Gospel and Acts list of apostles. To distinguish him from Peter he bears surnames meaning the Zealous, a translation of the Hebrew qana, marking zeal for the Jewish law before his call.

The name does not mean he belonged to the Zealot party, the entry stresses. Jerome wrongly took Cana for his birthplace, while Greeks, Copts, and Ethiopians identify him with Nathanael of Cana. Where he preached is uncertain, with claims ranging from the Black Sea and Egypt to Britain. Abyssinians tell that he was crucified as bishop of Jerusalem after preaching in Samaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-the:
Thomas the Apostle, called Didymus the twin, emerges most clearly in John's Gospel, despite a thin record elsewhere. His name stands in all Synoptic lists, but John gives him a distinctive part. When Jesus set out for Judea to visit Lazarus, Thomas urged his fellow disciples: Let us also go, that we may die with him.

At the Last Supper discourse he objected: Lord, we know not whither thou goest, and how can we know the way? Above all he is remembered for incredulity at the Resurrection, demanding to see and touch the wounds, then confessing, My Lord and my God, eight days later. Later traditions send him to India, where Christians still claim his name. The entry weighs Gospel portrait against legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stole:
The stole is a long narrow strip of cloth, worn as the badge of holy orders. This entry describes its form, use, and history in full. Usually silk and about eighty inches long, it bears a small cross at each end and in the middle, where the priest kisses it before vesting.

Deacons wear it like a sash from the left shoulder. Priests let it fall from the neck across the breast. Bishops wear it uncrossed, because of the pectoral cross. Ordination rites place it on the new deacon and priest with spoken formulas. Later sections trace its shape through the centuries, its colours for feasts and fasts, and the rules for blessing it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tabernacle:
Tabernacle, from Latin tabernaculum, tent, usually means the movable tent sanctuary of the Hebrews before Solomon's Temple. This entry gathers the Hebrew names for it. They run from ohel, tent, and ohel mo'ed, tent of meeting, to mishkan, dwelling, beth Yahweh, house of Yahweh, and hekal, temple. Each name tells us something about the building while raising problems for commentators.

Exodus places an ark tent outside the camp, guarded by Joshua, where Yahweh met Moses.
